review_text: The final is cumulative but only has multiple choice, fill-in-the-blank, and short answer questions. Frauwirth is a really nice guy, but his lectures are extremely monotone, and if you get the 2pm lecture right after lunch you’ll fight to keep your eyes open. He does Tophat questions for attendance purposes in lecture. He grades pretty uniquely that he has a set denominator in which he divides your total score by in order to obtain your final grade. This essentially means that if you do all the tophat questions, all of the quizzes, and any other extra credit activities, you get like 15 or 20 points of raw extra credit cushion points, so your ELMS score is usually lower than your actual grade. For exams, try to find someone who’s taken the class before. That will save you. We ended up running very late behind schedule in our classes, and we didn’t get to the last 8 lecture slideshows. I think part of this is because he spends the first 10 minutes of every 50-minute lecture reiterating the same points he talked about all semester (emails for missed Tophat questions, talking about the fact that he doesn’t round up, etc). The majority of the questions on the final exam were from the most recent unit. I honestly don’t know how you’d study for it except know every detail about the things presented from the 3rd exam to the final, and remember your basics of the other 3 units (like which type of mRNA does what, Km/Vmax, principles of regulation, etc). He loves to ask really detailed questions, unfortunately, but the lab grade cushions your exam scores. I heard they are separating the lecture from the lab next semester, so I’m sure he’s gonna have to curve the class after that change takes effect. Really nice guy, but quite monotone. Very accommodating though. I ended with an A.

I have very mixed feelings about this class because the content is really interesting, but the way these upper-level neuro classes are taught is honestly brutal. The worksheets feel kind of pointless and they are never really in sync with what we are learning in class, so you end up needing to know extra information for the tests, since of course all of that is fair game. The slides she gives out only scratch the surface of the material, and you really have to write down everything she explains in class if you want to do well. She does reuse old quiz questions from the ELMS weekly quizzes on the exams, so definitely review those and the worksheets really well before each test. The exams themselves are insanely hard. You need to know every tiny detail AND the big picture, and then apply it. The multiple choice questions are super tricky and sometimes ask about small things that were said once in class. I am a straight-A student and I still struggled in this class because the tests are just that annoying and difficult. If you are not a neuro major, I would not recommend taking this class. If you are a neuro major and you have to take it, make sure you truly understand what is going on for every single slide and concept. The TAs are not very helpful, so your best resources are the textbook and the professor himself. Overall, the class is really hard because of the exams, but the professor is a nice, normal guy who genuinely wants people to do well.

The content and the exams can seem a bit intimidating in BSCI410 at first, but Dr. Wu is extremely kind and provides a lot of opportunities to do well (from dropping an exam to providing extra credit opportunities) The exams are open note but that doesn't mean they are easy, so I recommend not solely relying on your notes!

he's a really nice person and does really want to help, but genuinely is a very physics based teacher, and will teach as so. it makes it super difficult to learn chemistry, as it seems he wants you to know chem on a deeper level than you're capable of learning in the period of time you have for class. this class legit made me realize that i didnt want to be a chem major and i changed majors mid year. if you spend all your time studying and legit dedicate yourself all week to this class you'd do fine, but other teachers for 131 were definitely better.

If you're considering taking this class, it's probably because its a required class for your major in which case you'll be stuck taking it in either case. So, I'm not going to tell you whether or not to take this class, I'm just gonna tell you what to expect. This lab definetely isn't easy, but it also isn't the hardest class. There are tons of office hours to choose from, so find a good TA to ask questions to and you'll be fine. Your experience in lab def depends on your TA (shoutout to Ireen--she's the best!), but again if you dont understand something in lab just ask your friends or go to office hours. You are going to have to take prelab quizes which are honestly pretty hard (her panopto videos can be helpful for these, but they can be long and hard to understand) as well as post lab quizes which I found less hard (but it is true that you take them three weeks after the lab). The post labs can at times take a really long time, but usually aren't too difficult. There are a few oppurtunities for extra credit, and our year she dropped the lowest quiz grade and lowest lab grade. Moral of the story is it's going to be a challenge but you've got this!

Honestly he was a pretty bad lecturer (mumbled a lot and went very quickly) but all slides are posted to Canvas and follows the textbook (which is extremely helpful in my opinion if you choose to use it, it's filled with videos and examples scattered throughout). As far as exams go, he posts one or two practice midterms/finals before-hand for each one that's is essentially the same as the real exam (slightly different). But as long as you prepare using these practice exams and fully understand those concepts, there is no reason you shouldn't do just fine in this class.

never saw her because it was a TA led lab. but the TA was really helpful and knowledgeable for lab reports. Lab reports took a while which were annoying. The TA Mya let us out early almost every time. We started the lab fast and she gave really good directions and therefore most of the time finished an hour or so early which was really nice.

Dr. H is an amazing professor! She’s so organized, approachable, and willing to help. Her lecture guides are so helpful; I’d upload them to my iPad and follow along during lecture so I wouldn’t have to worry about writing everything down. She also recorded lectures this semester, which was super helpful because I would re-watch every lecture and wouldn’t stress if I missed something important she said during the actual lecture. She also posts practice problem sets that she makes, along with answer keys and video explanations of certain problems. I don’t think I would have done so well without these! She is also so friendly during office hours; even after I asked the same question multiple times, she’d explain the answer to me in different ways until I understood. Definitely take advantage of her office hours and do the practice problems because this is a very hard course. I studied for hours daily and still had a lot of questions, but Dr. H was so supportive and acknowledged my hard work! You can tell that she really cares about her students because she tells us that! Her exams were difficult but fair for the most part. The only complaint I have is that she did not post her old exams, but given the rigor of her practice problem sets, I’m not sure how much more mock exams would have even helped. I’d take more courses with her if I could!
I have never hated a lab more; half the time things didn't work. But she curved my 80 to an A-
Nice professor but I wish he has homework or worksheets for completion to give a better buffer for exams.

Hirschauer's lab is night and day from orgo 1 lab in the best way possible. Her lab is so organized. The weekly emails were very clear in what exactly you needed to do to prepare for the week's experiment. I loved the variety in having LCTAs and post-lab questions. LCTAs mostly felt fair (put units in every step of calculations!) The PLQs always felt fair and relevant also. Her canvas classroom is well-structured and has a lot of supplementary material to help explain lab procedures as well. Watch the videos, they are *so* helpful. She even came into the lab once or twice and gave people some advice and checked up on us. The experiments themselves are kind of rough, but as long as you can explain a low yield or weird melting point, it's totally okay. You will likely be in lab nearly the entire time on most days though. The lab manual isn't completely updated to the current curriculum, but all the changes are on canvas and explained clearly (along with the reasoning). The best part about having Dr. Hirschauer is her open door policy. Even if it's not formal office hours, if her door is open, you can always ask for help! Take advantage of this if you're confused about a PLQ or even just the post-lab write-up.

Life is so much easier when you stop hating on Dixon... I don't know why people interpret "you have to go to lecture to do well" as Dixon being a bad professor. It means she is a good lecturer. I think Dr Dixon has an effective class structure and flow. Also, she emphasizes concepts that are helpful for future coursework (biochem) and exams (topics are aligned with the MCAT). Dixon's classes are hard, but not impossible. She is very available in office hours, she has CAN one night a week which is HW or exam-like problem review, and she posts outlines and supplemental videos for tricky concepts. Take advantage of the resources she provides, understand that you're going to have to lock in, and you can do well. Her homeworks are tricky, time-consuming, and sometimes ambiguous. I tried on all the HWs just based on what I learned in lectures and usually got like 2/3 of the points. But then I redid the HWs multiple times checking my work with the answer keys after she posted them, which was a great way to study for the exams, since the exams are like the HWs. I was okay with not doing well on the HW and just studying them after the fact, and making up for it on the exams. I'm not really an office hours person but people have said they are helpful. Exams are most of the course grade and they are very closely based on the homeworks. She puts way more points on the exams (like 115) and scores them out of 100, so as long as you are a fast test taker, you have lots of opportunities to get points, and can get a high grade while still getting things wrong. Also, if you get over a 90% you will automatically get an A+, and she doesn't do minus grades unless it helps you. If you came to college to learn, take Dixon.

Dr. Schech made 272 easy as a lab coordinator. If you really want to, you only have to go to the 272 lecture twice, just for her two exams, because she posts the actual lectures on Panopto. The exams were very fair, just with a few annoying questions occasionally. In terms of the actual labs, I felt like they were pretty easy to do, but this also depends on your TA. At least with the structure of office hours that existed, it made it very easy to go to ask a TA for help on any lab report, which made it very easy to get 26-30/30 on every lab report if you had the time to go to office hours. I would recommend taking CHEM272 with her if you can.

Overall great guy and a chill professor. The class has a ton of work, but he provides so many resources to study. Make sure to review old topics for each exam so your coding stays up to date. he records lectures and is extremely nice.

His lectures and slides were very good. The projects are extremely detailed and very useful for understanding the content. Make sure to go to every lecture and discussion because getting a 0 on a graded worksheet will heavily decrease your grade. Note that he does not allow students to use any devices during class, but this shouldn't be a big issue if you manage your time effectively outside of class.

He's quirky but a great lecturer (not a professor). Our exam Averages were lower than Kaufman who was teaching 216 at the same time, which is something to keep in mind. But imo the exams were generally difficult, but fair and he gives you a lot of resources to prepare for them ahead of time.

Decent TA, could greatly improve with managing many students and ensuring that everyone gets equal time/attention. It seemed like there was favoritism to some students and/or that she was chatting with those students so she wouldn't have to help others like me. Normally I wouldn't mind this, I get being a TA can be tiring. It's just that I had missed a week of lectures due to falling badly ill, so I wanted to talk with a TA about how I could get back on track with the content. I told her all this and she told me I had to wait in line after which she chatted with two students at the same time for an half and hour before rushing through my questions in five minutes. Mind you, there were like four more students in line after me who were also waiting the whole time.

I had the 2 PM lecture for this class, and it was the best decision I've ever made. His lectures are entertaining at times, and he's probably one of the funniest professors here at UMD. But I honestly don't think he should be teaching at all. He has a great knowledge of data science, but this was a class I was really looking forward to taking, and was really interested in the content, but Max, as the professor, was a big no. He doesn't know how to teach and is probably one of the laziest professors here. His exams are pretty hard, and he doesn't help you with review. He posts these like weekly recaps, but they are kind of useless because they are vague about what you should know. His practice exams are nothing close to his actual exams, so they are just useless. Homeworks were not that hard, and he gave a lot of time to complete them, which was great. But honestly, I barely learned anything from him and really had to teach myself everything. Max is a great guy, but he is not suited to be a professor.

Anwar is pretty good. Him and Cliff coteach so no difference as far as exams, projects, etc. He teaches really well imo when he goes off his slides, which is about half the time. And then the other half he just does random examples on emacs which can sometimes be helpful and other times just makes things confusing. But overall he is pretty solid.

This class is honestly a joke. You really don’t need to go to lecture at all because you can teach yourself everything. Each project took me maybe 2–3 hours max, and for the exams, you just need to study the day before. And by “study,” I mean memorize the format of the previous exams. I'm giving Nelson a 3 because he doesn’t seem very invested in what he’s teaching and tends to go off-topic a lot (another reason I skipped lectures. I didn’t feel like I learned much from them). I took this class alongside 330 and 351, and it wasn’t too much work overall.
Definitely overrated. 5/10 lecturer with good notes but I really don't understand how his rating is so high. Maybe it's more of a relative rating because most other CS professors are abhorrent.

Bahar is a very nice and knowledgeable professor. I would consider this course to be an intersection between computer engineering and science. You will go pretty far down into understanding different parts of a computer and how they work, right above the transistor level. Due to the low-level nature of this course, all of the projects are "simulation" rather than "development". (You aren't gonna build your own CPU pipeline lol). It relates to much more analysis of how different parts perform under different scenarios. They aren't very difficult imo. The exams are fair but are above average in difficulty imo. The difficulty isn't exactly hard because of the content, but because of the limited amount of time you have to finish. Work fast! This course is very content-dense; there is a lot of information that you have to learn. It can be easy to get lost in the sauce many times. Lectures are recorded, and they were an enormous help for reviewing material.

This is a horrible class. The projects are impossibly difficult and the professor is terrible lecturer. His stutter is distracting and notes are all over the place. Average for a midterm is around a 46/80. Exams are really difficut You will have to end up learning all of the material and then doing all of the projects yourself. Dont take this class with him if you dont have to.

His lectures were pretty engaging and he's clearly interested in the content, but the disorganization of the class left a lot to be desired. Stuff doesn't get graded for a long time, like one project that took over a month to be graded. The final ended up online with little warning. His grading was also messed up for the final, which he had to correct (to his credit, he did fix it). The last project was a partner project and my partner wasn't added to the gitlab for an entire 2 weeks, despite the emails he ignored. I like his lectures, but I wouldn't take him again due to the lack of care he puts into the administration of the class.

First semester teaching, course was poorly organized. She and TAs were not responsive. She's not great of a lecturer, she just reads off from the slides and doesn't make material digestible. She also did not give good practice for the exams, although she might use this semester's exams for future semesters.

Best professor ever. Makes content super digestible. He is very understanding, and he gives a lot of practice for the exams. He tried out a new structure for the class this semester which is why there are so many low-star reviews, but he has released a survey and promised to improve the course further.

Dr. Kim and Dr. Regli were co-teaching this semester (Fall 2025), so their lectures, homework, projects, and exams were the same. I think you should probably have some basic background in AI because I didn't, so that made all the concepts really hard to understand/follow. But this is a skill issue lol Some notes: - 3 coding projects. ACTUALLY DO PROJECT 1 WELL BEFORE THE DUE DATE PLEASE 🙏🙏🙏 It is the hardest project out of all 3. Even if they haven't taught the concepts yet, just use Google and stuff to learn, JUST DO IT EARLY!!!! All projects are coding + writing. For example, for Project 1, you had to write a full report alongside the code. - 4 homeworks. - 2 midterms and 1 final (non-cumulative). You're allowed a cheatsheet (front and back) for all exams. All exams are multiple choice, so no partial credit. - All lectures are recorded. - All slides are posted. - Optional 1-2 hour recitations/discussions where TAs or the professors explain some of the concepts or how to start a project. In my opinion, midterms 1 and 2 were too close together (I think they were a little over a month apart), but maybe my perception of time was warped lol. In either case, the content needed for the final feels like a whole year's worth of content with how dense it is. So don't be fooled by the "non-cumulative"; the final will always be hard for a conceptually challenging class like this one. Dr. Regli is an okay guy. His hats are fun. I haven't spoken to him one-on-one or asked for help during office hours, but I think he lectures okay...? The way he explains things can sometimes be contradictory and not that well-explained. I think to really understand his lectures, you have to read the book (optional), research/learn on your own, and review a lot. Piazza is not the greatest place to get clear answers. Dr. Regli tends to get a bit annoyed when students ask the same question, which is fair since there is a search bar in Piazza, but sometimes his answers to questions can come off as a bit condescending. It is kind of funny when he types out "sigh" though...

I think she is genuinely very passionate about the class itself and covered a lot of different topics which was nice. I do agree that it would have been nice to have some variety in the practice problem sets and some more fun projects because the material itself was pretty cool. She allowed for a double sided cheatsheet for every exam so saying that the exams are mostly "memorization" is a bit ridiculous like you probably could have copied the practice exam solutions and done decently on the midterms and final. Genuinely, if you look the midterms and final, it was pretty similar to the stuff we have seen in practice exams or homeworks. She said that the exams would be harder if people used ChatGPT to do the homeworks and did not really engage with the material, and the homework averages were very high. When you take a 400 level CS class, I feel like you should be more prepared for fast paced rigorous content, especially since this class was definitely not harder than like 330 or 351. If you plan to actually study the material and go to her office hours if needed, you will do fine.
I guess it's an easy but a bit boring class. The exams are a bit tedious because the grading is nitpicky.

Possibly the worst class in the computer science department. The course is horribly organized and the lectures provide absolutely no valuable information. The projects and homeworks feel very disjointed compare to the course content. The TAs are not very helpful when it comes to elucidating anything about the class; possibly the most annoying thing is the constant shifting of the goalposts and grading criteria. In previous semesters the grading was very forgiving, probably to account for the chaos. Over halfway through the semester, we are still left mostly in the dark. Absolutely do NOT take this class. You can learn everything you need about computer vision on your own.
Pierce is more responsible than DVH and is the most helpful TA I’ve ever had in a CS course. Dude responds to Piazza posts at 1am in 5-10 minutes. What else can I say?
Class itself is straightforward, but exams had tricky questions (even though they were open note and open computer)

As said numerous times before, lectures are pretty boring. I genuinely liked learning about HCI, so I found the class to be fairly interesting despite him being a boring teacher. He does make this class 10x more tedious than it has to be, project descriptions tend to be lengthy (I'm talking 7+ page descriptions) and convoluted, and it feels like you're hitting a "moving target" when figuring out what you need to do. I would highly recommend taking another professor if possible, but if you end up stuck with him, PRAY your group is a good one because that'll really shape your experience for the semester. Exams are pretty easy, but he is super nitpicky about your answers. Overall: easy exams, very tedious semester-long group project, boring lectures. Yes, it's an "easy A" but sometimes it would be better to take a "harder class" with better structure and avoid the headache this class brings.

This class isn't easy if you expect A with minimum. You will definitely read lots of documentation online and debug a lot due to syntax. AI tools are not completely reliable but they can be good templates. DO NOT PROCRASTINATE! Please follow the suggested due date for each phase. There are 6 individual phases total and a group project. Phase 4 is the hardest, so work on it as soon as you can.

Dave Mount is easily the best professor I’ve ever had. First off, he’s an awesome lecturer–no matter the complexity of the algorithm, proof, NP-reduction or whatever concept it is, Mount always manages to explain it and break it down until it’s totally intuitive. He’s also just a really nice guy. You can ask him really anything about the course material or homework and he’ll happily give you more information than you even needed and he never makes you feel like you asked a dumb question. With that in mind, I CANNOT recommend attending his office hours enough. The homework problems can get really challenging, but if you go to OH, he’s always willing to help lead you in the right direction, or quickly look through your solution and provide general feedback. The exams are admittedly kind of brutal. They were both 2 hours, but devising and writing out a description, proof of correctness, and running time of an algorithm takes so long that there’s simply not enough time to fully think over each question–you just have to see the solution immediately or you won’t be able to finish the exam. HOWEVER, Mount is an insanely generous grader, so even if you don’t see how to answer an algorithm question, he offers so much partial credit (more than I felt like I deserved) if you demonstrate even some knowledge of the base concepts. This class is really challenging and you will need to dedicate a lot of time to it, but I’ve learned so much and the help/resources Mount provides are more than enough to help you succeed.
Nice teacher. Records lectures which is very helpful and is very accommodating. Also knows his shit.

Fumeng is a new professor in the CMSC department at the time of writing, and she did not disappoint. She was clearly very excited to be teaching 471 (it was her first time teaching it) and she had a lot of the course materials put together and published MONTHS before it started. She has a bit of an accent but it's pretty easy to understand her most of the time. She puts a lot of effort into her lectures and clearly has rehearsed them beforehand, appropriately stopping for questions whenever possible. She's also young and like was a college student just 4 years ago so she knows firsthand what college is like from a student's perspective and incorporates that well into how she structures the class as a professor. The information she taught about data visualization was pretty interesting, and I think I learned a good amount. The class was on Mondays and Wednesdays, and it was structured as lectures on Mondays and labs on Wednesdays. Labs were self-guided exercises in creating a variety of different visualizations, and were graded by being in class and asking her or a TA to look it over, and they were basically automatic 100s. Besides the labs, there were three assignments and a final project, all focused on either critiquing or creating visualizations based on what was taught in class. Two of the assignments and the final project required working in groups, which I honestly didn't love, but admittedly I think it's good to encourage teamwork and it was definitely appropriate for the class. Take it with friends if you can and you'll be fine. There was definitely a lot of practical skill learned with this class and I like how it was entirely project-based. There were NO exams, which was excellent. I do think that Fumeng was expecting a lot from us and expecting us to put a lot of effort into our visualizations, and since she is someone who has seen a LOT of visualizations, including some really cool but really complex ones, it seemed to be hard to impress her. At times, she could be kind of strict with grading or passive aggressive if you didn't put a lot of effort into your visualizations, but honestly she's kind of the goat for that because it encourages you to work harder to make something really cool. She was very constructive and I felt encouraged and motivated to put more effort than the bare minimum. She gives a lot of room for creativity which I also appreciated. If you're looking for an easy Area 2 or Area 3 class, I'd suggest this class with her as long as you're okay with taking some time to put at least a little real effort into the assignments and final project, but it's definitely not a class that you can just do the bare minimum for and expect to do well. But I did learn a lot of practical skills for data visualization and she did a really great job as a new professor teaching the class for the first time.

This class is not too bad and quite interesting if you're at all invested in more complex machine learning techniques. I feel like the class's pacing could be better, as the beginning of the class is extremely slow, but the last few weeks are a bit rough with assignments, final project checkpoints, and the final exam all overlapping. The lectures can be dry and math theory heavy but if you're interested it's doable. And all the lectures are recorded and taught on zoom concurrently so you don't have to physically attend class. Professor Shrivastava is very kind and understanding when it comes to grade concerns or other logistical concerns. Almost no one fails this class. That being said, the TAs (for my class at least) were very hard on grading and rarely granted regrade requests. But like I said, it doesn't really matter unless you're trying to get a 95 or more because the curve is high. Overall, I recommend this class for those who are interested in machine learning/deep learning. If you're not interested in the topics you *will* be bored out of your mind.

I don't know how previous years went, but his semester teaching CMSC474 was an absolute disaster. The projects graded in a ranked scale where the students competed against each other for the better grades, he barely put anything on ELMS so we had no idea how we were doing in the class at any point, and most of us didn't even get our final grades unless we asked. He also gave us zero help in studying for the exams that were 60% of our grade. There was no topics sheet, there was no practice exams, there was no Piazza, and there was one review session for the midterm (and none for the final) that he didn't even attend. He also told us we should listen to his 12 hour podcast because it may be tested as extra credit... which never happened. And every time someone goes to him to ask for any clarification, he just tells us to "not worry about our grades". Well, I "didn't worry about my grades" and I got a D, so thanks for that.

I loved the class. he's a very caring professor, asked us how the class could be better frequently and actually took the suggestions. He asked us how the midterm 1 went and we said it was too long so he made the second one shorter. He just genuinely wants us to learn the material and was really helpful in office hours and doubts in class. I talked to him about philosophical questions and my career and academic plans. he helped a lot. the clas itself was quite interesting. Take the class IMO. it's fun (if u like math a little) , great textbook, and useful. I would recommend you to take the class!

I usually don't write reviews, but Professor Griffin receives lower than a 1 star if possible. He's extremely passionate about what he teaches in the classroom but his respect, attitude, and behaviors towards others (including his AMPs) are in the gutter. Like everyone else has said, he has assigned seats during lecture, takes attendance during every class, wastes the first 15 minutes of lectures just going over the syllabus, and treats students like children. I'm not sure if he's on some power trip but his attitude towards students is disgusting. One time, a student sat in with another student in an empty seat and he called them out in front of the class, felt the need to embarrass him, and kicked him out. He is extremely passive-aggressive whenever a student is a bit late and sometimes even calls them out in front of a full lecture hall. When a student was late for their exam, he had them sit in the front of the room and almost flung the exam in his direction. The students in his class are smart and capable but he does not treat them as such. STAT100 should be an easy A but Professor Griffin assigns "busy work" and talks/complains about the most useless and impractical things. Class is also never canceled in this class. When Professor Griffin was out sick, he had the AMPs and the TAs sit in front of the class and "teach" which basically meant students looked through the lecture slides on their own and completed an online classwork by the end of it. He's not understanding, he's not lenient, and he's overall just not a decent person. If you can take stat100 elsewhere or with anyone else, do it otherwise you'll spend the rest of the semester complaining about this dude

very easy one credit asynchronous class (i knocked it out in one weekend), structured into mcq quizzes (that have multiple attempts and show you what you got wrong and what the correct answer was, so you're guaranteed a 100% after the first one) and short frq assignments. only thing is i thought the slides were sometimes a bit confusing in their formatting, and her announcements were a little confusing but that's it

the projects took a lot of time tbh for a 1 credit class but they were fun and really helped me learn Python. I got good grades on all the projects so I'm sure they weren't tooooo strict with grading. pretty easy

Imo super boring class, but a pretty easy A. No exams and all project and homework-based. There is a final project/presentation for the midterm & final which build off of each other, and it's really just a standard data science exploration project. Sometimes the assignments can be confusing or mistyped, but they're not that difficult if you dont slack off. I stopped going to lecture a quarter into the semester, but I managed to stay on top of the work because of the resources he provides (websites & books). Literally everything you'll be doing will be in R(Studio) and with ggplot2 for data visualization instead of Jupyter notebook/Google colab (pandas). Professor is a really chill guy, but I guarantee you'll find this as more busy work than anything else.

Great man and a decent teacher !!! He did sometimes give out a lot of work but he also granted extensions if you asked him and if your reason complies with the syllabus. Would recommend this teacher if you are ready to do a lot of work..

DO NOT TAKE THIS CLASS!! As others have said assignment instructions were confusing and inconsistent. They would change on a whim with little to no prior notice and send half the class into a frenzy on disallowed terms (which were literally taught in the textbook). And, as everyone else has also mentioned she took the time to report half the class for cheating which severely impacted my mental health last semester. Imagine worry about your academics and then all of a sudden being accused of cheating (which i didn’t do and was eventually cleared of) which puts you into a 2 month long limbo period. That was easily the most stressful point in my life and I’m sure other students who also did nothing felt the same.

Professor Aditya knows his material and know-how to teach a class. He does live coding and walk through step by step if you get stuck. He's very helpful and knows that everyone in his class learning and understanding the Data Science concepts. He's the best professor for INST 414.

literally the best teacher ever. she makes concepts super understandable and the way she structured the course was really helpful for students. there's a quiz almost every week, but the question is taken directly from the homework (and homework isn't graded/submitted - you only do it to be ready for the quiz). the worksheets aren't difficult and can be done in groups. all the questions in the midterms are extremely similar to worksheet/homework/quiz questions, so you definitely want to go through all the material to be prepared. although the final is made by chadwick, her class prepares you well enough for it. i'm just sad she wasn't here to teach math141 in spring 26.

Super good lecturer who genuinely cares. Quizzes are much easier than the exams, although the homework does take a while. Exams are pretty hard, but he gives a list of suggested problems on Canvas. If you put in the work and do all of them, it prepares you very well for the exam because he'll make a lot of the problems very similar to the suggested problems. Also, I once dropped my keycard in class and he drove all the way to North Campus to return it to me :) very kind

If you're taking linear algebra, I highly recommend that you DO NOT take this professor. I know his ratings are good, and that's because he isn't a bad teacher; he knows what he's doing, but he goes extremely fast in lectures. His percentage distributions are terrible; the final is 30 percent of your grade, which is purely your score on the final exam. The midterms are very tricky, always testing difficult concepts and theory behind computations and have difficult true or false questions. Taking this class was draining; I studied so much to end with a B+. The concepts in this class aren't hard, but the tests he gives make it hard, and honestly, it is better to have a worse lecturer who gives easier exams. I recommend taking another professor who is more lenient with their exams, even if they have worse reviews or is worse at teaching. Lastly, his grade distributions on ELMS are wrong, and he purposefully announces it on the week of finals, when there is nothing you can do about it. Make sure to calculate your grade using the syllabus distributions and DON'T trust the score automatically calculated by ELMS.

I took this class Fall 2024. Brosnan was clearly immensely smart and incredibly good at math, but this unfortunately worked against him. He never really went over too many examples in class and only really derived the formulas from axioms. He also was not really great at answering questions or anything like that. The exams were fairly easy and the homework was optional, with the quizzes also pretty easy. The final that was set by the university was a bit harder than the midterms, but I wouldn't really say that the midterms were good preparation. Like many others are recommending, it is pretty necessary to use another set of notes, such as Justin's.

Very nice person, exams were fair, and I didn't have to dedicate much time to studying in this class (though I did come in with a strong foundation from previous math classes). She is very understanding about extenuating circumstances in life, hence why she decided to drop two quizzes instead of only one. I would definitely recommend this professor. She provided a lot of practice material, and the practice exams especially were very useful. I would recommend this professor to anyone.

I'm pretty sure this was her first semester teaching, and she did pretty well imo. Exams were fair, and actually got easier as the semester went on, but I think that's because of the nature of the class; you get better at writing proofs over time. Workload was initially a bit much, homeworks took up a ton of time. But she took feedback from the class and scaled them down. They're still really helpful to study. We had quizzes most weeks which were never too bad. Group works were good for grades and added a nice way to discuss the material with classmates. Lectures got better as the semester went on. Writes clearly on the board, and emphasizes theorems and definitions over just drilling examples. I don't know how she would teach a computational class, but her style fit 310 well. She speaks very quietly though I'd say I got a lot out of the class- I feel much more comfortable writing proofs than I did going into it, which is the entire point of 310. I recommend her, she'll give you a fair class

He is a very good teacher; what he writes on the board is not super overwhelming and can be pretty easy to follow along with. He is not that understanding so you should try really hard to stay on track and not ask for many extensions and stuff like that. The homeworks are super helpful and not too difficult, usually they are from Justin's notes, which makes it better. He drops two homeworks which can be a relief and he might curve the course depending on the average. The exams have been very fair, just computationally heavy which means work fast.

Honestly, he's not too bad. The first couple homeworks were brutal for me before the way the class expected you to think made sense for me, but the rest were probably 90 minutes total for each homework, once a week. Lectures are boring and the proofs are very confusing and I usually had no idea what he was doing unless I had read the textbook's proof prior. I don't think I ever got enough intuition developed to just freely following along with all the "obvious" insights he expected us to see. The first exam was a total freebie, I got 100% with very little studying and just glancing through the review problems was sufficient. Material difficulty greatly ramped going into the 2nd exam, with a lot of chapters covered and the most difficult material all condensed into one exam window. Everything from basic homomorphism facts to sylow groups and free groups fell here, and there was a heavy expectation on the second exam that your intuition be strong enough to work with very little given information in a problem and recognize the correct structure of a group to be able to reduce what felt like a complicated and near impossible problem to a trivial two line proof. Not kidding, all the solutions posted by him after were essentially a sentence or two. Lowest exam score of my life with a 58/100. My lowest grade on anything else in the class, including the final, other than the second exam was a 90% on the 3rd homework, and in general I got a 100% on just about everything, including the homework leading up to exam 2, so I wouldn't say that my understanding of the material was lacking so much as my intuition. If you're very comfortable with 400 level math, I don't think you'd have any problem and rosenberg is always willing to answer questions quickly when you email him, even before a homework assignment is due. The time spent on rings and fields was a little short and felt rushed due to the heavy emphasis on group theory, though the problems on the final did appropriately compensate by being very fair and quite straightforward and easy, so I won't complain too much. I think what we didn't cover that other professors did could easily be made up in a week or two of your own time, as we got a strong foundation in rings and just ran out of time to go into field theory. Would have liked to know earlier after the second exam that he thought he made it too hard and would be making the final easier and curving the class, as I had spent the previous several weeks before he finally told us during final review terrified I may fail the class.

I enjoyed him as a person, but his teaching style could be a bit disorganized. In particular, we didn't have our the majority of our homework graded until the last week of class. Also, he wrote pdf of lecture notes on the class material but only released them about two weeks before the final.

Overall, I would not recommend this professor since he made this class a lot harder and more stressful than it had to be. However, this was his first semester teaching at UMD, so hopefully the quality of his instruction will improve next semester. pros: - can be pretty funny and entertaining - did a huge curve for our class (thought I would fail, ended the class with a B+) - homeworks were reasonable, mostly graded for completion (except one problem is graded for accuracy) - exam problems were mostly reasonable and we were given plenty of time cons: - vague about what is on exams, which made it very difficult and stressful to prepare for exams. The structure of his exams was usually some definitions and 3-4 theorems from class or homeworks, but since his exams would be only 3-5 problems each, it felt very hit or miss - exam averages for both midterm exams were pretty low, around 65-70% - very picky about definitions and harsh grader for proofs - wasn't always fully prepared for lectures, would sometimes waste time during lecture trying to come up with proofs - wasn't very encouraging, during class he said our proofs were "disgusting" and ideally he would give most people zeroes on all their proofs and wasn't much nicer during office hours - not a good lecturer; his explanations and proofs were often confusing, his handwriting was hard to read, and would often block view of the board while writing - exams were worth 90% of our grade (50% final, 20% each midterm) - doesn't post notes to encourage lecture attendance

Dong was a really nice professor, and quite frankly, taking this course with him is an easy A. This course consists of 6 HWs, a midterm and a final. The HW contained a mixture of mildly difficult problems and very challenging problems. The challenging problems were very theoretical in nature. I will state, though, that he usually went over the challenging problems in class, and outright gave entire answers for those problems. However, I think the HW could have been a little easier and less theoretical. His exams are pretty chill. Unlike the previous semester (which had a take-home midterm and a final that was basically optional), we had an in-person midterm as well as a take-home final. The midterm was very fair - he gave us practice problems for the midterm that correlated very well with the actual exam. Most people got an A on the midterm. The final was a little harder, but due to it being take-home, it was very little stress. His lectures were not the best, but also not the worst. His accent is very thick, so it is difficult to understand what he is saying at times. I found it difficult to learn from his lectures, but it wasn't the biggest problem as the textbook contains the content that he covers in class. He also does not record lectures, nor does he post notes. I would prefer if he at least posted notes for his lectures, but again, because of the textbook, it wasn't that big of an issue. I'd like to note that he is very passionate about Number Theory. He also has an impressive knowledge of Math history, and often goes in depth into it in his lectures. This made his lectures pretty enjoyable, in my opinion. Also, the TA and the professor were extremely lenient with the grading, which made this course super chill in general. Overall, this professor was a life-saver for me this semester, as I was stressed out with other courses. I'd recommend taking Dong if you want an easy A. I would have preferred to learn a little more, but still think I gained something from it (got a lot of practice with congruences, and learning all the tricks and manipulation you can do with them). I would like to note that MATH406 is actually a really difficult course if you were to take it with any other professor - only take this course if Dong is teaching it.

Dr. G is quite literally the goat. He is very approachable, uploads all of his notes, and genuinely cares about his students. He consistently makes an effort to help everyone succeed and is easily one of the best professors I have had at UMD. MATH410 is infamously known at UMD as a difficult class, and Dr. G fully acknowledges that students have historically struggled with the material. Because of this, he makes every effort to make the course more manageable. He walks through proofs very slowly to ensure everyone has a solid understanding and goes through many practice problems during lecture. His quizzes and exams are also very fair. He clearly outlines exactly how to prepare for them, so expectations are always very transparet. He also records all lectures and uploads his notes, and is always happy to go over questions during office hours or after class. Overall, this course was taught wonderfully.

Berhanu is an incredible lecturer with a ton of experience and knowledge in a variety of analytical fields, which made this class feel more than bearable. I loved his teaching style, which focused very heavily on building the intuition behind understanding the problems instead of solely giving you a formula or procedure on how to solve them. A complaint I could see someone having is that he writes very fast during lecture and it can be hard to keep up, in which case I agree, but I would refer back to the previous comment I made about building the intuition and not copying everything he writes down word for word. He is not the most rigorous when it comes to proofs, as he is self-admittedly lazy when it comes to the formal elements of math, but I thought that this made everything about the class easier to understand as I wasn't always so stressed about trying to match a certain style. At the end of the day, if you can understand what the problem is saying and convey that you know how to resolve that problem, you will do great in the class. Just be aware that even if your formal writing is strong/rigorous, you will get no points on problems if your intuition is off. The exams were fair since they were completely based off of either the homework problems or the practice sets he would give 1-2 weeks before the exam. The homeworks were also fair and helpful with every problem assigned from the book so you had a clear idea of how you should solve the problem in relation to the section. My grader was clearly not that good with the material, as I had to visit them multiple times to teach the content (which is ridiculous). I got my points back on every problem I taught him about except for one, in which case Berhanu stepped in, resolved the issue, and fairly gave points back to me and other students who also suffered through the grader. This showed me that not only was he attentive to what was happening in the class, but that he also cared about the issues of his students. Some advice I have: 1. Show up to lecture: I feel like this should be a given, otherwise what else are you doing with your time? The lectures were interesting and Berhanu would frequently engage with the class and give opportunities for questions or clarification. 1.5 Don't be late: This is a point that he makes at the start of the semester which I didn't like. I interpreted it as "Don't barge in on me trying to teach and become a distraction". There is a difference between being a minute late from walking from another class and coming in 20 minutes after the lecture starts, a point which I thought was fair. Not sure what happened to students who came in late, but I would hope he was lenient to students walking from other classes. 2. Do every practice problem: They are relevant and will show up somewhere. 3. UNDERSTAND THE BALL: This concept is taught relatively early on, but if you understand the concept of the open ball, the rest of the class will come so easily. My thoughts on negative reviews: 1. "He will accept only a perfect solution." - Couldn't be further from the truth. I know some professors who would throw a fit if they graded some proofs that Berhanu marked as full credit. The difference is in what is valued. Berhanu values understanding, and he can tell if you do or don't. If you get points off, it is purely because it is clear your intuition wasn't there. Yes, it's harder than just memorizing, but then why are you a math major? 2. "Tough, difficult, many students dropped" - ??? Many students dropped my section and I wasn't sure why, but the exam averages were well above 80% and he will give an extra, optional exam if students do poorly that replaces your lowest exam grade. 3. "would talk poorly about students to other students in the same class" - He never did this and I don't know what he gains by gossiping with undergrads??? 4. "He deducts points for everything." - I disagree with everything about that post, but thought I'd include this example considering that I was deducted full points for an exam problem, which was totally fair considering my solution gave a calculation and conclusion that was straight up wrong, but he gave me half points back since I always went to lecture and was engaged with the material. 5. "He is self-centered" - Tbh I would be too if I had 40 years of teaching experience and had to deal with some of the ridiculous stunts some students would pull DURING LECTURE. A student in my class would consistently ask irrelevant or unrelated questions during the lecture and I thought Berhanu was more than justified in not giving a thorough explanation. With these types of reviews, I urge people to think about the variety of students a class can have, which will more times than not include someone who wants to be "main character" of the class. This class was so bearable. While I didn't see my graded final exam, I am pretty sure I got a B+ in the class because I didn't take the time to learn the integration section and also I just hate solving integrals. An A is very achievable if you go to lecture and do the problems he assigns.

While I think he understands and is passionate about the subject, I believe the way that he teaches the class is detrimental to the performance of those in his class. Homework assignments were not regularly spaced out, with grading not happening on time. While it was interesting to go from one concept to the next via deriving them via proofs and previous knowledge, there was a severe lack of examples to do in class or to practice with, which made me feel unprepared for the content on both the homeworks and the exams. I personally despise chatgpt but was really considering using it to assist me with homeworks. I appreciated the content he included in his notes, however, they were basically what we went over in lecture but more in-depth – meaning it was overwhelming to comb through to find specific things if you needed to look for something. There is a curve that he mentions, with the person with the highest grade guaranteed to get an A, however I genuinely cannot tell how the class is performing at this moment because there is rarely any class participation. Aside from my grades, I have not received any feedback on my homeworks, meaning I don't know what I have gotten wrong etc. I also had issues with him in terms of accommodations, he was very resistant to respecting some of mine which caused me trouble in the beginning of the semester. I love to learn more about math, however since exams and homeworks are everything in this class, I feel like the way he teaches is not fit for the structure of the class.

Great professor. His exams were very close to his study guides and overall fair. The only complaint I have is that he created a effectively down curved the class by changing the weights on assignments more than half way into the semester. In addition, instead of dropping two assignments (which is what the original syllabus stated), he decided to drop just one.

The reviews of his 246 confuse me, because I feel like he's the exact opposite of what's described. You can tell he cares a lot about the class. On top, he's very responsive and passionate about helping students. Lectures are clear and entertaining. Exams and homework are fair and graded quickly (we have a good grader too!). The text used really sucks but I can live with that. Overall the course is organized and enjoyable. Highly recommend.

Quite possibly the biggest disappointment of a class I've ever had. His class has no direction or structure. "Lectures" are just a discussion between himself and the 4-5 math geniuses in class who already know everything, while everyone else is left in the dust, not following a single word. This makes the homework problems and tests pretty hard. Finals are coming up and it will be interesting to see how he decides final grades, since everyone seems to be doing either really well or abysmally bad.
Excellent professor. Teaches so well and is always willing to help. But he moves pretty fast so make sure you're keeping up

One of the best professors I've had at UMD. You can tell he really cares about what he's teaching and the success of his students. The homework, term project and exams feel relevant to the course. The exam questions are really fair, you never look at a question and feel surprised and wonder if you learned about the concept. It's a really dense course and some lectures can feel overwhelming but just make sure you show up to class and be an active listener and you'll be perfectly fine.

Such a good professor, her lectures are quick, and she starts right on the dot, so don't be late. She posts her notes from every lecture and even curved our second midterm. She dropped the lowest midterm grade, I highly recommend taking midterm 3 as it covers easier chapters. She has HW assignments on Pearson that are easy and offer extra credit questions, which are really helpful. She responds to questions on Piazza quickly with helpful feedback. Your lab portion of the grade relies heavily on your TA, I had a great one, so that's all up to luck. Heidarian explains really well with helpful examples in lecture, and she posts practice problems for every midterm. I highly recommend her for PHYS121!

Such a good teacher, just follow her notes and review a couple times a week and you are set up for success. Review practice problems like your life depends on it and it will pay off not hard to not get an A, i just didnt put the time into trying.

While I did well, this class is horribly organized and should really be revamped. I did not do well because of Dr. Buehrle by any means—that was all my own prior knowledge and work. Dr. Buehrle simply cannot teach effectively: he spends lots of time on irrelevant information to try and build conceptual understanding but ultimately fails to make a conclusion in what he is teaching. There is little structure, and he jumps around clicker questions and long tangents about the ideas behind what we're learning. The textbook and required reading questions are so useless (except for the simulations) and is written very confusingly. I am good at physics, and have taken a more advanced class in physics than this before, so it's not just me; the textbook overcomplicates simple ideas. He seems to do this as well. The homework Expert TA questions were good for practicing, and were a much better source of practice than his lectures. If this class was a core part of the degree for life science majors in the same way that a class like organic chemistry is, the course would have been redesigned by now. No one complains about it because he curves the scores high enough each semester, but the class is treated like a joke, with ineffective teaching and no actual learning going on. Just read the other reviews: people barely felt like they learned anything from him, but he just curves them enough to pass anyway so nothing happens. Despite calculus being a prerequisite for the class, he acts like it's unnecessary during class, avoiding using it at all in practice problems and making a big deal out of the word "integral" during lectures. We are in college, and we can handle words like derivative or integral. He could have made the entire kinematics unit so much simpler by explaining it in that way, and the information was even on the slides, but he'd avoid doing that. The first week would have been better with a review of the basic ideas to understand the course as well, but he instead spent multiple lectures going over what a measurement meant and how to do an estimation. By this point, most students have taken difficult classes in chemistry dealing with this—and not once did we require multiple lectures on measurements and estimation. He treats us like we are incapable of understanding physics. Deleting those lectures entirely and dedicating a few lectures to going through actual practice problems would have been so much more useful. As for the grading: the way the curve works is absolutely no reason he deserves a good rating. Sure, he curves by a lot, but that is because he literally cannot teach and uses the curve to make up for it. No matter how low you score, he will curve people up to around a B average. He also grades on a bell curve, meaning you can get rounded down if you perform better than the average; this is also true for lab reports. The labs are also a joke and it seemed like they were just there to fulfill a requirement. The work we do is tedious and not helpful to understanding content in the slightest. The only good thing I can say about that is that the lab usually ends early if you have a better TA who can help out. If your TA doesn't know what they're doing, good luck, because the only other guidance for the labs is a file he puts on ELMS with unclear instructions. If you're someone who's between PHYS131 and PHYS161, and the professors are good for 161 and you're decent at physics and calculus, just take PHYS161. This class feels like a waste of time.

I didn't take PHYS131, so I was a little worried about how I would do in this class, but it was surprisingly simple. The lectures have all of the information you need to take the exams and complete the homework, so I didn't need to review any 131 topics that might not be covered in a conventional physics class. Dr. Severson was a good lecturer; he spoke slowly and clearly and sometimes drew diagrams to assist his explanations. I think he gives a little too much time to answer clicker questions, but they're nice as a brain break, and he explains the answers afterward. He's not the most passionate teacher and tends to read off the slides, but most of the class is just here for the credit anyway. He records his lectures. Attendance is not mandatory, and the in-lecture clicker questions can be completed outside of lecture. Doing the lab reports was a bit of a challenge since I wasn't used to their format, but I had good teammates who knew what they were doing, and I learned through observation. If you took PHYS131, the lab reports are in the same tedious format. Make sure you pay attention to the rubrics for the lab reports and try to do the modeling section in lab so you can ask the TA questions. The last couple of lab reports were easier than the first ones since they had you answer specific questions instead of a conventional report. All the lab reports were completed in groups, so make sure you pick good teammates. The lab scores get normalized at the end of the semester, so some people ended up with over 100% for their lab grade. There is a recitation you're supposed to complete each lab that's graded for participation, but some TAs don't really care if you do them. Lab content has no bearing on the exams. Other than lab reports, the only other assignments we have are the Expert TA homework and the TopHat clicker questions, both of which you have to pay for. The clicker questions (both in-lecture and for homework) are generally graded for completion. Sometimes there are TopHat quizzes in lecture graded for accuracy, but Dr. Severson warns you about them ahead of time, and they're not difficult. You can also talk to your classmates to verify answers. The Expert TA questions are graded for accuracy, so I'd recommend completing them on a sheet of paper, verifying your answers with a TA, then submitting them online. There are 10 graded Expert TA assignments, and some are longer than others, so make sure to check them before deciding to do them last minute. There are 3 exams total (2 midterms and a final), with the final worth 17% of your grade and each midterm worth 14%. All the content you need to know is covered in the lecture, so I didn't really use the textbook to study. To prepare for exams, I went over my notes, reviewed the Expert TA assignments, and completed the practice exams. The Expert TA questions and the practice exam are pretty close in format and difficulty to the actual exam questions. The midterms have retakes, where your final score is an average of your original exam score and the retake score, so I'd recommend only taking the retake if you did really badly on the original. Dr. Severson is pretty accommodating about finding times for the retakes, but I've heard that the retakes are a little harder than the original exams. The final focuses on the topics covered in the last portion of the semester, but there is a cumulative component as well. Dr. Severson gives out a list of topics to review for the cumulative part, so you don't have to relearn the whole class. All the exams have a lot of partial credit, so always show your work. Exams consist of multiple-choice, short-answer, calculation, long-answer, and estimation questions. You should have enough time to complete the exam within the allotted time; I usually finish a few minutes early. Midterm solutions are posted as a video walkthrough explaining them, which is helpful for studying for the final.

Lots of material for an incredibly difficult class, and I’m so happy with what she did give us. Lectures were fast paced, but the notes online were excellent to follow. The online homework was difficult but fair, and the written homework sometimes felt impossible, but that one was graded on completion so if I spent more than 3-4 hours I’d just phone it in and still get full marks. My TA was alright, but Girvain herself has wonderful resources and was amazing during office hours. It’s not a fun class, but Girvain is an excellent choice to succeed with. The curve was also pretty great, with only 5% of students failing, with her saying they were often students who didn’t try at all.

I had him for the lab period, but pretty much no one actually interacted in person since the TAs run the labs. I give this 5-star review because one, the lab was well run and my lab partner and I always finished within a reasonable time frame and the excel sheets were very well made. And two, someone posted a profanity-ridden ELMs post about the review HW having deductions (it was actually worth no points), and the professor responded with a brief explanation of the no points thing and ended it with "lol" full stop. Giga chad move IMO, A++ professor.

Baden's 270 is honestly the best version of the class and there's no competition. He posts all of his notes and the midterms are just pages of expertTA problems. Basically read his notes and practice the homework and they'll be fine. He also drops the lowest midterm. His lectures are very interesting but not very useful for the class. They're usually derivations and demos of the concepts he teaches. I eventually ended up learning everything outside of class from his notes and practiced the hw the night before the tests and did well on all of the midterms. On top of all of that he literally made our final just the three previous midterms stapled together, same numbers, bar for bar. Only minor complaint would be that he does grade on a bell curve and makes the average grade in the class a B. But he gives you everything you need to do well. Class would be difficult if you barely study but can't really blame him for that!

Only reason he got 1 star was because 0 isn't an option. If you have any passion or interest in physics do not take his class because he will ruin all of it. Horrible teacher so take literally anyone else possible. Tests are impossible and he is unreasonable. Stay away

Professor Turpen is by far the best physics professor I've had at UMD. I appreciated her pedagogical approach to physics where she emphasized understanding the material rather than trying to destroy our GPAs. It's quite refreshing to feel like I can truly enjoy the material rather than worrying about exams. For homeworks and exams she allowed us to revise them for half credit back, and her exams were very fair. I wish other professors in the physics department would teach like she did.

Kara Hoffman is the worst physics professor I have ever had at UMD. First of all, she is an awful lecturer. She only lectures from premade slides that move way too fast and anyways don't teach anything. She knows her lectures are bad, so she forces students to come to class by grading them based on their responses to clicker questions (this is 10% of your grade). None of this helps the actual issue, which is that she doesn't know how to teach at all. Another 10% of your grade is attendance for discussion sections, where the worksheets given are usually on topics that have not been taught yet, so that is not very useful. Indeed, this same issue was present in the homework. Also, Hoffman gave a more difficult first midterm than we were led to expect (average in the 60s and most people agreed with this sentiment), which wouldn't necessarily be an issue, except for the fact that she previously said we should expect a pretty easy midterm that most people can finish before class ends. Additionally, Hoffman also insisted on using the textbook of MacIntyre, not Griffiths. MacIntyre is a terrible quantum textbook because it derives next to nothing, so you are really left to just memorize formulas without understanding the underlying physics. Hoffman's lectures are somehow even worse, and explain absolutely no concepts and are all about calculations and memorizing formulas. On top of all that, Hoffman is rude and snarky in manner and not understanding at all. She does not care if her students succeed and seems disinterested in their learning. Anecdotally, for example, she wrote in the official syllabus that students could come 10 minutes late to the discussion section with no points lost. However, without telling the class, halfway through the semester she started taking off points from participation for students who were even just a minute late. This is a breach of the syllabus and therefore against university rules, but Hoffman doesn’t care. She insists we are in class for every possible second, which makes it all the more infuriating that being in her class is completely useless since she is a terrible lecturer. For a class as crucial for a physics student as quantum, it was exceedingly disappointing to have had such a bad experience and learn so little conceptual information. If you can afford to wait a semester and take quantum with a different professor, I would highly recommend doing so and wish I did so myself.

Professor Galitski is a okay professor, but I don’t think I could recommend him. The course structure as a whole was very well laid out. There were three lectures a week as well as a discussion section. Quizzes were given out during discussions every other week, and the alternating weeks had a worksheet that the TA would go over. The course also had two TAs. There was a healthy balance between grade weighting for exams, homework, and quizzes. The final was also made optional. This allowed for me to do quite well in the class despite struggling with understanding a few topics. The main problem with the course was lectures themselves. The professor would go through countless derivations in class without really getting into the reasoning for doing so. These derivations were also free-handed so we often had to make corrections to our notes when he made mistakes. His lectures would have immensely benefited from him reading from his notes more often instead of trying to do everything off the top of his head. This made understanding some topics or their relevance difficult. Despite lecture difficulties, the professor did do his best to make the class manageable outside of it. We didn’t have too many homeworks, and they all were manageable. Additionally, for quizzes and exams, a list of the relevant topics was provided. I personally had difficulties with the professor in terms of scheduling a make-up midterm where contact over email was a struggle, but I’m not sure if that was just a onetime event. Students with a good grasp of quantum topics will do well in his class given its structure. People who struggle more with quantum may want to invest in tutoring or visiting office hours to ensure the content taught in lecture is explained in more detail.

Truly, one of the best professors I have had for a course. No complaints, no regrets, makes the class fun with all the demos and also really cares about the students learning. Take him for at any cost.

Prof. Davoudi gives long homework assignments and very difficult exams. She is sometimes a bit condescending when answering student questions. There was a decent curve in our course given the pitiful exam and homework averages so she gets an extra star for that.

Loved this class, would definitely recommend. He posted all slides before class and slides would have good example questions. Midterm and Final were easy and had a lot of similar questions to in-class examples. Would start and end on time. Discussions were a little pointless if you had an okay understanding of R, but overall very easy A.

I think I'm of the minority opinion but I thought his lecture style was ok. You definitely need to put some time outside of class to understand the content though. Quizzes are super easy and I think the midterms were fair, but other people definitely have different opinions. The final is 40% of our final grade and it was absolute hell, but he gave us a gigantic curve so we all wound up getting a higher grade than expected. He's a prof will actually curve, which I can't say about like any of my math or cs professors I've had so far. Very nice dude who cares about your GPA, but don't expect the lectures to be enough to actually understand what's happening.

KYEONGWON LEE: Kind and understanding instructor who is able to address student concerns. There is more to be done to better this course, since it seems he is relatively new to the university, but it wasn’t bad towards the end. Things just got better. LECTURES (Rating: 4/5): Lectures are primarily based off of PowerPoint slides. This isn’t the professor’s fault but mainly that of the statistics department. It would have been more appreciated to have a curriculum where we have some practice in lectures. This eventually changed towards the end when we sent him emails. See the “Homework” section for more details about the R sessions, which were held occasionally. DISCUSSIONS (Rating: 4/5): It would’ve been nice to have two discussions for this class. We go over a practice worksheet and then head into a quiz (we leave early afterwards). The quizzes should only take 15 minutes, so it would’ve been more ideal to have the extra 5 minutes to go over worksheet problems. HOMEWORK (Rating: 2.5/5): There was only really one homework assignment for the course - an R Project that was worth 10% of our grade. The R Sessions that were intended to prepare us for this project did not help much, and it was not fun having to learn an entire programming language from scratch just for this project (I am new to R). I HIGHLY RECOMMEND TAKING DATA 110 AS A CO-REQUISITE IF YOU TAKE THIS COURSE. QUIZZES (Rating: 3.5/5): Quizzes were meh. They were given weekly in discussion and were based off of the practice problems. The class group chat panicked at first because of how unprepared the class felt for the quizzes. But eventually the averages got better over time and even I was shocked at how good I was doing. Because some quiz means were so low he plans to drop the lowest score. EXAMS (Rating: 5/5): The exams were not bad, I’m just dumb. (I also have neither the dorm nor the time to study.) Dr. Lee allows you to bring a formula sheet in for the exam. One side of a sheet for the midterm, and the whole sheet for the final. Oh, and did I forget to mention there’s extra credit? OVERALL RATING: 3.8/5 Structure for Fall 2025 - R Project (10%) - Quizzes (30%; weekly, lowest dropped - we had nine) - Midterm Exam (25%) - Final Exam (35%)

Almost nothing bad to say at all. Dr. S is very organized and invested in her teaching, it is honestly impressive. She had pretyped lecture notes, which were incredibly clear. Very friendly at office hours and cares that everyone understands the material. Homeworks were very helpful for exams. Not the easiest class, I felt like getting an A required consistent effort, but was definitely not impossible. She didn't have practice exams which I felt made exams more challenging than they needed to be. Definitely worth taking any class with her if you can.

This course is extremely difficult with the instructor; do not take unless absolutely required for your major/minor requirements. The content is not what makes the course hard; the instructor frequently gets into arguments with students, does not answer questions if the material has already been covered, and teaches the course in an extremely robotic manner (she expects your work to match her style exactly and does not tolerate any alternative solutions even if correct). Steer clear unless absolutely necessary.

Unfortunately, Dr. Sahinoglu made this class very confusing and stressful for no reason. The main issue is the exams. The professor would take the majority of points off for even the slightest mistake: the average for the midterm was 49%, and 39% for the final. We had practice exams, but she refused to provide the answer key for them and then proceeded to blame students for poor performance, saying it would be a “lesson” to us. To get any feedback on sample exams, we had to email her our work. To her credit, she did give feedback, but it was inconsistent. The coding part of the exams was ELMS quizzes, where you would get 0 points for the whole question if you rounded or provided more decimal places; no code was considered at all. Luckily, she provided the explicit instructions for the final. The slides were of poor quality with confusing information and inconsistent formatting. At times, the lectures were confusing and lacked coherence. Unless Dr. Sahinoglu changes the class structure/grading, I would not recommend taking this class with her.

Dr. G is a really great and kind professor. She's an amazing lecturer who made the class material really interesting and easy to understand. I actually really enjoyed the material in this class and felt like I learned a lot because of how she explained things. She's genuinely a nice person who wants her students to succeed. She focuses on getting her students to understand the overall concepts/big picture, so she's not nitpicky about small details when making questions for exams. Her exams were very fair and covered exactly the material she teaches in lecture. The only thing was that since she was used to giving exams for a 75 minute class but our class was only 50 minutes, the first exam was very long and most people had trouble finishing, but the other exams were fine. I highly recommend taking her!
Fairly easy class. Kind of seems like a filler class without real purpose. But I might be biased because I do not like ecology.

I was scared for this class because it was the only one left and had bad reviews, but I loved her. Mohan's class is extremely organized and structured in a way that makes getting an A so easy. Her exams are extremely straightforward as well, she doesn't try to trick you. I would say her exams prioritize memorization over deep understanding as she doesn't really ask you to apply concepts, but simply know them. She sometimes speeds through lectures but they're all recorded! Her problem sets and practice exams are almost identical to the actual exams as well. Definitely take this class!

this class really solely depends on your TA and who you sit with the first few classes. Your TA will be the only face you see for the entire semester unless you go out of your way to meet with Professor Mohan, then depending on the type of group you get or specific group mates will determine how fast you get work done.

Like someone said before, a lot of these reviews are harsh. Dr. Fox is reachable by email and does care about your learning. I'm convinced that everyone who rates Dr. Fox poorly does not put in the work that is needed for this course. Yes, there is a lot of memorization. I actually prefer it is this way because I feel way more prepared for professional schooling as someone who wants to work in healthcare. Also, it's an Anatomy and Physiology course... it is going to be a lot of work.
