The hard part about labs that I think people struggle with is that there are no out of class assignments besides the Pre-Lab assignments. You have to be self-motivated to do well and put in the work. The study guides are helpful, and so are the many many resources on the ELMS page. If you are reading this and planning on taking 201/202, don't be scared, if you get it the mindset it will be bad, it will be bad. Put in the work and tune out other people's negativity and you will be ok.

Dr Opoku is exactly who you want to take for anatomy. I took her for BSCI 201 as well, and the class is very easy once you figure out how to study. Take her "study guides" as gospel and you will do just fine.

Dr. Carleton is super sweet and she genuinely cares about her students. I just found these topics to be very boring and I had a hard time paying attention, since there aren't a lot of concepts- its more of "this plant is different than that plant which is the same as this other plant" which can be very dull. The cheat sheets are genius, she doesn't drop exams anymore, and homework is basically completion. the lectures can be very fast (60 slides in 50 minutes) and you really don't need all the info she gives. i'd recommend going back through the lectures and writing down the key things. memorize the concept checks, homework, and GAE's and you'll be okay! i thought the first midterm was really hard (but to be fair it was also my first ever exam in college) + the 2nd + 3rd midterms were both doable and pretty easy! bring an energy drink to class!

Do NOT take her. She reads off her slides, makes the exam extremely hard for no reason, and makes the exam questions confusing to trip us up. She doesn’t care about you passing the class I feel like she’s literally trying to do the opposite. And she confuses herself mid lecture and would asks for us to clarify what she just said. She also does so many mess ups in the exams. Like mid exam she will tell us a question was written wrong too and sometimes won’t give us grace for that question. Overall terrible professor for an already hard subject.

For those considering taking the class because of the high grade distribution, DO NOT BE FOOLED. I spoke with MULTIPLE TAs at both the undergraduate and graduate levels. The reason the grade data looks so high is that the exams were all ONLINE and OPEN BOOK for many, many semesters. Now that all exams are closed-book and in-person, the average grade is now in the B+ range. IT IS NOT EASY to get an A without stressing out of your mind. Now for my review: This class was genuinely not worth the amount of effort I put in and the stress it caused. I am a chemistry major, Pre-med (thus took this class), and this was the MOST time-consuming thing I had this entire semester. Not even research or Orgo 2 took this much energy out of me. You work in a group of 4 with the most incompetent people the whole sem (one of my group mates literally contributed nothing, and another just used ChatGPT the entire time) for a MAJORITY of the busy-work assignments. I wouldn't even have issues with busy work if it were like a worksheet or something related to the topics at hand, but having to work MULTIPLE times a week on a meaningless assignment with TROGLODYTES for a topic covered a MONTH ago, when we are doing something entirely different in the lecture, is insane. The "flipped classroom" layout leads to people not watching lecture videos for months on end, and the lab work doesn't even help you learn the concepts that well most of the time. The lab is basically just "can you read instructions" and "can you analyze research articles about random microbiology topics." The exams are also something I have a bone to pick with, because there was absolutely no practice for any of the exams. Granted, however, if you keep up with the videos and lecture stuff, you will probably do pretty well on the exams, and the exams are the most grade-determining assignments. The first exam was super free, but subsequent exams just got worse and worse. The second exam had an average so bad Dr. Tran had to curve by giving everyone 10 points (dub for me, but if you had C on the exam, it didn't do much for you). The final, which I just took today, was literally just the hardest parts of every single midterm plastered into one exam and you had to relate it to the new material. NO CONSISTENCY AT ALL. I wouldn't even be mad if the exams were slightly harder, but at least make them all similar so we know what to expect man. ALL IN ALL: Worst part of this class is the busy work. I maintained a 97 in organic chem 2 with no problem but this class's formatting and work is somehow 4x worse on my mental. Exams basically determine your grade, but they aren't the worst part by far. Take this class only if you need to, or if you really really like microbio and don't want to take the upper-level class for it. The A wasn't even that free, and it was way too much stress for this stupid class. The prof isnt bad, this overall is just a review of the terrible class layout, format, and assignments.

The material in this class is genuinely interesting, and Dr. Frauwirth does an excellent job breaking down complex topics into clear, easy-to-understand explanations. His slides are very clean and include a lot of diagrams, which really help with visualization. I felt like this course was essentially a summary of BSCI 170 and selected topics from BSCI 222, with some additional new material mixed in. Dr. Frauwirth also records all lectures on Panopto, which is extremely helpful for rewatching content. To study for exams, I would find a premade Quizlet and split-screen it with the Panopto recordings. I went through each lecture, added any missing information to the flashcards, and then drilled them until everything was memorized. This approach was usually enough for me to perform well on the exams. Studying for the final exam requires a bit more effort since it covers material from the entire semester. I reviewed around 600 flashcards and went back through all of my exams from earlier in the semester. The exams themselves include multiple-choice, short-answer, and one long essay question. Relying heavily on flashcards helped me get a 98% in this class. Another major plus is that there are many opportunities to earn additional points, such as TopHat clicker questions, lecture quizzes, “Cell Biology in Everyday Life” activities, and lab points. The lab portion of the class largely depends on your TA. My TA was amazing and graded very generously, but in my experience, most TAs are fairly lenient. Since the lab is worth 200 points, this can significantly boost your overall grade. Dr. Frauwirth also offered around 15 points of extra credit during my semester, including making one quiz extra credit and assigning a diffusion activity. Another important thing to note is that you don’t need to read the textbook. Overall, I found this class to be a relatively easy A for an upper-level biology course.

I think he did a good job teaching the course overall. The class was very structured and easy to follow, which made the material more approachable. My main issue was that the exams were fairly difficult and made up a large portion of your grade. Going into the course, I felt the material was straightforward and digestible, but the first exam made it clear that he was testing very specific details rather than focusing on broader concepts. That first exam had a lasting impact on my grade for the rest of the semester. And while it is possible to recover, it still weighs heavily overall. I would strongly recommend studying thoroughly for each exam. Even when the material seems easy, there are many specific details that can be tested, and a deep understanding is necessary to earn full points. It is also important to pay close attention to the experiments, as he often tested us on our ability to recognize experimental setups, interpret conclusions, and even design experiments of our own on the exam. Overall, I think he was a good professor who genuinely wanted students to understand the material. Though at times, the emphasis on memorizing detailed information made the course more challenging than it needed to be rather than focusing on general concepts alone.

Dr. Wu is a very supportive professor who truly cares about her students. The class is hard, and goes to over some pretty complicated lab techniques like melting curves for qPCR, but so long as you know how to apply what you learn, and take good notes, you will be fine on the exams. I highly recommend attending her office hours as she is the type of teacher make an effort to connect with her students. Whenever I went, she always checked in to see if I fully understood the concept even when there were 15+ people in her office. She also offers exam review to earn points back on the first exam and a extra credit presentation at the end of the semester. So if you put in the effort you will get a good grade!

Found her lecture style to fit my style of learning very well. She was very nice and used lots of non-chemistry examples to help you understand the material. There is weekly homework, but it was actually helpful to do and grades very quickly. Gave lots of example problems and even practice exams (old exams) with keys to help you study. The only downside is she only gives you a periodic table for the exam, so you had to memorize everything else, and you can't use a notecard while for other professors for this class, their students had to memorize less content, and it was given to them. Lectures weren't recorded but attendance isn't mandatory, so you'd need to get notes from a friend if you miss class. The discussions weren't mandatory, BUT I highly recommend going to them as the TA when I took the class was extremely helpful and went over content that helped you understand it better. You also could go to any of the discussions as long as they had space. There were 3 exams and a cumulative final with no drops. Overall, I really enjoyed learning from her, but you do need to put in the work to get a good grade in this class.

Class is pretty disorganized and the pre and post lab quizzes are difficult but doable. The labs are graded by TAs but you don't know the rubric so it's hard to get full points on them. The class experience itself really depends on your TA.

If you have him, take advantage of the online textbook review option on the homework website it basically saved me when I couldn't decipher the slides and it basically teaches you the stuff that will appear on the exams, as the slides have a lot of filler info that isn't brought back up ever again. I honestly learned more during my discussions than during his lectures so kudos to the TAs. Bonus points for the practice exams being basically carbon copies of the next exam, but doesn't make them any easier though. Tip: start memorizing the required memorization materials as soon as you can, there is a lot you are required to memorize and if you don't it will bite you in the butt during exams.

The professor for this class doesn't matter a lot because you won't see them unless you go to office hours. That being said, GO TO OFFICE HOURS. She gives a 45 minute presentation about how to do the lab report during her office hours. She gives you the calculations for the lab report and answers questions. The lab manual is confusing and it is hard to understand what many questions are asking for, but it is much easier when you go to office hours. Also, this class will take a lot more time than a 1 credit class should, but that's the chemistry department's fault.

Dr. H is an amazing professor! She’s so organized, approachable, and willing to help. Her lecture guides are so helpful; I’d upload them to my iPad and follow along during lecture so I wouldn’t have to worry about writing everything down. She also recorded lectures this semester, which was super helpful because I would re-watch every lecture and wouldn’t stress if I missed something important she said during the actual lecture. She also posts practice problem sets that she makes, along with answer keys and video explanations of certain problems. I don’t think I would have done so well without these! She is also so friendly during office hours; even after I asked the same question multiple times, she’d explain the answer to me in different ways until I understood. Definitely take advantage of her office hours and do the practice problems because this is a very hard course. I studied for hours daily and still had a lot of questions, but Dr. H was so supportive and acknowledged my hard work! You can tell that she really cares about her students because she tells us that she wants us to succeed! Her exams were difficult but fair for the most part. The only complaint I have is that she did not post her old exams, but given the rigor of her practice problem sets, I’m not sure how much more mock exams would have even helped. I’d take more courses with her if I could!

horrible ahh 1 credit lab. taq's are IMPOSSIBLE. genuinely no idea what was going on for any of them. average was a 5/20 so im really struggling to understand why they're even administered if everyone fails. i guess it helps if ur in her lecture, but personally i was not and i was taking these quizzes on topics i hadn't even learned yet. the plq's are also really hard some weeks. GO TO TA OFFICE HOURS THEY WILL HELP, but honestly it all depends on which TA is grading them that week, some are nicer and more forgiving than others. the lab itself was fine me and my partner made stuff up half the time and no one cared, as long as u looked like u were busy. curve was really good. i had an 85 raw and it was curved to an a, and i know someone who had a 68 and was rounded to a b-. i have heard shes very unapproachable if u ever have a problem, but my ta was very nice and understanding 99% of the time i asked her anything, but u dont get to pick ur ta so it's really all luck. honestly gl and study for those taq's to the best of ur ability- it will really help separate u from the average grades at the end of the semester

Awesome guy. I’m so glad I ended up with him even though I tried so hard to get Davis. His exams are so straightforward and just like the practice exams. He never gives trick questions and you’ll pretty much ace every exam if you attend lectures, because that’s when he tells you exactly what he’s putting on them. I had it so much better than people taking other professors, I would def recommend!!

This class was a night and day difference from CHEM232 with Koppel, which was a disorganized nightmare. Dr. Hirschauer made sure to post quality video recordings prior to labs so that we could prepare and understand the concepts behind what we were doing, she also corrected and clarified stuff from the lab manual which made the lab go more smoothly. The only thing that was unfair in this lab was the practical. Dr. S and the TA said to know everything we had been doing in lab but lots of questions on the practical were far more difficult than what we had been doing and there were no practice problems provided so no way to prepare. This practical was also a huge part of the grade, more than the practical in CHEM232. The curve is minimal. You can tell Dr. S is new to this as she really put in excellent effort unlike some other professors who have been doing this for a while.

This was my first time having Dr. Dixon as a professor, and I will say she's not as bad as her reviews make her to be. She is very straightforward, and she is definitely not going to tell you what you want to hear to make you feel better. Her class requires a LARGE commitment, which was sometimes very frustrating because it was a two credit class and it definitely didn't feel like it at times. Her 15 pt HWs were so tedious and took HOURS to do, but the worst part was you couldn't complete them until the night before because she was still teaching material for it that day or the CAN at 9 pm was teaching material on it. The class felt very disorganized, as we would spend two class periods on a unit then have to start a new unit, which isn't necessarily her fault but it was very rushed. She does offer office hours almost everyday, which I highly recommend going to. If you want her undivided attention then you should go on the earlier side for sure before it gets overcrowded and she gets overstimulated and frustrated with the overflow of questions. Her exams are definitely difficult and designed for you to be able to solve questions quickly, but a plus is that there was always 15 extra credit points built into the exam.
Literally a ray of sunshine. SO SWEET and is very helpful when it comes to questions. I love her so much; she is my everything. Take her!!!

Teaching & Materials: He is a good professor in terms of giving the content clearly and having a lot of recordings, slides, and practice to look at during the lectures and discussions. However, he was a bit monotone so every lecture I attended kind of went in one ear and out the other. Content Difficulty & Background: The content really was not that bad at all, but I didn’t take CSA in high school so I think seeing this for the first time might be the reason why a lot of people do poorly. Exams: The exams throughout the semester were fair for me, but I thought the final was much more difficult than the exams we saw during the year. Study Advice: Overall, I recommend reading through slides and watching through lectures to review. Practice exams/quizzes were way easier than the actual exams, so lowkey just focus on understanding the content, syntax, and definitions more than memorizing what’s on the practice exams because those concepts probably won’t be what’s on your actual exam. Overall Experience: I am taking him for 132 too, so I had a pretty good experience!

Herman's a decent instructor. He definitely covers all of the material you need to succeed in the class, but I've fallen asleep so many times in that class. I honestly didn't show up for most classes, and even though I did fine I would've been much better off just biting the bullet and going to class. He also didn't input grades for most of the projects until after finals, so I had no way of gauging how well I needed to do on assignments and exams. Otherwise, he does a good job at conveying everything you need to know for the class and for DSA in general. I agree with a lot of the negative points that people have brought up in the other reviews, but honestly I think his class is a hard, but fair class. Show up, read the lecture slides, do the (optional) homework, and you'll be set.
Larry Herman kindled my love for systems programming. He models what a lecturer should be: engaging and clear. I see now after many years that he's one of UMD's best.

Very boring lectures and sometimes doesn't explain the reasoning behind his work. You'll going to be doing a lot of self teaching compared to other classes because sometimes he'll mention an important topic or thing you'll need to know and never mention it again and sometimes skip it if its a step he taught. What makes it better is the lecture slides sometimes have no direct lesson or topic you pull out by looking at it. Instead you will need to go to his scanned pdf file of work done in class and scroll to find your answer you were hoping to get (Or sit there and open up the panapto recording and scroll through the hour and 15 minute video). Quizzes are relatively easy and thanks to the TA for babying our class or most would've struggled. The midterms are also really not like the exam or home works. They are a step above of what he'll teach or go over in class, some of it is already tricky but I really do not feel like spending hours everyday reteaching things that I need to get taught, not what I signed up. Takeaway: Knowledgeable dude but also so boring. Teaches like you already know all of the material. Do not take Teli for 250 unless you're into self teaching yourself a lot.

This is the first time I felt like I walked away from a class with genuine real world skills, and this is exactly what Max aims for. This class is completely what you make of it. If you do the bare minimum and want a free A from an elective, avoid. If you want to become a better Data Scientist, Max's course will take you to the next level. To me, the lectures felt like YouTube videos and I walked away having learned something new after every lecture. Max is very different from lecturers we are used to. He makes his exams extremely difficult to make you truly understand concepts instead of memorizing, but they get curved and you have a lot of opportunity for extra credit to make up for them. Tips to succeed: - go above and beyond on the projects and get creative with it, Max will give you a lot of extra credit and lets you put them on your resume - do every reading Max assigns and know the core concepts of them before exams, he'll ask related questions - expect really difficult exam. use the practice exams purely to test your knowledge rather than learn from. Much of the learning for me was watching YouTube videos to better visualize the concepts. - do NOT take if you're not interested in data science, but if you are, 320 with Max will be the best class you'll take in college - Attend lectures, they're super entertaining and gives you hints on the exams

Here is the thing, he really just isn't that good of a lecturer. He can be very disorganized, and he can forget to share vital information unless a student explicitly asks. I think his exams/projects were pretty fair. His projects can be a bit tough, but they certainly help you prepare for the exams so make sure to spend time on them.

As other reviews had stated, pretty good on the workload and the way the exams are similar, no curveballs. The projects all have bread crumbs so it's 80 percent copy and paste and 20 percent work. If anything his TAs are pretty decent and care easy to reach.

Ting is a very nice and kind prof and she really cares about her students. HOWEVER, her lectures are atrocious. She just reads of slides and writes over them with her mousepad so it is very messy. Additionally, her accent doesn't help either, so going to lecture and trying to pay attention is so hard. If you have Ting with 351 and Justin(the goat) is teaching, do yourself a favor and look at his notes and go to his lectures. I only went to tings lecture on the first day, exam review, and exam days. Moving on to exams, you will want to take her (if she is coteaching with justin) because her exams were easier than justins and more straightforward, no curveballs, and she grades leniently. Even for homework, I forgot to submit something once and she let me submit it late (whereas justin didnt let my friend submit late). Overall, she is a very nice and caring person but her lectures are not it whatsoever.

Like others are saying, he is a very kind teacher and wants his students to succeed, but he CANNOT teach. The course content is not particularly difficult to understand, but Yoon's lecturing and lecture notes are terrible. I don't even know if he has actually contributed to the lecture notes. They seem to just be copy-pasted paragraphs/examples from the textbook and previous professors' lecture notes. He sometimes will write examples on the board (which you will only be able to see if you sit in the first two rows), but then keeps writing over the examples with more examples until his work illegible. Even then, he doesn't fully explain his thought process, which leaves students more confused. You will sit in his lectures and not understand anything, then go home and read the textbook for 30 minutes or an hour and understand the content just fine. The projects are fine. If you start at least 1 or 2 days early, you can probably finish them with a 100%. There is a curve.

Professor: He does have a stutter, but if you pay attention you will have no trouble understanding him. This does however make his responses to questions slower than normal. He will also give tips on how to do well in his class and stuff like extra non graded assignments if you need more practice if you ask him. Coursework: Projects are very difficult. Start early (no really.) on all of the projects and be prepared to ask for help from the TA's. Exams are medium. He grades hard, but his cut offs are low. So even if you do bad on one test you can easily make it up. If you study you can do well on the tests. But studying can be a problem if you get behind on a project (projects are sometimes due 3 days before the exam date). Grades: He curves the tests and does something with the projects (I did badly on a lot of them yet still passed the class). He will not give you any extra credit or extra assignments if your doing badly. If you fail you fail. Bottom Line? It will take a lot of work to do well or even pass this class. However you will learn a lot about OS's. Its also looks good on the resume and can give you a idea of how good of a programmer you are. Not recommended for a senior class unless you need 4 credits.

Yizheng was really nice when I talked to her and willing to explain things to help; frequent pauses were made at lecture to ask for questions, and there were always a few active students who were engaged and had interesting conversations. A LOT of the class did not attend regularly (probably in part because the exams mostly graded on slides) but there were good explanations of how the relevant architecture and network protocols led to vulns and i think everyone who actually went to class did well in it. Abt the negative reviews below, I think the projects were relatively straightforward with a good autograder for the parts that were autogradeable. I will start this review by affirming that Justin is one of the best lecturers at all of UMD, and going to his lectures is the best way to experience the professor. On top of that, he has some of the most thorough online study material, which covers everything he lectures about, and more. He answers questions through email and piazza, and if you score poorly on an assignment, it's rarely due to ambiguity (I would say never, but his 351 exams had many poorly phrased questions that were revised mid-exam). Onto the structure of the class, this is where things become controversial. If you are in the third of UMD students that went to an MCPS high school, the class structure will be very familiar. There are seven total midterms, at least one being dropped. This means a midterm every other Friday, including the second, and last Friday of the semester. The course starts at full speed, and finishes at full speed. The entire semester is midterm season. There are numerous upsides to having this many midterms though, which other students fail to point out. Each exam is only worth 11% of the grade, and only covers two weeks of material. This puts much less weight on any individual exam, and I personally got a B on multiple exams and still finished the class with a high A. The constant studying does cause occasional burnout, but it also prevents the midterm season cramming that many students tend to do, and prevents you from falling too far behind. Justin is an amazing lecturer, and the midterm schedule may sound daunting, but the condensed test material really helps prevent bad midterm habits.

Dr. Truman is awesome. I've honestly had a blast, and that's largely due to how she runs the course. I don't think I'm particularly smart (or math-y), but I've found she makes the content not only accessible, but exciting as well (looking to future semesters). In particular, some of the stuff I find super helpful: - focuses on building intuition for what we're doing, and is happy to slow down and/or reexplain as needed. for more challenging chapters, we'd take it even slower than usual (1 week+ per chapter). - building off the last point, she really values understanding over semantics/the minutiae. The review below mine is correct that she doesn't curve, but that's because there's a curve built into the class! The majority of the points earned outside of quizzes/exams are completion-based, and even on the quizzes and exams the grading again mostly (~70%) focuses on understanding (rather than punishing algebra mistakes or a skipped minor step). this is something she actually emphasizes throughout the course, eg encouraging people to at least write a solid outline of the given proof and define variables to get partial credit if nothing else/the approach isn't jumping out. - the more or less weekly groupworks/quizzes are fantastic. the problems she's written have been great for both consistently challenging my understanding and reminding me of definitions/theorems/techniques I should probably spend more time on (and during the groupwork, she and her TA walk around the class, interacting/helping groups as needed work through the problems) - office hours are a great resource. she knows the common points of confusion for both course material and the homeworks, and is always happy to give that little (or big) hint to help you continue to progress through it. furthermore, she also has a pretty active Piazza class which she encourages people to post on as needed for homework hints, quiz/exam review, or just clarification. - i said it above but she really is just awesome. she's super personable, willing to negotiate deadlines if you have something pop up, and is just generally excited about the class. i know it's probably the millionth time she's covered the material, and yet she still brings energy and enthusiasm to every single one of her lectures. My advice (for anyone planning to take this class) would be to 1. take it with Dr. Truman (duh) 2. lighten your semester coursework if possible - this class is the foundation for the higher level math classes you'll take, it's worth the investment now to truly learn the material (vs just skating by) 3. start early on the homework - some psets can be long, all will be challenging, and the earlier you start the more time you have to get help in OH (and bonus) a number with two as a factor != an odd number (hint hint)

Like the 12/02/24 review says, the prof doesn't really give us example problems of the material when we are first introduced to it. He also does sometimes skip steps in his lectures and makes some things sound obvious when they are not. The title of the class "Applied Harmonic Analysis: An Introduction to Signal Processing," can be somewhat misleading. The exams and lectures are mostly theoretical and the homework include some theory and some application (mainly in the form of MATLAB coding). I'll break down each of these 3 components: Lectures: Pretty theoretical especially towards the middle and end. Expect to know linear algebra pretty well (Math240 material, idt Math405/401 is necessary). Czaja is a good lecturer though in that his lectures are very structured and easy to follow. He posts his notes online and his notes are very detailed (almost too detailed, but like one reviewer said, he sometimes writes certain things are "easy to see" when they aren't). You should still go to class though because he does say things in lecture that aren't in the notes Exams: This is what most people have mixed feelings about. Like previous reviewers mention, if you can see the trick/gimmick on each question, the exams are easy, otherwise the exams can be tough. This, on top of the fact that the prof doesn't go over many examples/doesn't make practice exams, means the only "real" way to study for these exams is to try stuff out on your own and study the lecture notes rigorously. While there are some problems in the profs lecture notes that do help, some exam questions will catch you off guard and there's no real way to expect it. Averages on exams are in the 60-70% range. Homeworks: Mostly chill, some are theoretical but not egregious and others are just implementing stuff in MATLAB. Studying the homeworks can sometimes help for the exams too. Pretty sure most of the class did well on the homeworks Additional Info: His grading is so that your lowest 2 homeworks get dropped and lowest midterm (out of 3) gets dropped. For Fall 2024, he again implemented the policy where you can take the grade of all 3 midterms and the first 8 homeworks as your final grade, and not take the final. However, for Fall 2024 our third midterm was NOT take home (and was also the day we came back from Thanksgiving Break). TLDR: If you care about/enjoy the theoretical math that propels signal processing and data representation techniques, this class might be for you. If you don't mind spending time on your own investigating these theoretical aspects, this class is for you. Else, I can understand why some people are frustrated with the way this class is taught and you might be better off taking something less stressful.

He isn't (in my experience) *explicitly* dismissive of student questions or concerns, but he just doesn't really try.

She is the best physics course professor I've had. She knows how to teach and has done an excellent job crafting this course's sequence and experience. This course was easier than other physics courses, but it was a nice break from tediously long derivations and gut-wrenchingly difficult exams. If you put in anything more than 1 hour a week for this course you are guaranteed an A.

Extremely lazy lectures. Slides are direct copy from the book but without the care and the detail. She also stumbles through HER own slides like she doesn't know what she's talking about. She is clearly very smart and is an expert in astroparticle physics experiments, meaning she is obviously well-versed in the subject. But she absolutely fails to convey that enthusiasm and knowledge through her lectures. We used some god-forsaken copyrighted material from some other university for our discussion session activities, which meant that she could not post the solutions on elms at the risk of being sued. She said she would have the solutions available at TA office hours but they did not, in fact, have the solutions. The homeworks were graded so slowly. I mean what's the point of getting a hw I submitted a month ago to be graded now? I don't completely blame the TAs because they had to hold office hours, show up for discussion sessions, etc. I think they should hire more TAs or reserve 1 of the 3 for just grading purposes.

Professor Jacobson has a very good approach to PHYS402. In my personal experience, the course was well taught at a perfect level of difficulty. The material we were taught was very relevant to modern research. The only thing that I was not a fan of was he skipped certain important topics like Bloch's theorem and scattering theory.

I've had Shawhan for 273 and now 410; he is the nicest and most understanding physics professor I've met, and he made my life a lot less stressful. No lie, both of these classes were difficult and took a bit of time, but I'm pretty sure that'd be true regardless of professor. The great thing about Shawhan is that he will work with you and around your schedule to make things work. I was out sick for a week around midterms, when I came back he was really the only professor that was flexible about makeup times, letting me take the midterm 1.5 weeks later and turn in the homework a week late. I'd email him about missing class or something and he'd be actually concerned and wanting to help out; he genuinely cares about his students and wants to see them achieve. He's very organized, records lectures and posts notes, and 410 followed pretty closely with the textbook which made it easier to learn and study outside of class. Homeworks are fair, a lot of practice so sometimes it's a bit tedious just having to do it. He does take attendance ~every other day, but it makes up only 4% of your grade I think. There isn't a lot to say about lectures, if you've made it this far you'll probably get the material (and 410 isn't as bad as other courses like 402); he's an average lecturer but goes through examples in class which is helpful. If it's an intro physics course I can understand the complaints about material going over the head. Overall good professor and love the guy, helped me a ton this semester and I won't forget it

Davoudi is a decent professor, she gets the points across well and uploads all her videos and notes on time. However, she gives incredibly difficult and long homework assignments and has very little flexibility. She would often add 3 or more problems to an assignment in the middle of the week, which could add hours of extra work depending on the section. Her exams are very difficult but I thought they were all fair except for one, where she did not test on most of the material we covered. Still, she delivered the content on pace and pretty clearly.

The class is the easiest math class probably ever. Look as long as you know how to do basic math and understand really anything then you should get a good grade. The professor while he is very strict, he does it so we actually do good. This is why exam averages were always above 80%, now if you don't like that he rambles about phones and whatever then that is your problem. Look go to GSS study sessions, focus like you're supposed to and you do good. There is no reason you can't do good unless you don't want to.

He's not the worst professor, and a lot of the reviews below are probably a little harsh. Early in the semester it was a little rough, with him leaning into theory on the harder side, but he began using more example problems to clear up concept confusion. He gave homeworks that were definitely tough, but began to give lots of bonus point questions on them. He also curved every exam to an 83 average. I think he can definitely improve on his teaching, but it is definitely possible to do well in the class if you practice concepts.

This course was kind of rocky at first but if you do the practice problems and have all of the important formulas written down on a formula sheet that you are allowed to bring into the exam you will be fine.

I'm giving a 5 because I think an accurate rating should lie within 3.5-4.0. Teaching: Overall, he's really sweet and playful. I personally found his lectures enjoyable to listen to because of his fun personality. His accent is not bad at all, even if u have trouble deciphering it, following his lecture slides while listening will make it a ton easier. Grading: For quizzes, we had them approx once every two weeks (although some of them got cancelled) and the problems were pulled straight from his practice problem sets. The difficulty was quite easy, nothing else to be said really. His first midterm had a median of 73 but I genuinely think that's just because most students didn't even come to lecture and only cared to pass this class for major requirements. The problems were reasonable and there was a bonus problem too. Students seemed to do much better for the second midterm, the median was a 98.5 lol. For the final, he was super generous. Most of the problems were from previous quizzes and the ones that weren't were from his practice problems. He even gave a ton of hints/clarifications for how to do them during the final. Just go to lectures and understand the material and for an easy A. Workload: No homework because he said there's no point now that AI can do all of it for u. Lectures were optional to attend.

I had a very disappointing experience in this course. The professor was often rude and dismissive toward students, frequently refusing to explain material by saying, “you should already know this.” As a result, I never felt comfortable asking questions when I didn’t understand something. Her grading was unusually harsh, with significant point deductions for very minor or seemingly irrelevant issues. Additionally, she regularly made mistakes on the board and reacted defensively when students attempted to seek clarification. One incident that illustrates the disruptive classroom environment involved her refusing to return an exam to a student, wrongly insisting they were impersonating someone else—even after verifying their student ID. Overall, the atmosphere was not conducive to learning, and I left the course feeling discouraged and less confident in my mathematical abilities due to the frequent verbal criticism in class.

horrible professor. her exams have almost nothing to do with lecture material and are unnecessarily hard and she is also very harsh on grading. Exam 2 and the final exam were extremely disorganized and everything about this class was just confusing and made way harder than it needed to be. For being a SAS programming class, I feel like I did not learn anything about SAS. There was also poor communication throughout the semester, we had no idea what our grades would be because of the poor averages on midterms and the final. This class was by far the worst class I have taken in my 4 years here.

Great professor. Really cares about his students, passionate and deeply knowledgeable about his subject. Makes himself available to students during office hours. Really kind professor too. Class work is fair - challenging but not overwhelming. Enough to help you learn and grow. Has patience of gold. Love him.

Hans is actually the lab coordinator but he ended up teaching my section instead of a TA so if you're in the same situation you got lucky! I thought he was a super nice professor who always tried to make the lab a little more enjoyable for everyone. He responds to emails super fast and leaves comments for why he took off points on each assignment so you don't make the same mistakes. Some assignments were harder than others, but none were horrible.

Dr. Keller is super nice and the class environment was pretty chill overall. Lectures can be somewhat difficult to follow at times, but they generally give a decent amount of necessary info. His philosophy is that he doesn't want to add unnecessary confusion and explains only the information that is critical for students' understanding. In terms of assignments, there are simulations throughout the semester that vary in length (expect to spend at least an hour on most of them, followed by a short check for understanding at the end); Worksheets (pretty much weekly), w/ in class work time; Weekly 10 point quizzes due every Friday (non-retakeable). These don't necessarily make or break your grade but a few poor grades on the quizzes does add up quickly. Exams went from going really well for me to not as well about halfway through the semester (went from higher end of class average to lower end, hence why I ended up with a C+). The content at the beginning was relatively easy to grasp with minimal studying, but got increasingly more overwhelming/content-heavy later on. Attendance isn't mandatory but there are a TON of extra credit clicker questions that can help your grade in the end. Slides and lecture recordings are always posted in case you miss class, though. Overall, the class wasn't horrible and Dr. Keller is amazing and super passionate about what he teaches, but it is a pretty large amount of content in a short amount of time.
This class is totally dependent on your TA, but Dr. Mohan is super organized and makes it easy. This is how a 1-credit course should be and all labs should be this way!

Dr. Goytia is an incredible professor, and anyone at UMD who needs to take BSCI201/202 would be lucky to have her. Anatomy and Physiology is difficult in general, but Dr. Goytia offers many resources, a very generous amount of extra credit (which frankly I didn't even need), and a cheat sheet for BSCI201. She has an enthusiasium for teaching that made me look forward to goig to her class. GO TO LECTURE. They are posted in this class and sometimes I would skip but the material sat better with me by going to lecture. The exams were very fair, and even though I hear they are a bit harder than the other professors who teach this course if you go to lecture an put in the work outside of class you will do good and it will set you up for success in 202 or whatever program you are taking this course for. You really do have to put in the work for this class, these are not exams that you can cram for or put everything on the cheat sheet and expect to do well. I strongly suggest following the study schedule that she shows you the first day of lecture. The practice tests were very accurate and helpful. I didn't go to GSS so I really can't speak on that but going to office hours is very helpful, and even doing the GSS worksheets at home. Overall 1000/10 take Dr. Goytia!!

I've taken Goytia for both 201 and 202 and can without a doubt say she is an absolute gem of the UMD BSCI department. I've had great professors before, but her level of understanding, passion, and care for her students and anatomy itself is truly remarkable. Dr. Goytia wants her students to succeed more than any professor I've seen, she understands this subject is difficult and requires time/dedication, and offers students many ways to make up points (extra credit that allows you to see what you got wrong, multiple attempts on quizzes, offers old exams for studying, and more)! Her lectures can get a bit complicated, but she mostly tests you on big picture ideas, and I think she gets especially excited talking about certain topics (because a lot of the processes are really cool). I have and will continue to recommend her to anyone looking to take 201 and 202 in future semesters, Dr. Goytia truly is one of the best.

I wouldn’t take this class unless you really need to. There’s an intense amount of content, and it’s not just memorization, you have to actually understand it well enough to apply it to new situations on the exams. Also, ignore older reviews saying you can drop an exam, I took the course fall 2025, and that was no longer an option. That said, Dr. Carleton is genuinely very kind and responsive over email. She clearly wants students to succeed and is a great person overall. The lectures are recorded, but they’re very information-heavy, so I personally found it much easier to watch them on my own time and pause to take thorough notes. There are graded in-class activities where you get full credit just for showing up, and the homework is completion-based, which helps balance things out. The real challenge is the exams, there’s no test bank, and the in-class activities don’t really prepare you for the free-response questions. Still, if you put in the time to study, you can definitely do okay.

An HONEST review from an AVERAGE Student: I honestly feel like the people who complain about this course really just never want to learn or do work. Unlike previous reviews, I have not taken orgo or upper level BSCI courses, and this was my introduction to it. With that being said I still got an A in the course. The Course is very content heavy and exams were hard. Exams being hard is expected in a BSCI class though, as it is not pure memorization but rather actually learning the content. Yes there were trick questions, but the same can be said about any upper level course. Dr. Mutz was very open to questions after class and in office hours. There were many opportunities to gain free points to boost your grade, through both lab and quizzes. The class was not easy by any means, but the course was extremely fair. Dr. Mutz is an amazing professor who seems to get a lot of unfair hate due to students wanting to be lazy or just never putting in effort to understand the concepts (just memorizing words will not get you far in this course). I am very grateful to have taken Dr. Mutz rather than the other prof who apparently did not even teach the correct content. Overall, Dr. Mutz is good at lecturing and wants students to actually learn about what she is passionate about - good qualities about any professor with content you actually want to learn. I feel like I actually learned so much about genetics in this course and am prepared for future BSCI classes - Thank you Dr. Mutz!

Dr. Tran is clearly passionate about her subject, which is refreshing compared to many other professors at UMD. However, the current class structure leaves much to be desired. Lectures often feel unproductive, as little useful material is provided to help students succeed on exams. There is a lack of helpful resources, such as study guides or previous exam materials, which makes exam preparation more difficult than it needs to be. At times, it can even feel like the grading system is set up to be unnecessarily challenging. I hope Dr. Tran considers being more lenient on the final, and for future classes, I strongly recommend rethinking the course setup to better support students' learning and make the experience more manageable.

Dr. Frauwirth is the best!! He is so approachable especially during his office hours, and he will always answer your questions in person or through email. His exams can sometimes be challenging on the multiple choice section, but the free response are very fair as long as you pay attention and study. He will literally tell us during class "When I ask you on the exam... you should say this..." He is very transparent about what to know for the exam and what to skip. In office hours he once said " I don't want you to memorize every single thing and lists of things that you can look up on google, but I want you to understand the main ideas and their importance." Lab is very dependent on your TA, but everyone typically does really well as long as you show up and put in effort on the assignments. Your exams are also graded by the TA so that could affect how much partial credit you get for the written portions of the exam. Overall, this class was definitely my favorite class that I have taken as a biology major besides BSCI170. We learned the typical transcription/translation and other foundational units of biology that you cover in every past class, but it never felt like anything we were learning was a waste of time or useful small details of information that we would never need to know again. I would highly encourage taking this class. You will definitely get the grade that you deserve through this class. I think it's very doable to get an A coming from a student that is never within the top percent of their STEM classes.

This professor is all nice on the outside but is harsh in the inside. His lecture slides are just images with little descriptions and tell us to "Figure it out". He does not provide any directions or assistance. His worksheets are impossible to complete in the 75 minute time constraint. His exams are hard but the final exam was worth 30% of our grade and some of the materials we discussed for one lecture was worth over 30 points on the final. Overall I do not recommend this professor at all.

Dr. Wu is an incredibly kind and supportive professor. The material in BSCI410 is challenging and fast-paced, but lectures are well-organized, and the exams are fair and application-based. She is very approachable in office hours, explains concepts clearly, and provides helpful resources throughout the semester. The extra credit opportunities are especially helpful if an exam doesn’t go as expected. If you’re interested in genetics and willing to put in the effort, this is a very rewarding class.

Dr. Schech is a phenomenal lecturer and the best CHEM131 professor by far! When she goes through lectures, she uses lots of analogies, makes things simple to understand, and doesn't do as much historical background and more useless stuff like some of the other professors do. She records every lecture, and posts her notes too which are useful! Overall, I found that most midterms, besides the last, and the final were all super easy. On top of that, she gives you plenty of resources in discussion with the TA to practice, and even a practice exam with a key. She curves the class too! She truly sets everyone up for success and is such a positive light for everyone.

If you don't put any effort into this class, then call it wraps. In order to do you well in this lab you need to put ALL your effort into the pre-lab quizzes, lab reports, and ESPECIALLY the reflection quizzes. The pre-lab quizzes were sometimes hard, only because topics weren't covered in lecture yet, but very doable. Lab reports should be an easy A, except for the time you get graded by a TA who prays on your downfall and takes off petty points (I swear some TAs have massive egos and need a reality check). On that note, the TA that leads your lab is not always the person who grades your lab reports, however, if you had a GOATED TA like I did, then you shouldn't have to worry about it because they can easily look over you lab report and make any changes to the grading as needed. Something that WILL kick you in the ass is the reflection quizzes. Since they are only 2-3 questions if you get one question wrong your grade gets TANKED like fucking D-Day. Expect to get a 0 or 50 on a few. I ended up getting one 0, one 50, and the rest 100 because I locked in. At the beginning they were really hard and were designed to trip you up, BUT as the semester went on they got significantly easier. And if/when you get those low reflection quiz scores, getting really good grades on the lab reports will balance that. Dr. Guest ended up dropping the lowest reflection quiz, so she is goated for that. She also decided to drop the lowest lab report and pre-lab quiz which brought my grade to an A+. Overall, my tips to succeed in this course is to find a TA that actually cares, is willing to answer your questions, and go to their office hours for help on your lab report. Before you know it lab will be over and you will be FREE!!!

Andrei has a heavy accent and mumbles throughout his lectures, which makes them pretty much completely useless (I went about two times total). That being said, the online textbook (which you have to pay for and is expensive) is quite good, and the class can be self-studied from that. He has a more than reasonable curve policy, and his exams are very easy (especially compared to the other CHEM135 profs). He posts old midterms in ELMS, and they are literally the exact same as the exams you will have to take, making it easy for you to know if you are ready. Overall, the dude cannot teach at all but the exams make up for it somewhat in my opinion.

CHEM136 is definitely worth more than 1 credit, but that reflects the course, not the professor. Will you have to put in a lot of effort into the lab reports to do well? Of course. Will the professor and TAs help you? Absolutely! You'll almost never see her in the lab because her TAs run it for her, but my TA, Jonathan was the absolute best and he helped out a lot when I reached out over email, no matter how late I sent the email. I went to the weekly review sessions that she had about each lab, AND THOSE WERE WORTH IT! Go to her in-person review office hours each week and she will basically give you the answers for calculations in the lab. Once you start going every week, she just gets funnier and she's really nice to those who consistently go. The pre-labs are about 5 questions and you have 3 attempts and the highest score is kept, due the night before the lab. A lot of it is either from the lab manual or you can look it up online. Her last review exam was just a bunch of pre-lab questions together and you had two attempts to do it and she opened it for an entire week. I'm giving her a 4 instead of a 5 because the lab manual was poorly worded and even the TAs had trouble figuring stuff out at times. But overall, definitely a good professor for CHEM136 as long as you put in the time and effort for the lab reports!

imo Dr. Hong is a great professor and I'd recommend him highly. He explains things well, puts effort into making lectures interesting/entertaining, clearly cares about the students, and is just a chill guy. Some folks blame him for speeding through content - that's fair, but I feel like it's not his fault. OChem is just a hard class with a lot of material to pack into one semester. Going to class is not gonna be enough; no matter how good the professor is, you gotta familiarize yourself with the material on your own. Besides, I'd rather get through all the material a bit faster and have some time for review than be scrambling close to finals because we didn't cover the last couple topics in time. To his credit, Dr. Hong gives a LOT of practice material: between weekly homeworks, practice exams, past exams, past discussion worksheets, etc. (all can be found in ELMS), he makes sure students have many chances to grapple with material and really lock the concepts down outside of lecture. I know it's tedious but you should do that extra practice, it will be a huge help. (also, Dr. Hong seems to like reusing questions from practice worksheets/tests to reward you if you did them :D ) I should also mention that his TA / GSS leaders (Dennis / Ariana & Sophia) are super nice and helpful, I'd definitely recommend going to discussions / GSS if you want help with a particular topic, have questions about the material, or just want even more practice. Exams are not easy but they are definitely fair. Usually there'll be a few tricky questions but nothing egregious. He also emails a list of exam topics before every exam, so if you just follow that you should be good. I'd recommend going to all his lectures (as aforementioned I think he explains things clearly and thoroughly, plus he sometimes gives hints for bonus points) and sit in the front rows if you can (so you can hear him better, and so you can participate). TLDR: Dr. Hong is a very solid professor and a lovely person as well. If you lock in for lectures and use the resources he and his TAs provide, you'll definitely do great in his class.

As a 1 credit course, like the other reviews say, this class is a LOT of work and very disorganized. Oftentimes you will find yourself writing the same things in many different places. But really, it is not horribly difficult, just rather time consuming. Points go as following: 5 points for the pre-lab quiz (pretty straightforward if you read the procedure), 5 points for the notebook pages (pretty straightforward too), 20 points for the worksheets (straightforward as long as you did the experiment or the makeup), and 20 points for either the PLQ (post lab questions) or TAQ (theory and applications quiz)...and no, they are not as notorious as people say. All you need to do for PLQs to do well on them (coming from someone who repeatedly scored 90%+ on them) is to understand the procedure of the lab: not necessarily which chemicals were used, but the objective of the lab. Essentially, they are to apply the objective of the lab to a different set of chemicals, as a sort of "what if" situation. Office hours help A LOT. Sometimes they were very confusing, other times pretty easy. But do not ever wait last minute to do them, that's how you screw up. TAQs are like PLQs, but instead of having a week or two to do it, you have only 10 minutes in class. These...are horrible to say the least. Because they are so rushed, getting a 10/20 or above will feel like luck. Class averages for these being under 5/20 are no exaggeration. Overall, it is possible to do well in the course. You just need to be able to understand the objective of each procedure to pass.

I wish no bad feelings toward Dr. Isaacs. That being said, the current rating is too high/deceiving. Dr. Isaacs does put in some effort, but honestly, it seems minimal. The slides are mostly just reactions and mechanisms with barely any explanation or details we actually need for the exams. I get that we’re supposed to take notes ourselves, but there’s not much space on the slides, and he flies through the material fast that it’s easy to miss key points. He didn’t post most of the lectures, and there were only two midterms plus a ridiculously long final exam which means if you mess up one exam, you're cooked. The content is the usual overwhelming amount to memorize, which is typical for organic chemistry, but he adds more unnecessary information we need to know. For example, the nomenclature section on exams often required memorizing how to draw random molecules from scratch (and he wouldnt just tell us which 20 we should know…he would take random ones from the notes or book). This distracts from the important concepts we should focus on, and it doesn’t help for things like the MCAT either. I bet everyone has already forgotten them by now anyway. Not that this is unfair, but just a warning: there are already tons of reactions and mechanisms to learn, and he throws in tricky questions that require knowing minor details or exceptions about them. Exams are very difficult. The second exam was the only one that was reasonable in my opinion. Our final was the first year he did it in multiple choice format, and it felt harder due to the sheer number of questions and options. A lot of us ran out of time and had to guess on many questions. I would’ve much preferred fewer questions that required written answers. Also not that this was a big deal, but he lowkey abandoned us on finals day. Overall, Dr. Isaacs doesn’t teach as if students are learning the material for the first time. You’ll have to teach yourself or go to TA hours like everyday, which makes it very difficult to balance with other classes. Dr. isaacs section ended up being way more time-consuming and difficult than I expected, and I thought I knew what to expect after orgo 1. I don’t want to be too harsh, but it felt like everything was on us, and if we did badly, it was made out to always be our fault…but he could’ve done more such as review common issues/problems/concepts students struggle with on exams more frequently, provide more practice problems for the final, send out helpful advice and resources to the class, etc. I did appreciate him holding review sessions and trying to make the times available for everyone, but they were canceled many times and did not help much. At one point I just read the textbook like he told us to and did well, but it took so much time to do that +take notes + practice (i spent 140 hours studying for finals and passed) and I did not have the hours to do that for the entire semester. Also, just look at the withdrawal rate…it’s clearly not normal. The curve was large, but I think we should’ve gotten at least a slightly bigger curve, given the new final format and how low the average was. He also needs to add more graded assignments since the three exams are all that count. One bad day and you will be forced to drop. He’s not a bad lecturer and can explain things well, but other chemistry professors I had put in much more effort and care with their teaching methods, course materials, and helping their students succeed. Expect much sacrifice or suffering if you take this professor. I’m not exaggerating.

Dr. Hirschauer actually made an effort to periodically pop into lab sections to help around (including helping a student clean up shattered glassware so that the student could continue their experiment on time), which is more than I can say about any other lab coordinator. This is her first semester for 242 so she used the old curriculum, but I believe she said she will be writing her own in the future, so I don't know how things will change. There's definitely at least somewhat of a curve at the end of the semester because my 92% got bumped up to an A, but I don't know the exact cutoffs or anything. Overall, Dr. Hirschauer always tries her best to allow her students to succeed and is just so sweet to everyone.

Genuinely the worst teacher I have ever had in my entire academic life. 0 stars if that were possible. Anyone giving her more than one star is either a teacher’s pet or completely delusional. This class will consume your entire existence, say goodbye to your other courses, your sleep, and your sanity. Unless you want to live, breathe, and suffer through chemistry 24/7 while everything else in your life falls apart, DO NOT TAKE THIS CLASS WITH HER!!! Absolute nightmare of a professor.

Loved it! Labs were easy but interesting, and lab reports were time-consuming but also pretty easy because the instructions walk you through them pretty thoroughly. Dr. Schech is so sweet and her lectures are really well-done, and my TA (shoutout to Rachel) was the best! The exams were easy if you study (and take the practice exam!) so overall a great class. Also - I didn't take 271 (lecture) at UMD and had no trouble with this class, so don't be afraid to take 272 without 271.

Great professor. really chill guy and good at teaching. posts lecture recordings and slides as well as sample code to help. exams are hard and you have to handwrite code, but that's just what it is in cs. doesn't curve unless you are in between a letter grade then rounds up. 92.9 isn't a 93, but 89.6 is a 90. programming assignments are easy and a great grade booster (25% of grade). They also help with reviewing for exams and quizzes as the material tested with the code is what you're learning in class. Didn't go to office hours until final review, but he was helpful there too. Quizzes are announced and closed note. Labs are unannounced and open note, so go to discussion. Final was super easy compared to the midterms, was about 1.5 times the length of the exam but given double the time. Overall, if you can take him, take him. Easy to get at least an A-, even if you bomb exams. Kinda annoying he doesn't curve, but you shouldn't fail the class even without it, as long as you submit everything and show up to exams.

Larry Herman has a lot of quirks, and I can see why most people seem to dislike him; I, however, thought he was overall a good instructor. His lectures are well taught, and he explains concepts very well. Discussions are spent doing worksheets, which are occasionally graded for completion. He also will occasionally and randomly hand out graded worksheets during lectures--this, combined with the fact that he doesn't record lectures, means you should definitely attend as many classes as you can. His project descriptions are incredibly long and often repetitive, but this is also an advantage; you're essentially told exactly how to do each project in the description. I personally didn't find his exams to be challenging--anything he says in class or writes on the slides or handouts is fair game, and he will definitely test you on even things we spent the smallest amount of time on, but he gives a LOT of good exam prep, from the practice exams, the homeworks, and the discussion worksheets (he even admitted in lecture that he will sometimes pull exam questions from discussion worksheets, so definitely do the worksheets!). He has some negative quirks, such as not allowing electronics in class, having an interesting participation system, and being really touchy over being called a professor for some reason, but honestly the only strong negative I have for him is how incredibly long it took for everything to get graded. We had a total of 10 projects throughout this course, and by the time finals came around, we still only had the first three graded; it can be stressful, because you really don't know how well you're doing in the class if you can't know your grades until the very end. Overall: Good lecturer & exams are very passable once you understand his format, but he has a bunch of odd quirks and he's an INCREDIBLY slow grader. He's not the best instructor out there, but definitely not as bad as some of the other reviews have said. If you're forced to take his class, don't fret! Put in the work and you'll do fine. I'm giving him 4 stars because I can't give him a 3.5.
First exam took me from feeling like I'd get an A to feeling like "lets pray for a curve to a C-" even after doing great on the quizzes. Class is abuse.

Max when I catch you!!! Do not take this class with him I'm begging you. He is the most unserious professor I have come across. And yeah he's funny... i guess! But really and truly just take another professor it will save you the headache. A hard class like this you need a serious professor and max is not it I fear...

He will make you truly love data science. However, his exams tend to be quite challenging. tl;dr: If you are wary of group work or minor disorganization, then perhaps he might not be the professor for you, but otherwise, I think he was great. Difficulty (for a senior-level math class): 3/5. Topic Interest/Usefulness: 5/5. Course Materials & Organization: 4/5. This class was essentially flipped, which meant some troubles during COVID: It is much more likely for people not to show or not to participate when they're sitting, camera-off, behind a screen. In any case, when it operated properly, it went very well, and I won't dock him for a global pandemic reducing student participation. Essentially, we would have a worksheet every week or two to work through in small groups, with him popping in periodically to answer questions or provide guidance. Then, we would reconvene into the full session toward the end to go over what was on the worksheet. His exams were both take-home, and they were fair in their difficulty and scope, very comparable to the homework. Both exam and homework consisted of guided, long-form problems, often proving fundamental results or exploring a toy example. I generally prefer exams to be of this kind, perhaps with some quizzes on very basic material to check students are actually familiar with the content. The nature of the course content made it such that he could get away with this without worrying much about cheating. The two exams and homework essentially comprised the grade in equal 1/3 parts, except there was also a 5% participation grade. The exams and homework are longer than most senior-level math classes', but it is very light outside of that and the assignments are not particularly difficult; it is a class with relatively little theory, one where it is even easier than usual not to read at all, where perusing a completed worksheet for five minutes would catch you up on the essential information to do the homework, and the rest is your own perseverance and ingenuity. His arguments are not always the most polished. He seems to prepare mostly by having informally looked over the day's worksheet and then doing additional thinking in-real-time, which mostly led to clear, precise proofs because, of course, he knows the material very well (and indeed uses combinatorics in his research). Still, because of this, there were times where he had to develop arguments on-the-spot a few times, which is naturally a non-linear, somewhat clumsy process. He always eventually prevented a clean solution, however, and for some students, I suspect the humility of seeing their professor make some silly mistakes or have to take some time to think over basic material can be nice, as can just seeing the thought process and participating in it (he would welcome student ideas and discussion in the few times he briefly got stuck in this way).
