Would give him a 0 if I could. The Wendell Hill experience guarantees: 1. He tries to solve a problem on screen, but does it incorrectly, taking away time the next lecture to correct his mistakes (which was for a problem ripped straight out of the textbook!) 2. Has to "correct" some things in his slides from when he last taught this course (10 years ago!) 3. Mumbles a lot AND refuses to use a mic (in a lecture hall!) AND has horrible handwriting. Even if you are sitting in front row, 50% of the info will not be coherent. 4. "Walk us through derivations" by putting up symbols on the board and telling us to "turn the crank" (Thank you Professor Hill for walking us halfway through a textbook problem! PLEASE don't go through some problems similar to ones that show up on the midterms....) 5. Maybe was special case but Midterm 3 had 4 types (including a missing question???) 6. Literally saw some questions for the first time on the midterms 7. Participation grade (5% of total) was literally us writing our name on a piece of paper (RIP if you missed lecture that one random day) 8. Tried to get us to buy a clicker at start of semester, never used it at all. Bright spots: TAs were fine, taught me more in 30 mins than in the lectures. Gave pretty good exam and lecture reviews, though prepare questions to ask during it or they will just leave. Lowest midterm got dropped Generous curve (85+ is an A roughly) Cool demos if the equipment works (~50% of the time) Summary: Hill makes the class harder than it needs to be, just read the textbook and do some textbook/expert TA practice problems, ask the TAs questions during discussion.

I never actually met him, since this was just the lab section of Physics 260, but the labs were alright. Not too hard, but nitpicky with the grading. I liked that the final exam was online. Don't worry.

Buehrle was a good lecturer and made the content interesting. While he used generic slides, he usually used it for discussion and did his own practice problems. The class was pretty doable and didn’t feel rushed even though it was summer session. Exams were okay but it was hard to get a feeling of expectations. Quizzes were the worst part because they were mostly obscure theory that wasn’t covered in class. Pretty decent curve on exams. Despite some reviews, he’s a pretty good instructor but won’t do any miracles.

It takes a while to get used to his accent, but once you do he's a pretty good teachers. Lectures can be boring; i often did homework during lecture. However, he uses detailed powerpoints and will post them online so you can look over them. There are random lecture quizzes, but just for completing them you get a 9/15 so they help boost your grade a little. Also the weekly problems you get for hw are often taken right from the book, so take a look in the book to see if there is anything in there that might help you solve the problem. Also Min makes sure that students know he cares about their grade and wants to help them succeed, and this was good to have from a professor.

Dr. Turpen is the absolute BEST! The list of amazing things she does is quite possibly endless, but I will do my best to list them anyway! She adapts her lectures based on what would be most helpful for us, meaning she will completely derail her own lesson plans to have review days as needed, and she will still make sure to get us where we need to get to by the end of the course. The best educators are ones that are able to take students of varying levels and equip ALL of them with the knowledge they need by the end of the course, and Professor Turpen could very well be the best educator. She gives us practice exams with solutions and writes incredible homework that greatly enhances our learning. She never leaves a student behind and makes special relativity (which is not by any means an easy thing to understand) so digestible it might as well be ice cream. All because of Dr. Turpen, I was able to achieve a level of mastery and understanding with this material that I haven't really had since high school. I can confidently say that I understand modern physics in its entirety, and every single professor at UMD--nay, the WORLD--should be taking notes! Professor Turpen literally does research in physics education, so it makes sense that she's so awesome, and all of my wishes every time I blow out birthday candles--mine or somebody else's--will be for whatever physics professor I have next to have a fraction of the teaching talent that Dr. Turpen has.

I have nothing but praise for Dr. Hoffman’s PHYS401 course. Every element of this class was useful for learning the material. Homeworks were legitimately helpful for both learning and studying. Friday discussions repeatedly hammered concepts into my head until I genuinely understood them. The textbook choice was great. Exams were just the right level of difficulty. Dr. Hoffman even went the extra mile to post exams from previous years for us to practice with, which was a great study tool. I haven’t taken the final exam yet, but Hoffman said she’s willing to replace our lowest midterm grade with the final exam grade. If you have the chance to take PHYS401 with Dr. Hoffman, you should do so with no reservations!

Probably the worst professor I've ever had. He had unrealistic expectations of the students, a monotonous classroom experience, and did not provide nearly enough support to his students. His exams were purposeful attempts to fool students, a fact of his teaching strategy that he shared with us. Moreover, he made me really dislike QM, something I would have thought impossible. Avoid at all costs.

I didn't do well because I am. Professor Jacobson is one of the best professors I had. He answers students' questions through piazza almost 7/24, and his lecture is unique and clear. He also gives you notes written by him, basically a textbook. Probably you find it is hard to read, by it is very concise and include everything you need for this subject(just need a full insight to read). is class is very challenging, don't take the class with him if you just want an easy A. But if want to learn some real physics, definitely choose him.

He explains things well and knows the material extremely well. On top of that, he's a friendly guy who's willing to help his students in any way he can. He had this one inspirational lecture that actually made me want to go home and do some physics. He's an award winning physicist, which is great, but this means that he travels a lot and misses a lot of class. When he isn't in class (which was in total about a third of the semester), he has one of his two post docs teach the class. As a result, the class material gets really fragmented. This is the main reason I'm not giving him 5 stars. Homework takes forever and tests are difficult, but this is no reason to downgrade him. This is just a forewarning.

I am really happy that I had Professor Griffin for STAT100. He is extremely organized and gives plenty of opportunity for extra credit. There are two tests and a final exam which he provides plenty of resources to be very well prepared for. The class was SO easy and as long as you show up and put in minimal effort you will do great!

It was his first time teaching STAT400, and he didn't know how to format exams, curves, and lectures. He's a nice guy, though his lectures are pretty boring, and most people ended up skipping the lectures towards the end of the semester. The quizzes are simple(depending on the TA). I ended up skipping most of the lectures and going over the practice questions that he gave us, and did decently on most of the exams(around a 85% average). He also gives bonus points on homework towards the end of the semester, and some quizzes get dropped. The final exam was just a copy of the practice exam he gave us; some of the questions were exactly like the practice exam questions. From what I saw, most of the class felt good about the final and thought it was the easiest exam they had taken. I'm sure in the future his class will be more organized, and the lectures will be more thorough. Overall, I would take him again because(at least for me) it was an easy A.
The absolute goat. Explains material so well. Records all lectures. Exams are super fair. Homeworks are long but still fair. Take STAT401 with no one else but the legend Danul.
Not great TA. Very not lenient. Very not thorough in grading. Talked to him many times, very not humorous guy.

One of the worst teachers I’ve had the displeasure of taking. She often fails to explain things clearly and then blames the students even if she makes the mistake. There is no regrades and no arguing, and her grading is beyond absurd. You must complete every problem exactly as she does, correct alternative solutions will yield you zero points. While the class isn’t that difficult, she makes it immensely frustrating as you can do a problem 90% correctly and make small numerical errors and get no points. The exam averages were in the 40% after curves, and while the problems are similar to the HW, she often changes the numbers in such a way that a completely different method is required to solve them. You are allowed a formula sheet, but even though she isn’t clear, she will give you a 0 on exams for the smallest dubious infractions. The final exam does replace all grades, so getting a decent grade isn’t that hard, but once again it is just not an enjoyable class. Take it if you need it for the math major, but just be prepared for a very unpleasant experience.

Honestly she’s fine; not the greatest not the worst. Pros: really cares about her students, is invested in your success, approachable and accommodating. Homework, in-class work, attendance, and the project were basically free points. Easy to get 100s. Extra credit opportunities that can make a difference. Cons: exams are little more than rote memorization, the first exam was riddled with obscure questions buried on the slides. Way too heavily weighted at 30% for each exam. The slides themselves are a disorganized mess and need updating. The homework assignment instructions are even worse in this regard. The professor is clearly wayyyy too comfortable with the format she’s set up and kind of goes through the motions in terms of teaching. Easy enough A or B for a 400 level UMD mathematics, but the class could use some retooling in general.

She's great. The exams are pretty easy, and they only test you on content covered in the review guide, but they do take up a large portion of your grade. She drops the 3 lowest homework assignments, and none of them take much time. If you've taken AP Environmental Science, this class is very similar and covers a lot of the same content. She covers everything you need to know very clearly, and none of it is truly very hard anyway. The class isn't very time consuming and the content is pretty surface-level. My only issues were that the homework assignments from SimBio weren't very useful, but they were short. The exams also test your ability to apply the content instead of the content itself.

I've never met the man. Keller is kind of non-existent when it comes to the course, but I guess that's just the way it was designed. The TA does most of the brunt work. In terms of the actual course, I really liked my TA, and I haven't heard of anyone not liking theirs. You have weekly pre-lab and post-lab assignments that can take anywhere from 5 minutes to an hour depending on the assignment. You also need a lab manual for the course which explains the material pretty well for the most part and is very Maryland-specific which was cool. IF YOU MISS MORE THAN THREE LABS (even if it's excused) YOU WILL AUTOMATICALLY FAIL THE CLASS. I don't know who this would happen to but it seems important. The lab period itself typically lasts 2-ish hours, so you get let out early a lot of the time. The final is a lab practical of 12-13 questions split into stations. You get 3 minutes for each question and 3 minutes to check your answers at the end. You get a calculator or access to Appendix C and D for the questions that you would need them for which make it a lot less stressful. It is VERY fast-paced though. They do post the questions in advance though which helps though many of them are meant to apply to specific scenarios given to you during the exam.

She's really nice and doesn't give any "useless" info during lectures; you'll be tested on all of it. Her exams are really fair and are all based on her lectures. I have no background in biology, but I found most of the content easy to understand. You would have to memorize/understand every lecture because on the exams (which are multiple choice, fill-in-the-blanks, sometimes graphs, as well as written explanations), some questions aren't straightforward; you would have to have a good understanding of the topic to answer. The first midterm was the hardest for me. I got a 66 on the first exam, 88 on the second, 92 on the 3rd, and a 91 on the finals. overall highly recommended, plus she records her lectures, and I found myself not having to go every time.

This review is pointless to Dr. Mohan because you don't ever speak or meet her since it is ran by a TA. Your experience truly depends on how good your TA is. As long as your TA knows what they're doing, you should do just fine. Your grade, however, depends on your group. Make sure on the first day to sit with the students that know what they're doing. You don't want to get stuck with a deadbeat group all semester. The labs can be very annoying and very long but should not be too difficult. The practical and class itself was fairly easy so I recommend you take it!!

First off, sorry for the long reveiw, I just want you to get a full picture of her class and my feelings on it. I will say that anatomy isn’t necessarily a hard class, but a tedious one. Despite my review, if you have to take Goytia, you are not cooked or finished by any means. I just heavily suggest Justicia. I believe that Goytia’s class is very doable; my issue with her is that her exams are not true to her words, and her practice tests are useless. Still do the study guide but remember that they aren’t representative of her exams. She has a very bothersome tendency to make one topic out of the two to three she talks about the dominant thing on the exam, which is usually the most recent topic she discusses. This makes it hard because you wonder why you even bothered learning a topic when she only asks questions on one. She did this very heavily on this year’s final exam, where she only asked about two to three topics out of the ten learned about. Some topics only had one to three questions dedicated to them out of the 78 questions asked. On the final exam, she said there could be images, and there were no images, and seeing the useless study sheets of mine and my colleagues was baffling. The study sheets seem more helpful than they actually are; please do not take this class for that reason alone, because of how inconsistent her exams are—you may end up putting yourself in a hole if you rely on them. She asks too many questions in such a short amount of time; your study sheet should be used only for glancing. Her practice exams give you a false sense of confidence. They are so much easier than the actual exam it’s not funny. Her slides are not that useful—just research the topics on them. Her lectures are boring, and she does not do nearly as good a job as people say she does at breaking up topics. I once asked her a question with a straightforward answer, and she convoluted the answer, making me wonder why I even asked. Sometimes she gives helpful responses, but it’s 50/50. I can’t comment on GSS and its helpfulness. Her extra credit is not as good as Justicia’s (hers are 10–20 points built in). For the first exam out of 50 points, there were 2 points of extra credit; the second exam, I think, was 10 points of extra credit out of 120; the third exam was 140 points and only had 14 points of extra credit. To do well, really be confident in every topic, especially the more recent ones she teaches, and feel comfortable walking in without a study sheet except for any images with answers. She has quizzes that are easy but tedious and help your grade if you do them on time and don’t sacrifice a single point. But these will hurt your grade, despite the dropping of four of them, if you miss them. These are due early in the morning and during weekends, which makes them easier to miss. She does record her lectures, so you don’t have to go to class—just make sure to watch them. Start early with your studying, especially using the study guide. Pay attention to lab a bit more than lectures, as your lab grade is very important. Please study at least one week early for her exams, but more importantly for the practicals, as they are what get some people. P.S. Don’t miss a practical—the lab coordinator is harsher than the TAs. Goytia is nice, but not as great as I feel the reviews below me say she is. I was warned about her by people in person and used these views to sway me. I regret that now, as my friend has an A in Justicia’s class and I have this grade in Maira’s. Justicia is straightforward—what’s on the slides and her study guide is what’s on the exams. She overprepares you for her exams. Everyone left their final exam for Justicia super early, as she didn’t want to stress her students. She’s also funny. Justicia’s main con, in my opinion, is how exam-reliant her class is. If you tend to do very poorly on exams in general, then you should take Maira. Lastly, I want to say that Maira’s exams come much sooner than in other classes, so be prepared for that. TLDR: Goytia has weak extra credit, a boring class, unevenly distributed exam topics, easier practice exams than the actual exams, sometimes convoluted answers, and you shouldn’t take her class for the cheat sheet. Choose Justicia if you are good at exams and are taking other difficult classes.

Doesn't give cheat sheets but the class is still really good. not mandatory lecture, easy to learn at home, practicals aren't bad. gave 20 points extra credit on exam 2 and 25 extra credit points on exam 3.

Absolutely love Dr. Fletcher!!! He is such an amazing professor and is truly passionate about what he does. He is also genuinely one of the nicest professors I have ever met at UMD. He makes the content easy to understand and his exams are very fair. Would definitely recommend taking him!

I took this class in Spring 2025, and it was easily the hardest class I’ve taken so far—harder than Orgo I, Orgo II, and even BSCI 330. As someone who wasn’t a fan of the material, earning an A required a ton of work. I didn’t attend lectures because I quickly realized I needed to rewatch the Panopto recordings anyway. The professor talks very fast and has a thick British accent, which honestly made the material much harder to understand. Listening to the recordings for long periods genuinely drove me a little crazy. I don’t have a strong opinion on Dr. St. Leger as a lecturer since I rarely went to class, but my friends said that he tends to call on students sitting in the front rows. Also his slides are so cheeks cause they literally have paragraphs on them. To succeed in this course, I mainly relied on a Quizlet someone else had made. I would split-screen the lecture recording and the Quizlet, editing or adding cards as needed, and then spamming the flashcards until I memorized everything. I’ll admit that I made things harder for myself by procrastinating. The day before each exam, I’d end up watching around five lectures (each about an hour and fifteen minutes), finishing my flashcards, and then reviewing them—all in one day. As a result, I would have to pull an all-nighter just to memorize all the material. Despite all that, the exams themselves were actually pretty fair, and I rarely used the posted practice exams. The final exam includes around 32 bonus points, which essentially acts as a curve for the class. Even though this course caused me a lot of stress, I still finished with a 94%, so if you’re stuck with this professor, an A is definitely possible. The discussion section was probably the worst part of the course. There’s a lot of busywork, but the upside is that it helps boost your overall grade since the TAs don’t grade too harshly.

The flipped classroom is not helpful because she doesn't actually teach in class, just goes over practice problems. Easily 7+ hours of homework assignments a week, that is just busy work. The exams were ridiculously long, and no one finished the questions in time. I studied the slides, and it didn't seem like the content reflected in the tests. My TA was also not helpful and didn't take the class here, so she basically said I have no information on the tests and wouldn't show us how to study because there was no study guide, and the professor didn't acknowledge that there was even a test. The labs were twice a week, but half the time we got out in less than an hour, which is great, but why have two labs a week, which is a waste of time? Overall, this class is not a class you want to take unless you HAVE too,

As someone who was reading reviews for this class and super nervous because I was also taking a bunch of other content heavy classes at the same time, I am so happy to say I'm ending with an A! I actually did below average on the first exam, but I was able to do much better on all the other exams and in lab and that's what brought my grade up. Don't feel discouraged if you don't do great on the first exam! The class can be interesting and conceptually isn't too difficult to understand. It's just a lot of content that you need to know in depth. Dr. F's exams consist of multiple choice, short answer, and a long answer 18 point question at the end. My advice is to find as many practice materials as you can so you have some exposure to these types of specific questions. I would go to class and get exposure to the material, then rewatch lectures before exams, then do practice problems until I was getting them mostly right. Don't get discouraged! My only gripe with this class is how much content we are expected to know just a short time from being exposed to it and how specific and detailed the questions are when they weren't gone into that level of detail in lecture. I think this is unfair and as a result you have to put in hours and hours of work that I feel is unnecessary. Overall, Professor Frauwirth is a very funny and kind professor from what I've seen, and he makes classes enjoyable by making jokes and interesting analogies. I highly recommend you take BSCI330 with him.

BSCI353 with Dr. Butts was a very interesting class. His excitement about neuroscience (especially in the later units) clearly showed in his teaching. This class requires a lot of work, but Dr. Butts is very helpful in office hours and in his review sessions before the exams. Lectures are recorded, and the recordings have been very useful, but please still go to lecture because there are clicker questions that boost your grade. Additionally, there are 5 or so in-class group worksheets that you should get full credit for if you complete them, and I wish more professors gave them out – they’re a great opportunity to learn from your peers and shore up your understanding. These worksheets are also very helpful for exam prep. Speaking of which, the exams are on the harder side, as they ask you to think more about applying the concepts you learn in lecture rather than rote memorization, but they’re fair and he provides practice questions as a discussion board.

Very kind and supportive professor. Incredibly understanding and very student friendly. This is a very difficult class in terms of content and the degree of complexity. However, she records her lectures, posts all of her lectures accordingly and on-time, provides a lot of student-friendly extra credit opportunities, and is very approachable. I had a pretty difficult semester in a lot of ways and she really helped alleviate some of that burden by being a great and compassionate professor. Would recommend but don't fall behind with notes, it is a 400-level biology course for a reason.

If you can take any other professor, please do. While his lectures are easy to follow and he is a good professor overall, his exams are extremely hard, with the average grades being 50%. If you ask him a question in lecture, he will give you an attitude back in front of everyone but claim that he's not giving an attitude. Overall, if you're willing to put in the work, which will require a lot of separate practice and textbook practice, because I didn't find that the two hour homework helped much, you should be fine.

Like other people said, your lab experience mostly depends on the TA. 132 was timed really badly with 131 lectures so we would do the lab a week or two before the lecture so we wouldn’t know what we were doing or the science behind it until after the lab report was submitted. The TAs do all the grading and I lost a bunch of points on dumb stuff but my TA Docia kindly looks over any requests you have and will most likely give you points back as long as it’s sort of reasonable. Post and pre lab quizzes were BS where you could lose a bunch of points easily. The post lab quizzes are taken in lab 2 weeks after you do the lab, so you forgot everything already. They are each 3 questions worth 10 points in total, so it’s really easy to get a 0, 3, or 6 out of 10 which will lwk tank your grade since each of the 10 labs is only worth around 30-40 points. Lab reports are all done essentially as worksheets with written responses and math work shown. They’re okay, kind of time consuming but not terrible, though it's so hard to get all the points since we never get to see a rubric beforehand. I lost tons of points on significant figures in my data sheets and other small mistakes. All the labs we do are kind of boring and our data is always wrong because we suck and all the equipment is broken. FYI for resources you do need goggles, lab coat, the lab manual and a lock (any lock is fine it doesn’t need to be the bookstore one) . You don’t need a special calculator (I used TI-84 but any graphing or nongraphing will work) or a flash drive

Best chem professor for this class, but the class is super difficult. At the end of the year, he'll curve the entire class (50% was passing for us), but during the semester, it's unlikely he'll curve individual exams. Approachable guy, super kind and fun to talk to, and responds to emails fairly quickly (unless he's busy with grading around finals or midterms). Overall, I highly recommend him, but be prepared to study heavily for this class, especially if your chem knowledge isn't well defined.

So I will say that the reviews stating that you never see the teacher are true, but that is true for any lab, and not indicative of the teacher. However, there are several other reasons that I have decided to score Dr. White low. Firstly, her labs are incredibly poorly worded, both in the instructions, pre-lab, and post-lab questions. However, I think most people’s saving grace was the move of pre-lab questions to a virtual format, which included 30 minutes each attempt and 3 attempts. However, I know several people did not even get full points with this, as these are often her own designed labs, and she expected us to know the right calculations and conclusions to the labs already (which, in my opinion, should be the point of doing the lab in the first place). And the labs themselves were designed poorly, for example, our second lab had us doing analysis, and according to our TA, one of the first things she told them was that everyone who got X chemical would have several lab errors, yet I know she took points off those groups for said errors. In addition, another lab’s post-lab was entirely calculations, which she spelled out everything to do in the instructions. However, the instructions did not align with the rubric and neither aligned with how she phrased certain things. Plus, she was out during this entire week and TAs are not allowed to send out announcements without permission, so anyone unable to go to TA office hours got that wrong. In addition, my TAs sections were told to use a particular number of significant figures, which apparently did not align with the rubric (but how were we supposed to know that?) and so got points of for following our TA and she refused to give points back for that. In addition, in her review session (the day before the final exam), she told us that we needed to memorize the common names, formulas, reactions, colors, smells, etc for every single product and reactant over the course (probably about 50 reactions, although some compounds overlap). Now I would be annoyed but it would be reasonable if she told us this ahead of time. But the day before the final is not the time to do so. The only reason I gave two stars instead of one is that she was occasionally decently helpful when I emailed with questions.

Take this professor. I attended GSS weekly and did the practice exams, and I was always well above the average on the exams. Lecture can be a little confusing at times if you don't review the material beforehand, but as long as you keep up with the content, you will be fine. I would definitely recommend taking Koppel! - I thought her exams were fair, and the curve is very generous. She offers Zooms at night with extra practice problems before every midterm and will answer questions. She clearly cares about her students a lot and keeps lecture interesting. Most of these bad reviews are for lab, which was a different story and unavoidable... I still did well in it, but found it to be even harder than lecture. Make sure to go to the TAs with questions, and they can help you out.
Lab over the summer felt like a fever dream. It was so fast-paced and fried me. My TA also didn't quite seem to know what he was doing! Just come prepared for each lab.

Here's the thing the difficulty of this class depends on how much you keep yourself accountable. There's only 2 midterms and a final so there's not much work for this class but if you want to do well you need to spend a good amount of time every week learning and understanding the material. Personally I did not spend as much time on this class than I should have and that's because the structure of Isaacs class made me unmotivated. Lectures are kind of pointless, everything I learned was from the textbook which he straight up teaches from in lecture. He doesn't record lectures or give much practice though which sucks because that's the best way to understand the material. His exams were hard but make sure you look at his practice exams, they're super helpful. The reason I give 2 stars is because I felt like I was my own teacher and Isaacs himself contributed nothing to learning or studying. But if you believe you can make time for this class every week and not just right before an exam you should get an A. A 50% is a guaranteed C and 80% is an A (not minus). But his final was so cooked that he curved a little extra and my 74% turned into an A-, so do what you will with that info. This class is mostly memorizing reactions and when to use them, it's lowkey not that bad it's just a LOT of reactions, so the more time you spend on the material the easier it becomes.

Even though it was Dr. Sonia's first semester as a lab coordinator, she proved it was possible to set an example for other lab coordinators despite the class itself being the hardest lab I had taken before. She actually visited sections and answered questions during labs, which shows that she cares unlike previous lab coordinators, who we never even saw! However, this class is hard; there's really no sugarcoating it. Labs always took the full time (reaaallly long), and the LCTA quizzes (and practical) were relatively difficult. Nonetheless, Dr. Sonia wants you to do well, and she'll try her best to accommodate any hurdles during the course. Overall, it really helps to have a chill TA and create a light mood with your lab partners to ease the annoyance.

Here is the most honest review you could read about Dixon... I took her CHEM271 class, she was the only professor at the time of this class. I have never done so bad in a class, I am a straight A student and this class sucked the absolute life out of me. I spent countless hours on the homeworks, studying and so much more. She basically begs you to come to office hours, but there is already a ton of people there for a small office. This is a two credit course, so its only twice a week, but then she posts asynchronous videos which she expects you to watch because its material you need to know, she posts asynchronous "lectures" (I say this is quotes because she can't claim they are lectures but if you don't watch them you won't know half the material). Also almost every homework, lecture or asynchronous lecture has mistakes, which she realizes then fixes at the end leaving you more confused than when you started. She is incredibly disorganized with ELMS and makes homeworks due without receiving half of the content for the homework, leaving you to search stuff up or just have no clue how to complete it (also homework take upwards of 10 hours, sometimes longer, and half the material on the homework she hasn't taught yet). I personally think that there was way too much content for this class. (also she added a whole pharmokinetics unit... I asked other people who took it before me and they said they never had to do any of that, so idk what that was all about.) The exams... first off, she forces you to sit packed like sardines in the first 5 or so rows in the chem building, its incredibly hot and cramped, and those desks are too small for the 10 page packet she gives you to complete in 55 minuets. Everyone I talked to said they didn't finish the exam. Which leaves the exam grades so low, if I had an extra 20 minutes, the exams would be fine. The only nice thing is, she will tell you what you need to study, which is very helpful. Another things about the lectures is that the first exam was almost 2 months into the semester... so it was incredibly content heavy so be prepared for that. Now I know this class is extremely hard, and she honestly wasn't a horrible teacher, I personally enjoyed the lectures, she answered questions, and always asked people if they had questions. I am sure that the chem department threw her upon this class because there were no other sections, she was the only teacher for this semester. So if you don't have an option of professor like me, Id would still take the class, but I wish I knew this before taking the class. Just be prepared to spend a LOT of time on this class (and the lab is arguably worse). But don't let my bad grade fool you, this class is very passable, there is a very decent curve. Grades are based on the 2 exams, 10 lab reports, pre-lab notebooks and quizzes, and data & observations. The pre-lab notebooks and data & observations are pretty much graded for completion. You had to pay for LabArchives, which is an online lab notebook, which I found pretty nonsensical. We could have just as easily submitted the pre-lab notebook and data & observations through Canvas. The pre-lab quizzes are easy as long as you pay attention to the lectures and complete the optional pre-lab walkthrough. The exams are pretty close to the practice exams Dr. Schech posts, and people generally do well on them. I'd study for the exams by reviewing the lectures, completing the practice exam, and looking over previous lab reports. Like others have said, lectures are recorded and optional. If you get stuck on the lab reports, reviewing the associated lecture and pre-lab walkthrough should show you how to do it. The lab reports can be time-consuming, but as long as you attend office hours to verify your answers and double-check your sig-figs and math, getting 100% should be pretty easy. The labs themselves were kind of boring, but many groups got out early for most labs. Overall, the workload for this class was on the lighter side. Dr. Schech was very approachable and welcoming during office hours, and she was thorough when answering questions. She was also available for a little while after the lectures for questions and was quick to answer questions on the class Piazza. She has a 24-hour grace period for late lab reports, during which they're not marked off for late submissions, so you essentially have 8 days to complete every lab report. I felt like lab reports were graded in a timely manner; grades were always sent out in time so that your lab reports could be used as study material for the exams. If you got points off, there would be an explanation why.

This course was significantly more difficult than other sections of the same course due to the instructor's exam design and grading policies. While rigor is expected, the level of difficulty combined with the lack of dropped assignments (even one quiz would have helped) created a grading structure that was inequitable across sections. Although this course was described as "beginner-friendly," in practice, it was not due to the nature of the harsh exams which did not reflect the difficulty of the practice he had provided. For students new to the subject, this made the course especially challenging to navigate. As a result, receiving one poor exam score had a disproportionate impact on your final grade. This leaves no room for error for future assessments. Students should carefully consider their coding background before enrolling in this section. Given the exam difficulty and grading structure, I would not recommend this course for beginners.

I think people are too harsh on Herman; his average here is a 3.14, which isn't terrible, but the way I've heard older CS students speak about him is as if he is the teacher of doom and despair. (Note that I called him teacher DO NOT call him professor this will be the first thing he says on the first day and he may even spend 10 minutes giving a whole presentation on it later in the sem!) The project descriptions are quite lengthy, but personally I would prefer this to vague descriptions where you have to figure it out yourself. There will be pretty much no questions left unanswered. Some projects are quite difficult, but honestly some of the ones I struggled with the most were also the ones I left until the last day or two, so I would recommend starting around three to four days before the due date. Also, make sure you read through the whole project description before starting, I know it's annoying but it's better than if you start to code and then realize you're violating project requirements, because sometimes you are prohibited from doing things that may be intuitive. Overall though, some projects were hard, some were easy, and also bombing one or two projects is really not detrimental to your grade. He also has some nice extra credit for a lot of them if you do it early and only submit once which is super nice. As for exams, I genuinely think his exams were extremely fair. Herman gives super long practice exams that I usually found to be harder than the actual exam, if not about the same. To study I typically reviewed his slideshows, which he posts, and then did those practice exams and I did pretty well on all the exams. Even questions I got wrong on exams, I felt like they were fair questions to have been asked and things I should have known. One interesting policy to take note of, though, is the grading of multiple choice questions. These were usually the harder part of the exams. They are multi-select and you get 1 point off for selecting an incorrect answer and 2 points off for not selecting a correct answer. This is super important because if you are truly unsure, you should just select an answer because you lose less points if that's wrong than if you don't pick it and it's correct. The lectures themselves can be pretty boring, but I do think they are super helpful. In hindsight, my worst project grade was definitely as a result of me zoning out in class when going over that topic. If you listen in class, you will be pretty set because he does explain concepts well and often uses people in the front row as examples, which helps get the point across. Also, he does like to make jokes sometimes during lectures and personally I really enjoy his humor. The lectures are not necessarily mandatory, but there are graded worksheets that pop up both during lectures and mostly during discussions which are about 10% of your grade, so you really should go. Also, those worksheets are super helpful to understand what exams are like. As for homework, I'm ngl I did like 3 of them and there were probably around 10-12 not quite sure. The ones I did were helpful but they're all optional and really can just be used as additional studying. Finally, just some interesting policies that Herman has. No phones, laptops, iPads, etc. If using technology is important to you definitely don't take Herman because he is very serious about it and will call you out every single time. Don't sit in the back row because he will tell you to move up. The damn pdf password really got me it's really annoying to have a locked pdf but also thats not really that deep. There is a participation grade for 3% and he is more likely to call on you if you sit in the front (not really that crazy but good to know). He doesn't do Canvas announcements but instead has a newsfeed that won't notify you when he posts and instead you have to remember to check (this really pissed me off but also not that deep, not sure why he does this). You also can't email him or message him because he won't answer, you have to go to office hours to ask any questions and such. Finally, he has very specific style requirements. Most of them were pretty intuitive to me, the only one that sucked was that you aren't allowed to have multiple return statements, that was always so annoying but I got used to it. Overall though, I thought Herman was a very good teacher and I can honestly say I learned so much this semester. Coming from AP Comp Sci A in high school I think it's super important to have a good teacher in 132 for these foundational concepts. I know a lot of people where 132 was more review for them, but for me it was all new and I feel like I learned it very well. I recommend Herman for 132!

Whether I end this class with a C- or an A+ I'll leave having learned the exact same amount from the lectures and projects: absolutely nothing. The fact UMD is ranked as high as it is for CS and then has professors for lower level classes that cannot teach and TAs which vary from "make the class easy as pie" to "Lecture round 2 with no benefit to the students at all" is rather insane. You would think it in the school's interest to attempt to give students a strong foundation so they can confidently get internships, do research, do well in later classes, but I'm pretty sure the avg student coming out of this class will only have gained the knowledge that "they don't like C/assembly" based on a bad prof.

It's been a very fun and rewarding class!

Goes at a great pace, great at explaining, super positive attitude, and a pretty lenient grader I would say. Deserves 6 stars for being the first math professor Ive seen to not use a chalkboard and instead use a tablet and upload the lecture notes.

Everything from 5/17/2025 with some additions. 1) the important content was not covered (no hwk on Lagrange multipliers, the very last lecture covered surface integrals, green’s + stokes’ theorems and that too by the TA), no questions on the final about mean value theorem or actual understanding of differentials — we would get taught some sections in class but have no assigned hwk 2) hwk was entirely computational and barely proof based 3) a lot of the theorems were actually taught wrong in class or glossed over — only reading the book made more sense 4) >75% of the class got <55% on the final 5) he hasn’t announced grades yet but kept saying he would increase the weighting of future midterms/exams after m1 (avg was 12/20, avg was 15/20 for m2) rather than curve 6) I knew most of the material very well prior from other classes and still struggled because of his unfair exams/grading 7) no partial credit on certain final questions, and even graded different students’ exams differently 8) I used to love analysis and now I am just genuinely repulsed by it. A professor really DOES make all the difference.

Things to note: 3 midterms one of which is dropped; 10 hws 2 of which are dropped In our class, the third midterm was a take-home free one (basically guaranteed 95+) and so, the best of Midterm 1 and Midterm 2 (which are legit midterms) along w/ M3 are going to make the 2 midterms that count for your grade. He will offer an opportunity to drop the final and take the score of the 3 midterms and the first 8 hws if you want to take that opportunity up. Regarding the homeworks, most of them are pretty chill -- he doesn't really offer help in OH though so you gotta learn through Stack Overflow, GPT, and just trying stuff out. The midterms are challenging asf -- the thing is they aren't really anything like the homeworks and are way more proof-based than what you'd expect given what he describes the midterms as. Only 1 or 2 of the questions are "here, do it" questions, the rest are showing some type of property or proof question which is significantly harder. As others mentioned, if you can notice the gimmick fast enough, it's normally a 2-3 liner. If you can push yourself through, it can take 10-15 minutes sometimes and you can get the answer. But chances are, you might just f*ck it up because there's no really good way to prepare (you just have to remember and notice the right things in the moment). Definitely use the practice problems from his notes though because they are somewhat similar to the actual midterm (the homework problems that he assigns aren't though). Lecture-wise, he's pretty good. Just, it gets a bit tiring after a while especially because a lot of the content is cumulative (especially near the end of the course), so if you forget things from previous lectures, you're kinda F-ed. That being said, the accent isn't really an issue and you get kinda used to the whole structure of the course after a while. All in all, I'd just suggest being TOTALLY aware that you're interested in DSP stuff before taking this course becuase while the material can be extremely interesting and fun to learn, if you're not interested enough for it to motivate getting through the times where you're misunderstanding things or have to read through the notes, you'll ultimately end up hating the course and neglecting it leading to not great outcomes. Overall, pretty good course, but requires more mathematical maturity than just a MATH240+MATH141 prereq (I think he should also add a MATH401 or MATH405 pre-req as well since some of the linalg does get a bit crazy). Make sure to attend lecture and focus/lock-in on the shit so you don't fall behind.

First off I must say that people must account for the class she is teaching when thinking about taking her class. I took the upper level geometry course with her and she would occasionally complain about how bad her calc students were. She seemed to like us a lot more. Lecture: Was a little dry, but she gave good examples and explained things very well, things get a little strange when we get to non-Euclidean stuff which is weird. Homework: Was hard. About 85% of the homework problems she made up, which were often pretty hard, if she assigned work from the book it was often pretty easy. There were also three computer projects with Geometer's Sketchpad which were somewhat difficult. Office Hours: Very helpful, in the beginning most people didn't know how to write a proof so she would more or less just do it for us. Tests/Quizzes: Quizzes were fairly easy, just basic test to make sure you are keeping up with the material. The midterm was pretty easy too, the Final was a little harder because it had some crazy hyperbolic stuff. The layout of the midterm and final were something like this: 1) Some true false (no justification) 2) fill-in-the-blank proof 3) Do it yourself proofs 4) Some computational stuff or short answer Grades: 25% = 12 Homeworks assigned on Friday due the next Friday (drop 2) 10% = 3 Geometer's Sketchpad projects 35% = Final 20% = One midterm 10% = 4 In class worksheets and 4 quizzes (lowest dropped) Again this review should only be applied to her upper level classes.
The one and only. Class was easy and relaxed. Having background in a lot of the material, I only wish the pace was a little faster so we would be able to cover more interesting graph theory topics.

Josh is a great physics TA; unfortunately this isn't reflected in the grades his section got this semester. He is very good at explaining concepts, going over practice problems, and helping with lab procedures.

I took PHYS121 with her and now 122, she is a wonderful professor! Really helpful and explains all the topics, even content covered in labs. Her practice sets and solutions are super helpful in studying for exams and I feel that the grading is very fair.

the man can not teach for the life of him. at one point i stopped attending the lectures and just did the top hat questions during the class time to get participation. he would constantly belittle himself if got something wrong, telling himself that he is stupid and this is why he drinks OUT LOUD. overall he just scared me. but when it came to exams, the curves were amazing, usually around 30 points added to your raw score. the final was god awful though and he was not even there when we were taking it, literally just a TA watching over us. the homeworks were time consuming, but the most helpful material for studying for exams. he gave practices exams, but they were from another professor and most of the time had other material on it that we have not learned. he's all that is there this upcoming semester so just hope the curve is good and good luck!

Fahad was a great TA! He is very knowledgeable and always happy to help. He is also super understanding and flexible with deadlines. His recitations were always helpful for reinforcing content from class. Even though our lab was at 8am, he always brought positive energy. Definitely lucky to have him as a TA!

I will preface this with saying that I took Hailu the previous semester for 161, that class was easy and thought he was chill so I went with him again. Hailu's lectures are very hard to get anything out of, in the end you just learn the content through the homeworks and videos, at least that's what I did. As in 161, he again goes through derivations of equations, but they go on for so long that it's pointless and he shows you more than what you'll actually need. Just look at the equations on his slides and write that down. As usual for Hailu style, his exams are fair but do make sure to write down equations that you may think are useless as anything is "fair game".

Severson did a really solid job setting up 261. Every lab is done entirely through Excel and LoggerPro, with instructions on Expert TA. Prelabs are also on Expert TA, and you do get penalized for incorrect attempts. He gives you an Excel template for each lab which is very straightforward, there's just a lot of copying and pasting and typing out complex formulas, but nothing challenging. The instructions for each lab are easy to follow so there's no issue getting out early. After the first 5 labs, there's a makeup week for anyone who missed one of those labs, but if you didn't miss any you get the week off. There's another makeup week after labs 6-9, too. After that, the next week is a review for the final, and the week after that is the final, which takes place before the usual finals week. The final is not bad at all, and he gives you a bunch of practice questions (though not the answers to them), a couple of which were on the actual exam. The final was originally going to be in person, but he moved it online and mentioned that he'll probably keep it online in the future. One thing to note about 261, though, is that it may be the physics 2 lab, but the majority of the labs are on physics 1 concepts, like momentum, centripetal motion, and pendulums. Only the last two labs were on physics 2 concepts, waves and the ideal gas law.

Great professor. He seems to genuinely care about his students and their learning. He is obviously very passionate about physics which makes his lectures somewhat interesting. Exams were all multiple choice, and the final was just repeated problems from the 3 midterms. Grade scheme is a bit weird and nothing gets put on canvas until the end of the semester, but if you do okay on midterms you will be fine.
This class was very tedious and time consuming but I had an awesome TA who made it bearable. The culminating labs were not bad since we all worked together.

I’m honestly just bracing for the whiplash of not taking a class with Dr. Turpen next semester — this professor should teach every class in the department. She’s one of the only professors I've had who truly sees her students as human beings, not robots. Lectures are not just 50 minutes of force feeding material like other classes — she stops frequently for questions and polls the class with interactive comprehension questions to make sure that we're really understanding what's going on. Homeworks are expertly crafted to actually support our learning process and I always know that, even if I didn't understand what's happening in lecture, I'll understand it after the homework. Her exams are incredibly fair and she provides such an amazing support system with her review sessions, practice exams, homework corrections, test corrections, and TAs. She sincerely wants to see everyone succeed and, if you put in the work, you'll learn so much from her class. I hope I get to learn from her again at some point — seriously, take a class with Dr. Turpen if you can :)

I thought this class was very well-taught. I've come out of it with a strong understanding of the fundamentals of QM and feel like I was able to follow along with the material without having to fake it. Homeworks were usually helpful and suitably challenging, albeit often computationally intensive and tedious (don't shy away from using Mathematica/integral calculators). Exams were very fair as long as you went over the homework and understood it. There were a few lectures (spherical harmonics, harmonic oscillator) where she just quickly went through a complicated derivation, which I didn't find particularly useful, although I don't really know how I would teach those in an engaging or memorable way either. Most lectures were engaging and comprehensive. I know there was a lot of frustration from the class over the fact that 20% of the grade was participation/attendance. 10% of the grade came from attendance to the weekly Friday discussions/group worksheets. She dropped one of these at the end of the semester if you missed it but wasn't really communicative or forgiving if you had to miss more than one, so just don't be sick on Friday more than once I guess. Another 10% of the grade was "class engagement" through Piazza, which she graded based on whether or not you were responding to the in-class clicker questions because people weren't posting questions/discussions outside of class enough. She didn't tell us this until the end of the semester, so lecture attendance was being secretly graded.

One of the best physics lecturers I had: 1)extremely thorough and clear presentation of QM, with lecture notes posted; 2)put effort into designing the course, supplementing Griffiths' textbook with his own derivations which are often more insightful; 3)challenging but well-written homework problems focusing on physics concepts. That being said, he held (perhaps righteously) high standards for his students therefore gave difficult exams. But, even when the problem seemed really hard, you could manage to solve it if you followed and understood all his lecture notes (which I should have done but didn't). I definitely learned a lot in his class and did not regret taking him. It's not an easy ride, but neither is QM.

Jacobson gives way too much homework (expect to spend over 7 hours a week if you want to get above a 90), but I honestly thought he did a very good job of explaining the first 2/3rds of the content. Especially when we started going into Hamiltonian Mechanics, I struggled to follow what was going on in the homework and his supplied notes didn't help much. I did very poorly on the final even though I had the 3rd highest grade on the first exam. PHYS410 has a lot of great content by itself, and Jacobson tries to teach all of it and more, never skimping on homework along the way.

This was a really hard class. The material was very difficult. I'd like to say that this class was like a vector calculus boot camp. Problems commonly included partial differential equations, integrations in spherical/cylindrical coordinates, Legendre polynomials, Fourier analysis, and alot of other fancy stuff. The homework problems (from Griffiths) were long and tough, and Jacobson also created his own supplementary problems to add to the fun. They were actually sometimes easier than Griffiths'. Overall, Jacobson is a good lecturer. He presents the material quite well, and is very sharp when answering student qustions. If he can't properly address a student's question in class, he'll email the class later on explaining a concept. He is very nice and respectful of student concerns. Instead of just re-writing notes on the board, he actually interacts with student questions. He answers emails quickly. He does alot of interesting demos. His grading scheme is nice; grade is broken into 4 pieces: homework, midterm 1, midterm 2, and final exam (NOT cumulative). Your two best each count 35%, two worst are 15%. Very fair grading scheme. My only comment is that his final was really difficult, and I probably got like a 15% on it. Luckily, he seems to curve exams ... Overall, very fair professor. I may take PHYS410 this fall with him if I can fit it into my schedule. I'd recommend him.

One of the best professors Ive ever had. Griffin is a good professor, but is very picky when people don't follow his directions and don't come to class. He makes attendance a big thing during discussions and lectures. Every lecture, you are given a worksheet, and if you complete it early, you get to share your answer with the class and earn extra credit. Discussions werent that bad and were mainly similar to how the example tutorial for the discussions was. Exams were very straightforward. The exams were very similar to the previous 2 semesters, with a few changes in numbers. We also had MyLabs from Pearson, and it was pretty petty, but we didn't really utilize all the resources in there.

At first, the course was unreasonably difficult and very disorganized. I think this professor is just new to teaching, so it was a rocky start. Near the end of the course, he improved significantly in his lectures and on top of that, the last few exams were more representitive of the material covered. The homework used to be insanely difficult too, but near the end it was starting to become more managable. I think there is still room for improvement, but throughout the semester he actively worked to improve the course based on feedback.

TL;DR: Lectures can feel a bit slow or boring at times, but he genuinley cares about his students and is good and explaining things slowly Pros: - Exams were very very similar to practice exams - Homeworks were a little tough, but doable - quizzes were either once a week or once every two weeks depending on how he was feeling. Usually similar to an example in class though, so they weren't bad if you showed up to class. - Genuinely great at explaining things starting from the basics and working up - Works almost 1:1 from the textbook, so even if you miss class, you can read the textbook to catch up. Cons: - Lectures can be kinda boring as he is a little monotone and lecutres can move slow a lot of the time.

Brutal midterms and final, but from what I've heard all 410 classes are difficult. Struggled to pick between 2 or 3 stars but ultimately decided on 2. He is actually a pretty good lecturer but it's external factors that make the class worse. Lack of online notes: he loosely follows notes from a different university (and I mean loosely, sometiems he'll just ignore stuff or teach something else) and doesn't post anything else. If you're like me, online notes, namely readable slides, are almost always the most useful material for any class. He does not have them, period. Additionally, the grading is very unhelpful. I suppose the expectation is to check with him if you want specifications but I expect more than literal nothing other than being marked off on my test sheet for how much we have to pay to go here. I was probably also the wrong audience for this class, however. I took it because it fit into my schedule and I needed a stat 400+ class. Don't take this class with half-hearted expectations and you'll probably have a better time than me, but I can't say I didn't have a bad experience.

This was the hardest course I have taken at UMD. Prof. Xu is very knowledgeable about statistics, seems to genuinely care about the students' learning outcomes, and had some cool stories he occasionally mentioned. I found lectures to be somewhat dry and hard to follow, and homework assignments challenging and time intensive. That said, the exams were quite fair and similar to past exams available on the Testbank. I finished with a C but if you actually put in the time to study for this course it's totally possible to finish with a solid grade.

Yeah I really can’t say I’m a fan of this professor. With her class times being so late it’s hard to pay attention to what she’s saying and reviewing the material is impossible cuz her slides don’t cover everything, her exams are way too heavily weighted and they test you on stupid vocab that you haven’t heard, she also doesn’t give you any practice material for exams, and won’t give you your exam back to see what you did wrong, I’m sure she doesn’t change them every year. Overall very disappointed with this class.

Dr Shapiro is deeply passionate for the subject he teaches, but doesn't seem to understand that we don't all feel the same. I attended all lectures and studies very hard for the tests, but he makes them quite impossible to do well on. The questions are asked a very overcomplicated way so no matter how much of the material I actually know, I can't understand what is being asked of me. His questions are also very specific, so if you missed even one small example in class well that's likely 3 points off your test. I will say his final exam was much easier than the rest of his exams and he does drop one.

I've never met the man. Lemke is kind of non-existent when it comes to the course, but I guess that's just the way it was designed. The TA does most of the brunt work and unless you're making up an absence, or Lemke is your "TA," you won't even interact with him. In terms of the actual course, I really liked my TA, and I haven't heard of anyone not liking theirs. You have weekly pre-lab and post-lab assignments that can take anywhere from 5 minutes to an hour depending on the assignment. You also need a lab manual for the course which explains the material pretty well for the most part and is very Maryland-specific which was cool. IF YOU MISS MORE THAN THREE LABS (even if it's excused) YOU WILL AUTOMATICALLY FAIL THE CLASS. I don't know who this would happen to but it seems important. The lab period itself typically lasts 2-ish hours, so you get let out early a lot of the time. The final is a lab practical of 12-13 questions split into stations. You get 3 minutes for each question and 3 minutes to check your answers at the end. You get a calculator or access to Appendix C and D for the questions that you would need them for which make it a lot less stressful. It is VERY fast-paced though. They do post the questions in advance though which helps though many of them are meant to apply to specific scenarios given to you during the exam.

The GOAT. DO the Simutexts. They are graded(easy points) and are pretty important to the content most of the time. Exam 1 is shorter than the rest and the easiest, in my opinion. Exam 4 was personally my hardest and probably had the lowest scores. Be careful of trick questions. He likes to use a barrage of easy questions, then hit you with a hard one that you really have to think about, and where one answer is more true than the other. Homework is decently easy if you pay attention in class, albeit lectures can be a bit fast, but that was mainly because my class was allergic to asking questions. Exams always covered the study guides mainly, but it doesn't hurt to study the full unit. Clicker questions are a great grade booster. Overall, I would definitely retake with him.

The reviews are right that you never interact with this professor throughout the semester, unless you have her for lecture. Your grade is heavily based on if you get a good TA and a good lab group, both of which I did not get. However, it is still possible to get an A if you work hard. I found the labs sometimes confusing and the post-lab assignments sometimes unnecessary. There are also a lot of literature-based assignments where you have to background research, which was really annoying. Besides that, the lab practical is easy as long as you pay attention and participate in labs. Also, never ever be late.

Dr. Goytia is definitely one of the best professors I have ever taken and I thoroughly enjoyed this class! She is passionate about the material and her students' comprehension-- she is enthusiastic and always prepared to explain concepts at any time. I am not one to use office hours often, but I would go up to her before class and felt comfortable asking her questions, knowing she would take the time to help me actually understand. This course has LOTS of material, but it's structured in a manageable and honestly enjoyable format since Dr. Goytia's slides have various examples and memorization tools. She takes familiar concepts and relates them back to the new material which makes the class very cohesive and tougher concepts easy to understand. Dr. Goytia is an amazing lecturer and provides great study guides, and practice exams-- paired with the lab there are so many tools provided that will help you succeed on practical and lecture exams. I also noticed she has many regulars and previous students visit during her office hours-- she also knew many students by name which demonstrates her passion for teaching. It is clear she has a true impact on her students, and I 1000% recommend taking her for this class!

What a roller coaster of emotions throughout this semester. Weekly assignments very easy, as well as pre and post labs. But exams were VERY difficult. Would give extra credit to get average to 70 (had to retake exam for points). Ended up with a D+, missing the cutoff by 0.12%. Final grade was put in as D+. With a random change of heart, I checked a few days later and bumped to a C-. Very difficult course as you would expect. Exams much different than study guides and practice exams. Overall okay teacher.

As much as the class is difficult, Dr. Carleton is extremely nice. If you are a first semester freshman taking this class as I was, do not underestimate the first exam and be sure to take your time writing good notes during lecture. (I prefer using a google doc/typing, I used an iPad first unit and there was too much material and lecture went to quick to write quality notes) Expect that this class will take a lot of studying, but if you do it you will do well.

This guy is interesting. I was originally gonna give him 1 star but in the end he curves like crazy so I am not really complaining. However, bro puts me to sleep in every lecture and I have to spend time studying on my own after class. Take this guy only if you're a hard worker.

A lot of people don't like her because of the way the class is structured, and I do have to admit - this class IS really tedious. There are so many assignments that it starts feeling like a drag, especially in the back half of the semester. However, Dr. Tran herself is actually really lovely. She clearly tries her best, and in my experience has been perfectly willing to hear out students' concerns. I've emailed her several times with issues and she's always been very patient and understanding. Additionally, her actual lecture content is well structured. Sometimes the content can be really vague though - so if you don't understand something, make sure to look it up yourself. Additionally, some people are upset about the second exam in the Fall 2025 semester. The exam WAS really long, but I'm here to tell you that she heard people out about it and ended up bumping the grades by 10 points, which was VERY generous. Additionally, people don't like her flipped classroom style, which is fair because she also forces you to come to lecture for clicker questions. In general though, the clicker questions are actually pretty helpful in terms of both reinforcement and preparing for exams because they show you what topics she thinks are important, which people either don't realize or ignore (?). In general, she's pretty great and I think I would give a full 5 stars if there weren't as many tedious assignments.

Dr. Frauwirth is def one of my top 5 BSCI professor at umd. He is a kind and goofy guy but can really break down concepts concisely and accurately. He also gives a ton of extra credit around 17 points. The exams aren't too hard as long as you study for them you will be fine. The lab really depends on your TA if you have Shruthika Nallamaddi one of the best TA's at UMD lab will literally be a breeze if you have her. Overall fun class and not that difficult if you study for it.

Gives in-class worksheets that are too long to finish in the time we are given, which causes a lot of stress. I also was laughed at by TA's on some occasions for asking questions, and at other times, they did not know how to answer my questions. Additonally, I was graded harshly on a single question on the 2nd exam, which brought down my grade significantly.

Dr. Wu is one of the most nicest and sweetest professors at umd she really does want everyone to do well in her class. However, she cannot really teach that well and usually just reads off the slides so you must self study for the most of the class. The exams are hard but you only really need to score a high C or above to get an A there are a multitude of assignments and extra credit that help your grade a lot. Its not too hard of a class you just need to put in the work.

Amazing professor! So glad I took chem131 with her. Her lectures are very helpful and she gives lots of analogies and examples for concepts that will appear on the tests. The tests were a lot like the practice exams and as long as you do well on those you should do fine on the exams. She’s also genuinely such a sweet lady and is very approachable.

This was one of the most disorganized classes ive ever taken. The content itself is manageable, but there are always problems with the lab materials and sessions, and quiz grades are extremely unfair (3 difficult questions that tank your grade). Honestly it all depends on your TA, mine was a man who couldnt care less about the class, and never knew what was going on. If you have a good TA who gives you resources, you should be fine.

Lascio is a great dude and is definitely the most effective CHEM135 teacher. He spends a little bit too much time on some topics, but I'm sure he'll get much better every semester. It's very clear he cares about his students, and he always sets his expectations higher than reality. His curve at the end of the year was very generous, and as long as you stay on top of each lesson as it is being taught, you'll be fine.

There is not much you can do to make sure you do well in this class except try your best and remember it is a one credit class. The instructor is pretty nice in office hours but your TA may be a problem. You will spend hours on lab reports just to get low grades because things are unclear but if you stay ahead and go to office hours before a report is due they are very helpful in answering questions and clearing up confusion. The curve is great, I went from a 77 to an A-. Try and stay above average on everything and double check your submissions and make sure not to submit at 11:59 pm the day it is due because they do not give you anything if your submission is wrong or late.
She’s a a little intimidating but a really good teacher. I learned a lot and would definitely recommend her!

Arjun is a very patient and upbeat TA. He made all the labs feel like they went by quickly, even though a lot of them can be rather dull in content (waiting for reaction to go through). His office hours were really helpful for the PLQs even though a lot of them are quite confusing.

Going into this class, I had heard a lot of positive reviews about Dr. Davis, and I also had a strong chemistry background (all As up to that point). First off, Dr. Davis is incredibly kind—honestly one of the nicest professors I’ve ever had. He explains concepts clearly, takes time during lecture to answer student questions, and you can tell he’s an expert in his field. That said, the class itself is somewhat disorganized. His notes aren’t great, and lectures can feel scattered. At times, he would lose his train of thought and jump to a new topic unexpectedly. On top of that, the class meets at 8 frickin AM, which made it so cheeks to attend, so I stopped going after the first couple of weeks. In terms of grading, your final grade is almost entirely based on exams, which is pretty standard for chemistry courses. The best part about Dr. Davis’s grading policy is that he allows you to drop one exam—including the final. The exams themselves are fair, and if you understand the material and complete the practice exams, you should be in good shape. The first midterm is very easy, and you should absolutely take advantage of it to buffer your grade. The only reason I earned an A in this class was because I did extremely well on the first exam. The second exam was by far the hardest for me, mainly because I wasn’t prepared for the jump in difficulty. Each exam gets progressively harder, so you definitely need to increase your studying as the semester goes on. The second exam ended up being my dropped exam. The third exam and the final were similar in difficulty, and I scored in the top 25% of my class. Dr. Davis also offers bonus points for completing practice exams—nine points total, with three points per midterm. I initially thought I would receive an A− since I narrowly missed the 90% cutoff, but Dr. Davis adjusted the grading cutoffs after the final, which ultimately earned me an A. For studying, I started about three days before each exam. I made a review packet based on his in-class notes (which was often my first real exposure to the material since I wasn’t attending lecture), made sure I fully understood the concepts, memorized key information, and completed two to three practice exams. If I could do it again, I would definitely make time to complete more of the practice exams to feel more confident going into the tests.

Hirschauer is one of the best professors in the Chemistry department, hands down. She is very kind to her students and is always willing to answer questions. She is also the only lab coordinator I have had that I have met. I highly recommend going to the TA office hours. My only complaints were that the LCTAs (quizzes) and the practical were harder than expected.

Please don't take this professor it will hurt you. Dr. Dixon is clearly a very rounded professor, with great knowledge of chemistry, but her class feels like you're on a time bomb. She will only assign 5 HW for Gen Chem 2 but they will be one of the most torturous and time consuming work out there taking up to 6 hours to complete with perfection. You might be asking why an assignment should take this long? Well, her homeworks always contain some mistake or typo. She will sometimes update the homework questions without giving students more time. You're only given 1-2 days to complete the homework essentially, since she will fully cover the material on the HWs by then. In some cases, she makes you watch asynchronous videos which some are very time consuming to complete the homeworks. Dr. Dixons exams are easy but you have to be born knowing the answers or you'll run out of time (most students can only get through half of the exam). Tho the only pro for this class are the large curves. If you can survive being low on time and want extra challenge, this class is for you.

The class isn't hard, but rather a little tedious. Lectures are recorded, so attendance isn't mandatory except for exam days. The lectures provide context for the lab, pre-lab quiz, and how to do some calculations on the lab report, but honestly, most of it you could get without watching the lecture if you have a general idea of what's going on. Your grade is made up of 2 exams + 10 lab reports. The lab reports are long and a little annoying, but not hard. The exams aren't too hard either, and are based on the calculations done in the lab report. Dr. Schech is also pretty chill and is willing to answer questions. The class is very doable, just a little tedious.

Pedram is a good CMSC131 Professor. The lectures are really good at explaining the concepts. As a person who never took AP Comp Sci and wasn't familiar with OOP, he did a really good job explaining it and other concepts I wasn't familiar with like recursion. His drawings of memory maps really help you understand what's going on. The other reviews are right that his lectures can be a bit monotone and on days where I was a bit tired it was easy to drift off. The projects are nice and straightforward and you shouldn't have trouble finishing them if you start on time and get help if you need it. The quizzes and exams are all doable. He also gives you nice review material for each quiz and exam (except for the final). Tips to succeed: - Attend every lecture. Attending them in-person helps you learn all the content at a nice pace. - Attend discussion. Before quizzes and exams, they are very useful for review and letting you know what will be on the quiz/exam. They are also helpful for learning specific things you may need for the projects and giving extra examples/questions to solidify the concepts. Some content (not a lot) is only taught in discussion. - Start projects early, try not to push them to the last minute. You’ll learn more from them. - Have a plan to study for each quiz/exam. This doesn’t have to be super thought out, but plan enough that you don’t need to cram the day before/of. At least, give yourself enough time to work through all of it without rushing. Do all the practice he gives you. Going through the code examples in the zip files provided with each slide and making sure you understand what’s going on can be helpful. Exams and quizzes combined are a large part of the class grade so prepare for them well.
