As I am writing this, Justin's average rating on Planet Terp is a 4.69, which is even higher than Christopher Kauffman's average rating (4.63). I had Kauffman for CMSC216 in Spring 2025, and he was one of my favorite professors of all time. Needless to say, given all the hype around Justin, I had high hopes going into his Summer 2025 CMSC351 class. Now that everything's over, I can say in short that I am disappointed with my experience. To be clear, Algorithms as a Computer Science class is commonly agreed to be a terrible class pretty much everywhere (based on talking to many people from many different universities). A large part of this is due to the fact that those with minimal experience in algorithmic programming find the class extremely difficult, while at the same time those with a lot of experience in algorithmic programming (i.e. competitive programmers, like myself) often dislike how it is taught very mathematically rigorously yet with little intuition or application at all (in other words, this class will not get you through a coding interview). Yes, Algorithms, the Computer Science class, is more of a math class than anything else. Yes, Computer Science is not just programming, and Theoretical Computer Science consists almost entirely of pure math. All of this I knew going in. None of this prepared me for when I lost over half the points on a problem from Homework 1 asking me to prove the Big Omega of a certain function. I approached it as almost everyone intuitively would; like almost everyone had been taught to solve an inequality since middle and high school. Set up the inequality. Turn it into an equality, and solve the equality. Determine which side of the solution to the equality contains the solutions to the inequality, and turn the solution to the equality back into an inequality. Apparently, this wasn't rigorous enough for this class. Perhaps this is just how this kind of stuff works. But we were never told that solving it this way would lose us points, and the "correct" way shown in lecture seemed unnecessary and unintuitive. Instead, Justin complained that many submitted solutions to such Big-Omega or Big-O proof problems looked the way AI would solve them, and that such proofs "were generally terrible", citing several reasons why. Okay, fine. If you take Justin, make sure you explain the hell out of any answer you give to a problem. One problem on Exam 1 asked me to find a lower bound for something and to show my work. I later received minimal points for my answer, despite the fact that the work I had shown lined up almost exactly with a potential full-score answer as described in the rubric. Upon submitting a regrade request, I was told the grader had no idea what I did here at all, since I had no explanation at all. But the question never asked me to explain! Too bad. There was an Exam 1 MCQ problem which asked whether a certain algorithm was O(N^2) in the best case. The algorithm in question was O(N) in the best case and O(N^2) in the worst case. As such, most people in the class answered incorrectly, as technically an algorithm which is O(N) is also O(N^2). A big stink was made on Piazza about this being a trick question hidden in a sea of 50 multiple-choice questions, designed to make students lose points even if they understood the concepts it was supposed to be testing. One student asked, to avoid confusion, why didn't Justin instead ask if the algorithm was O(N^100) in the best case? Another student literally included a screenshot of the Merriam-Webster entry for "trick question" in their post. In the end, Justin's response was that technically the algorithm was indeed O(N^2) in the best case, and that he didn't expect his students to autopilot any questions in his class. On top of this, there was a question on the Exam 2 MCQ which, depending on your interpretation of the question (the wording was not specific enough), could have had two different answers. However, if you picked the wrong one, you had no recourse, not even through Piazza. By this point, people had long since stopped posting on Piazza about questions like this. They knew nothing would result from their efforts. On Exam 3, there was a free-response question which essentially asked us to find the shortest path between two points in "a simple, connected graph" (I'm simplifying greatly). Many test takers realized quickly the looseness of this wording and realized that, to cover all graphs which could potentially be described as "a simple connected graph", one needed to run Floyd's Algorithm, as a simple BFS would not cover the case of a weighted graph, and Dijkstra's would not cover the case of negative-weight edges. Once Exam 3 was graded, everyone who wrote such a solution to that problem lost points (there was a special "tier" in the Gradescope "rubric" for Floyd/Dijkstra solutions). I asked in my regrade request what the issue with my answer was. The response was that I needed to specify what my input to Floyd's Algorithm was or what graph I was going to run it on. I responded that in my answer I had specified running Floyd's algorithm on precisely the graph described in the problem statement. The response? "It does not define distances". Confused and a little frustrated, I wandered over to take a look at the official Exam 3 solutions. The official solution to that problem? Run a BFS. This course had the potential to be much more engaging, but I found the content covered to be overly theoretical and not particularly useful in a practical context. While theory certainly has its place, the class focused almost exclusively on it, which made it difficult to stay engaged, especially when I heard that Professor Wiseley Wong’s section explored more hands-on, practical topics. There were daily in-class quizzes and homework assignments roughly every 2–3 weeks. However, the lectures themselves were quite dry and didn’t connect well to the homework assignments. To make matters worse, only 3 of the 6 homework assignments were graded by the end of the semester, which was frustrating. In terms of performance metrics, the average final grade was around an 83. The first midterm average was a 76 (including extra credit), while the second midterm average dropped significantly to a 57. I’m not saying that they were impossible to do well on, because people did, but the averages were bad. The uniform grade distribution mentioned earlier is not a joke. The first exam average was about 12/20 and the second exam average was 15\20. Also Exam 2 had about 10 points of matrix operations, which was trivial since all of us had taken some form of elementary linear algebra. That doesn’t seem too bad right? Well, it is. Every point on the exam in his syllabus was listed as 1% of your overall grade. So the average student by the end of Exam 2 was already sitting at a total loss of 13%. Seven people dropped after Exam 1–this accounts for the higher average for Exam 2–and then one more after Exam 2. So really the score of new material was about 50%. Out of 35 students, a 20% drop rate for a class that is taken by relatively mathematically mature students is abominable. The actual exams were not well put together. For the first exam, he walked into the room late, opened his laptop, turned around, and proceeded to slowly write the questions on the blackboard. Each question was weighted equally, so a definition or simple calculation that was briefly discussed from the first day of class and seemingly brushed off as unimportant was weighted the same as logic-based true/false and a proof. The second exam, only had 5 points worth of true/false justification and the rest of the 15 points were calculation. At least he gave us paper copies of the exam. This wouldn’t seem too bad but he graded them extremely harshly. He was hesitant to give partial credit. Comparing Exam 1 and 2, I believe he did not grade consistently. This is easily the class I have studied the most for. The amount of effort out towards this class is not a reflection of the grade I will receive. After both exams, he encouraged people to drop the class, using phrases such as “you’re just torturing yourself if you stay,” or “I rarely see students rally for the final.” The final was very bad. He did mention that he might consider reweighing the homework, and potentially adding bonus points to the final, but did not do the latter. With what appeared to be a grading scale of <70-No credit/70-C/80-B/90-A as listed on his syllabus, it feels nearly impossible to do well in this class. So, -1 star poorly designed exams, -1 star for inconsistent and harsh grading, -1 star poor preparation (constant lateness to class and poor time management of the content), and -1 star for his disinterest in supporting his students’ success.

416 content is definitely challenging but Czaja explains it very well. Content is genuinely interesting. He writes exams so that all questions have 2-3 line simple (elegant) answers, especially proofs, but if you don't catch it at the moment exams are hard. Cheat sheet is allowed and he drops one midterm. Getting a good grade in this class isn't hard if you keep up with homework and average 70s on exams. He changed the final to be optional for our class.

Her tests are unreasonably difficult and often do not reflect the material taught. Homework is assigned almost every class and she always ran 5 minutes over. Didn't learn much, but I wasn't really interested in the class.

Lecture: Adams was always willing to experiment and investigate students ideas that we come up with during lecture. I actually learned a lot during these little diversions. We did a lot more combinatorics than graph theory, but Adams said he might start with Graph theory next time to ensure that he covers it in more detail next time. Homework/Book: We used Brualdi's textbook and it was alright. Many of the questions were vague which made it hard to figure out what the questions were asking. Look over the homework the class period before it's due so you can ask Adams about it during lecture. Overall homework wasn't too difficult, it was assigned once a week and took 4-8 hours depending on what you are covering. Homework was usually about 70% application and 30% proof (but this was dependent on the topic, partial orders, recurrence relations, and graph theory were a little heavier on proofs) Tests: Two midterms and a final. All of Adams test follow a similar set-up. Some medium difficulty problems, then one problem that is rather easy followed by a problem that is really hard. The easy one is "free points" so you don't feel bad about not getting the hard one. No quizzes or anything like that. Grading was 100 exam 1 100 exam 2 150 final 100 homework (2 dropped) and he curved a little to make the median a 75 on both exams (and probably did the same for the final). I really enjoyed this class, Adams made it fun and the material isn't terribly rigorous. It would be good to take this class with the rigorous courses like MATH410/411/403/etc.
Talks super quietly and monotone. Stopped going to lecture but he doesn't post any notes just the slides. But I guess hes probably the best option.

Took PHYS121 with her and currently taking PHYS122. She is a great professor and makes sure you are on track. She provides practice sets for each exam which is similar to the actual exams. Also, she is accommodating to the exam scores and will curve if necessary. Very patient and overall a great professor.

Dr. Buehrle is a very smart and enthusiastic professor, but he seriously lacks in his teaching skills. If you're the type to download powerpoint slides and take notes on them, I found it really annoying when the slides weren't in order or when some were missing. He goes over practice problems during lecture which I appreciate, but I found them to be unrelated to the homeworks and the exams. The labs are dependent on your TA and the people in your lab. Even though my TA was smart, there was a time where we had to work with more complicated microscopes and he didn't know how to use them. Before exams, Dr. Buehrle would ask us what topics we wanted to go over which I appreciate. You get to have an equation sheet (one side of printer paper) for the exams and the final, but I found that despite how much information I put on them, there were questions that I wasn't sure how to solve. The weekly homeworks on ExpertTA were a little helpful, but the reading questions on TopHat were of no use at all. I found it annoying to have to pay for two applications for this course. Some advice: - Try to do well on the homeworks and TopHat questions. The homeworks will definitely help boost your grade up if you do well on them. - For exams, study the homeworks!!! There are questions on the exams that are similar to the homework questions, so write down the concepts on your equation sheet and the steps to work through them.

This class is whatever. Physics itself is cool, but like a joke, once you explain it, it loses its silliness. PROS - His exams are fair, he gives partial credit, and regrades are available. He also offers to retake the exam, but just an inside tip in case he doesn't mention it... don't do it. He said statistics show most people don't do much better, and since he takes the average of both exams, it doesn't really help.... so why does he offer it??? lol - The exam content matches up to his slides, HW problems, and somewhat to his practice exam. - If you score above the mean, you get an A; otherwise, you have to score close to the mean to get a B on exams. - Go to office hours for homework 'help' (answers) and to clear up misunderstandings. - Records lectures - A lot of buffer points like PHYS131 - Attendance isn't mandatory, but there are TopHat questions that are free points that you'll miss out on CONS - Unfortunately, he's very monotone. Not as engaging, although he has his moments. Sit at the front if you need to force yourself to be engaged. - He's also a little unclear at explaining at times, which I blame more on the content being hard to explain - There's a good bit of outside reading and homework assigned, so prepare for that. - Have to pay for TopHat AND ExpertTA :( RIP my wallet. - The HW has point deductions, so don't just guess. - Lab is so much work, also half of the materials used never work, like the computers or microscopes or cameras or software or or or.... - Lab can also be difficult, but it depends on the TA, mine unfortunately wasn't all that helpful

I would not recommend taking Hailu for the basic fact that he is beyond lazy with the materials he provides for his students and you can basically teach yourself significantly better with the textbook in the time it takes him to work through a problem in class. If you took him for 161, imagine that class but sped up with harder content, however the textbook is fairly comprehensive and has all the examples he pulls from for the class. I will say the homework is excessively long and tedious and isn't a great teacher of the test material and concepts, so be sure to do challenge problems from the textbook before the exams, which will be make or break for your grade. This class is much more conceptual than 161 so find a good TA to help you digest content wherever possible. Only take this class if you plan to learn out of a textbook anyways, and even with that the content is tough. Good Luck
You never actually see Severson, but he posts some hilarious announcements and makes the course very clear. The labs are pretty much filling out Excel sheets and its very hard to do poor.

Baden was a great professor. His lectures were engaging and he really cared about us learning and understanding the physics and being able to apply it. He almost always threw in some physics history or a practical application into lectures which I felt made lectures much more interesting. His lectures often started with the first 10-15 minutes being a review of the previous class which personally I enjoyed because it felt like I was really cementing my knowledge, but many of my friends would say that was why the lectures were boring like many of these reviews say. The homework was pretty straightforward and all the questions from the homework became the midterm questions which became the final questions. One midterm is dropped and the class is fully curved so the only way to know what your grade looks like is to look at how well you did compared to the average. The class is set up for you to do well in and is pretty manageable.
For a what can be a tough class, a pretty good professor. He's really helpful whenever you ask him questions, and his exams are of middling difficulty.

Professor Turpin is one of the few professors in the physics department who genuinely seems to care about you learning concepts. Exams were very fair- often times, other professors seem more interested in over complicating problems, or tricking you. This is absolutely not the case for her class. There is lots of TA-student interaction time outside of class (if you need it). There are weekly office hours dedicated to group solving homework problems. Just make sure you show up to class because attendance/participation is a surprisingly large percent of your grade
Best prof I've had, makes class entertaining and clearly cares about students. Also exams never require memorization at all, only test for understanding.

Definitely the best undergrad physics teacher I have had yet. Tests were hard, yes, but they were either open book or take home. hes also the director of the JQI (joint quantum institute), meaning he really knows his stuff.

I took PHYS410 with Hassam during the online fiasco that was Fall 2020. I really enjoyed his class though - his online teaching style is not my favorite (reading from prewritten notes) but his explanations of concepts are very good and his tests are remarkably fair and educational. I found that with his open note tests this semester that I was actively learning new things through his problems while still being able to get good grades. PHYS410 with Hassam is a very stress-free way to take PHYS410 while still walking away from the class with a much better understanding of the subject.

Professor Ott is one of those professors who is too smart for teaching. The fact that he is not aware of the class's understanding, or lack thereof, is also clear. He writes on the board and blocks what he writes with his body, talks into the board, and often mumbles. Medians of the exams were in 40s and 50s. You are better off taking a different professor.

Great professor!!! Take him for stat100 if you can. He is pretty strict about attendance and gives a graded assignment every lecture but the assignments are easy and sometimes these assignments count for extra credit especially near midterms and finals. He is a really good teacher and explains concepts well. The practice exams are EXACTLY like the actual exams and there are plenty of review sessions that the TAs do and every discussion session right before the exam is a designated review session. So as long as you know how to do the practice exam you should be set for the exam. He doesn't give answer keys for the exam but i just uploaded the exam into chatgpt and made it give me an answer key. The discussions are annoying since our TA didnt let us leave early even if we finished the assignment early but all the assignments are easy. I highly recommend taking the class with him.

I'm writing this review just after the final exam for Stat 400. It being his first time teaching at the university, Zheng started the year off rough, with confusing lectures, he was initially bad at explaining topics and gave no insight into what was going to be on each exam. After students expressed their complaints, he really cleaned up his act. For exam #2, he told us what type of problems would be on the exam and gave out practice problems similar to ones on the exam. He also began to give out extra credit points on the homework, which made it easier to recover points. For the final, we were allowed a double sided a4 sheet of notes, and he gave us in-depth practice problems that were very relevant to the problems on the final. I'm giving him a 4 star review because he really turned his teaching style around and doesn't deserve many of the 1 star reviews he was given by students early in the semester, when he was still acclimating to being a teacher for the first time. He also responds quickly to emails and is generally a pretty funny guy in lecture. Please don't shy away from taking his class because of the people who gave him low ratings early in the semester who were upset by their exam 1 results.

Dr. Khurana is a wonderful professor. Her selection of topics for the class is thorough and encompasses what I hoped to learn in a Statistics 2 class. She provides notes for every topic that are detailed, organized, and easy to refer to. I found her lectures and explanations to be very helpful. I frequently saw her in office hours, and often times asked questions outside the scope of the class, and she was always able to help me. She is very patient and truly wants each of her students to succeed. No matter the class or student, I have seen her sit down with students very patiently in office hours and explain a concept to them until they get it. Like any math class, they key to success is practice - and she provides an abundance of practice problems in the form of worksheets, quizzes, and old exams. I do think the class could benefit from being just slightly more theory-heavy - thought this is a change she has already expressed interest in making.

I feel bad doing this because the professor is genuinely a kind person, but he is truly a horrible professor. What he teaches in class and what shows up on midterms and quizzes could not be less similar. When he starts teaching a new topic, his explanation is purely mathematical notation and proofs. Not a minute of the lecture is spent explaining why this content makes sense conceptually (I mean it's introduction to probability, talk about drawing cards from a deck or something please I'm begging you). Even the most simple topics at the beginning of the class (I'm talking how many ways can you rearrange the letters ABCD) are explained abstractly. When I go to class I learn nothing. The reason he's not a one star is because I believe there is a way to do well in his class, and it can be summarized very easily: problem sets and ChatGPT. Here's what kind of worked for me: plug his 50-slide-long notes into ChatGPT and tell it to generate a page long summary for each chapter (about 3 chapter per unit), ask Chat abt anything you don't understand. Then, do the problem set based off of those notes. Luckily, almost every question on quizzes and exams are drawn directly, NEARLY WORD FOR WORD, from these problem sets (I basically just memorized every single problem set). Finally, pray you beat the average and get curved up. I'm sitting at a 90 right now, taking the final in a few days, and am genuinely beyond stressed about it because if the final isn't like the problem sets I am beyond screwed (so maybe an expected grade of an A- is optimistic).

I had previously taken STAT410 with him and really enjoyed the class, and I wasn’t disappointed this time either. His lectures aren’t recorded, but the in person classes are very valuable to go to, and he takes his time to answer questions so everyone is on the same page. Homeworks are typically given weekly and contain problems that were hard, yet really fun to work through. Quizzes are every Thursday and usually consist of a basic example that he likely already touched upon in the prior lecture. Exams are fair, and some curve will likely be applied at the end fo the class. I would highly recommend any class taught by him.

I’m not one to write reviews, but I have to say — I’ve never taken a worse class than this one. Pros: The professor genuinely cares about her students and is a very kind person. She often brings in cake and cookies to class and gives off a very sweet mom-like vibe. Cons: Unfortunately, the way the class is structured made the experience incredibly stressful and frustrating. STAT430 is typically considered an easy course, but she made it unnecessarily difficult. The exam averages were a 34.5 out of 70 on Exam 2 and a 23 out of 60 on the final. What made things worse is that after grading Exam 2, the professor expressed disappointment in the class’s performance. Honestly, if everyone is doing badly, it says more about the instruction than the students. Coding assignments are submitted through Canvas quizzes, where even a tiny error results in zero points. There is no partial credit, which feels unfair when your code is mostly correct. Additionally, written exams often fail to accurately reflect the practice material, and lectures are frequently rushed, making it challenging to learn the material effectively. Overall, despite her being the sweetest and kindest professor I've ever met, she makes this class harder than it needs to be.

Pros: - He is a great lecturer who explains concepts in high detail. - Homework (15%) and the final project (10%) are straightforward and easy to score well on. - You get an index card for midterms and a full sheet for the final (don't rely on these like i did, make sure you acc study and understand everything) - He drops 1 midterm that you scored the lowest on (i failed one so this one got dropped) Cons: - 75% of your grade is based on exams. - He tests on tiny details (like a 5-second video) rather than his long tangents - Slides have almost no info. If you don't go to class and take fast notes, you’ll be lost. - He uses Excel, so your Canvas grade may not be accurate. You have to calculate it yourself. Tips for an A - Don’t rely on TA review slides to study: Although these help with the sample exams, they aren't enough. Go through every lecture slide in depth. - He talks too fast for writing on Goodnotes. Record the lecture and move the info to an organized Google Doc. - The cheat sheet won't help if you don't understand how the systems work and affect one another. - He only gives two extra credits in the beginning of the sem that can only bump you 1% - i needed a 96 on the final to get an A which is crazy but somehow after putting in a lot of work, i got it! throughout the sem i believed i was gonna get a B+ because i was doing alright, however, I started studying earlier and a lot more which helped. - Make sure you understand every single example in class

I had Professor Lemke for my lab and it was absolutely awful. He is unnecessarily harsh with grading and doesn't explain why he took points off. He also gives vauge instructions and then takes points off when you can't read his mind. He is gets very defensive if you ask him a question and gives sassy and unhelpful answers. If you are unfortunate enough to have him, switch to a TA IMMEDIATELY.

Let me be the last person to convince you NOT to take this class with Dr. Haag!! This class genuinely had me bawling at South hahaha. Everything the other reviews mention is 100% true. Dr. Haag makes BSCI170 overwhelmingly difficult for an intro level class, especially considering many non-bio majors have to take this as a requirement for their degree. I'm glad to know I wasn't the only one who consistently had to reteach myself everything from the 40-70 slide lectures. Haag usually goes slowly reading slide by slide until he realizes he only has 30 mins left to cram a dozen+ more slides then proceeds to zoom through the rest of the lecture. When my friend showed me her exams in Keller's class, I actually laughed with despair because the exams were so much easier. Meanwhile, we'd be tested on something barely discussed in class and he'd have to clarify his strangely worded and complicated questions 5+ times DURING THE EXAM. There was not a day in the semester where I didn't nonstop think about bio. I genuinely thought at one point that I wouldn't make it. If you wanna build some grit, take this class.

This lab section is completely run by your TA, you will probably see Dr. Mohan once if it all. If you get lucky and have a good TA they can be very helpful during labs and with assignments. There are quite a lot of assignments for this course, but I wouldn't say any of them were insanely difficult. You are required to do pre-lab quiz every week before your lab, and a couple assignments during lab each week. Some of the work is busy work, but again nothing really challenging. If you get assigned a good lab group you will be set for the semester pretty much. Labs are a bit tedious at times, but again if you have a good group and TA you can all figure it out together. The amount of work may seem overwhelming but genuinely if you turn everything in on time and do what the assignments ask you to, you should get an A. Also don't be intimidated by the practical at the end of the semester, it's actually much simpler than you would expect. Most people in my class got A's so as long as you review a little bit you should be fine.

Boring class, 3 exams and a final. I will say that her class is manageable and she did make the final pretty fair, however, if you are not ready to spend hours outside of class learning and retaining informatio,n I would not take her. But Opoku is a good person, just not the best lecturer.

A&P 2 was much, much heavier on the physiology aspect than A&P 1. However, the anatomy portion and lab practicals were a lot easier and there was less to memorize. For me, it was a harder class overall. The lab practicals were weighted a lot less than the lecture exams (compared to A&P 1) which ended up hurting my grade. I would HIGHLY recommend going to class as professor Goytia is very knowledgeable and explains concepts well. Learning from just her lecture slides won't get you an A on exams because she adds in questions to her exams that she says in class, not from the slides. You also need to memorize every diagram in the textbook because she takes diagrams from the textbook and adds it to the exams. I thought that her exam questions were confusing at times. I would know the subject material well for the question she was asking, but would lose points because of the weird wording in her exams, especially on multiple choice and matching. I think that she writes the exams last minute and doesn't have time to really think about if the questions she is asking are clear. However, she does offer extra credit depending on how well the class did. The averages for each lecture exam, AFTER extra credit was added, was 82%, 70% and 76%. No extra credit was added for lab practicals and the average for those combined was a 78%. The hardest exam was the second lecture exam where everyone basically failed (63% average before the extra credit). There are 7 exams total, same as A&P 1. In terms of extra credit, the exams are not curved, you actually have to put in work and print out a scantron, retake the exam and submit it to her in person during lecture time. If you get everything right the second time, you get full extra credit points. If you don't, you will only get a little bit of extra credit. There are pre-lab quizzes every week before lab, post-lab worksheets usually around 20-30 questions (multiple choice, written response, matching), clicker questions, quizzes due before lecture. The final is cumulative. :( Anywho, overall, this class is hard but certainly doable if you go to lecture, actually listen and take notes.

Great prof, she's super sweet and fair. Midterms are only worth 65 pts, with the final being worth 125 pts. Homework is basically just based on participation. Lecture is a little slow and boring, but I wouldn't say its the most interesting class anyways (imo). I'd recommend looking over the key concepts at the end of each lecture since she bases her exams on those questions. The concept checks are also pretty helpful. Overall, I'd highly recommend Dr. K

Agreed with a lot of the complaints about his teaching for the fall 2025 semester, especially the ones about him being condescending and harsh with exam grading. The general format of the midterms is overall predictable since they consist of definitions, short answer questions, a bit of math, and an essay. It just sucks that he's misleading about what will be on them and in my opinion, his lectures are at times too messy for me to comprehend...so here are some tips if you take him: 1.) Check out past exams he posts! Some of the questions may even be nearly the same. 2.) If you can remember anything that involves math, that's pretty much free 20+ points for you 3.) Vocabulary is important!! 4.) Write as much detail as possible. Even if something looks "easy," and even if you blank - helps to at least get a few more points instead of zero 5.) Think about the "why" behind the details instead of getting lost in them, that makes all the jargon he throw at you make more sense.

Apparently Dr. Tran and Dr. Buchner swap teaching BSCI 223 each semester, so take Dr. Buchner because this class was a living nightmare and worse + more time consuming than my level 400 chemistry course. The lecture is modeled after a flipped classroom, which is weird because you are required to attend due to graded clicker questions (and UMD doesn't pay for PointSolutions anymore so go figure). If you don't know what a flipped classroom is, you learn the lecture material on your own through her posted slides and recordings, and you review that material during actual lecture. I highly dislike this type of classroom model because it's double or triple the work and I have other things to do. There are two midterms and the final, and she literally gatekeeps the format or anything specific about the exam. She didn't tell us the length, how many questions, or what types of questions would be on there. (No calculator, no formula/cheat sheet. She gave supplemental material like cycles and a codon chart for the two midterms. Some multiple choice and true/false, but mostly free-response questions, long and short. Exams took the entire 50 minutes.) Like someone else said, she complained that the mean score on exam #1 was too high (83%) so she ramped up the difficulty on exam #2 and basically everyone did bad (72% average). She gave us a 10-point curve out of 150 on the second exam. FORTUNATELY there are so many other assignments she gives you that can pad your grade in case you fail. Lab was ok but you need to print out the material yourself and get a binder and lab coat. The TAs were helpful but their start-of-lab lecture sometimes took more time than it takes to finish the work for the day. Lab is 2 hours but I usually got out within an hour. Like the lecture it's also busy work This course was so much busy work and so much self-studying that it left a bad taste in my mouth regarding the biological sciences. I'm sure Dr. Tran is a good person, but she is not fully equipped to teach this course. Take someone else.

He's an incredible professor and an even better human being. I loved coming to Cell Bio and I learned so much from taking this class. This was one of the best classes I've taken at UMD so far and Dr. Frauwirth is the best! Take this class with him - you will enjoy his class a lot.

This class was way harder than it needed to be. The professor intentionally made it more difficult than other sections because of how important the class seemed to her, and it ended up taking an insane amount of time every week just to earn a mid grade. Lectures were tough to follow since she talked way too fast. Exams were the worst part and graded with extreme strictness. She said everything in the textbook and slides are “free game” (which meant 30–60 pages of dense material per week), but she gave us very little practice. The worksheets she provided were not only easier than the exams but also not really like them, so they weren’t real preparation. Exams were so detailed and specific that it felt impossible to do well no matter how much you studied. On top of that, she gave almost no partial credit, if you didn’t use the exact vocab word she wanted, even if your answer was basically right, you’d get a zero on a big question. Her exams are mainly written response too with a couple MC. The reading and memorization load was ridiculous too. We had to know every little detail from the textbook, including things she never mentioned in lecture. This was exhausting because I would go out of my way to learn things in depth and would never see it again. Felt like a waste of time. Honestly, it felt like she made the class harder just for the sake of it, which left everyone drained and stressed. If you can take this class with another professor, DO IT! this by far is one of the most time-consuming and frustrating classes I’ve ever taken. However, If you're stuck with her. Here is what I have to say: She posts lecture videos. Good luck :)

Dr. Wu is an extremely kind and generous professor. Her exams are open note, and they can be a bit tricky to finish in time. She drops the lowest exam and there is no final. She offers extra credit throughout the course- some extra points are built into her exams, some are in home works. Then, at the end of the semester, you can opt in to doing an extra credit presentation (in person or you can submit a recording to the class discussion) which is worth 10 points, and we can get 3 points for asking questions to the in person presentations, and another 3 points asking questions for the online presentations, and on top of that you get 1-2 points for answering questions on your own presentation. That being said, Dr. Wu is truly an awful lecturer. She often mumbles, gets flustered, and goes on tangents. I tried joining the lecture through zoom which helped a little bit for clarity, but ultimately putting the slides through chat and generating summaries helped me understand the material. Besides that, the only downside to the course was the bioinformatics assignments. The assignment was poorly made, the code that was given to us never worked, and it took hours to complete. On top of that, the TA in charge of assignment & the person who created the assignment, Adena, was an incredibly harsh grader and she wasn't very helpful at all when it came to trouble shooting. She also barely responded to the piazza questions when we needed help as well. The assignment was a supreme waste of time. Most people who take this course are bio majors, who need the class to fulfill a major requirement, so no one wants to be coding. If we did, we would take the upper level bioinformatics course offered to us.

As someone who didn't take any Organic Chem or AP Chem in high school, I was really nervous for this course. Throughout the semester, I learned that Dr. Friedman tells you everything you need to do to succeed. First week, he told us that we would need to do practice problems, COME TO LECTURE, go to GSS (guided study sessions), and do all practice exams. I did all of this and ended with a 93 in the course. Fortunately, I am someone who really enjoys math, so that part was easy (ish) for me to understand with practice. There is absolutely not a topic in this course that you can just "know". You must know the ins and outs and manipulations for literally EVERYTHING. I would say that GSS is going to be your saving grace, especially with Amy. The exams, in my opinion, were fair if you studied at least a week in advance and did all of the practice exams and worked on everything he throws at you. I thought the final was unfair and I felt unprepared, but the curve helped. Do the best you can to do well on all the midterms so then you have a lot of wiggle room as you enter the final.

You will most likely never see Mrs. Guest unless you meet with her outside of the lab. The class is hard but manageable with weekly pre-lab quizzes, lab, post lab questions, and reflection quizzes. Mrs. Guest records videos to watch before taking the pre-lab quiz and they almost are never helpful for the test. Though, if you have a good TA you will do good, and make sure to visit office hours for help on the post lab questions. Only TA’s grade the post lab questions, some are forgiving and others not so much, getting random points off that I didn't even know I needed to include in my responses. Overall, the class is manageable if you put in the effort.

Lascio is one of the better 135 professors. His lectures are pretty decent for the most part, although he poorly planned/paced some of his lectures. This caused us to fall behind at the start, and we kind of had to rush things/play a game of catch-up for the rest of the semester. Towards the end, leading up to the final, he skipped/rushed through a lot of material simply because he did not have enough time to teach us. His exams were pretty hard, and the sample/past exams were not the best at preparing us for the actual test. I would get high 60s to mid 80s on the practice exam, but would do terribly on the actual exams. Exam averages ranged anywhere from the 50s to the 70s. The class average was around 70% before the final. Homework was only 80 out of the available 580 points. There were 3 exams, each worth 100 points, with the final worth 200. You could bring a single index card to each exam, which had to be provided by him. Homeworks were somewhat hard and would sometimes stray a little from the lecture or exam material. However, he was very accommodating and understanding with deadlines. The final was absolutely brutal, with the average being in the 50s. Lascio curved a total of twice during the semester, once before the final, dropping the C- cutoff from 70% to 61%. After the final, grades took forever to release, but after he finished grading them all, he posted an announcement stating how he was dropping the C- cutoff down to a 50%. Overall, it's a really challenging class with a lot of material to cover in a short period of time. Lascio is a very understanding professor and is very easy-going and approachable. The curve saved me from failing the class, as I had a high-50, which ended up curving to a C.

Prof. White takes a hands-off approach to running the lab. She implemented Friday review sessions that were phenomenal; I finally began to understand the experiments. She is a great teacher, so attend her office hours and review sessions. Exams are extremely difficult. Reports are graded harshly. However, the course is curved 8-10%.

If you get stressed easily by professors that have a disorganized way of teaching Dr.Koppel is not the teacher for you. She begins each topic with the general ideas and then focuses in on smaller topics but there are no order or outlines to follow. Looking back over my notes was a nightmare and if you miss a class and look at her posted notes, you will be beyond confused. I highly recommend the Orgo as a second language books if taking this course. The curve is based off of class average which was decently high for my class but I passed with a C with a 58 somehow. The online quizzes and assignments boost your grade but the exams and TLQ in lab are challenging and she does not give you any type of review and will usually be 1/3 of the way through new material, before the exam which gets hard to manage. If you dedicate the time and are good at self-teaching she's not a bad teacher but you cannot slack off or have a bad week you will fall behind orgo is alot of material!

Debleena is probably the best TA you could get for a lab. I was scared going in because people always say the TAs are of no help and leave you in the dust. Debleena clearly cared for her students and made it very known. There was never a time you couldn't ask her a question or for help. She was always looking out for her students. I don't think I saw her sit once during lab because she was always helping someone or making herself available. Considering she was constantly busy with her own PhD she made this class very manageable for the students. her kindness and support never went unnoticed.

Dr. Davis is a great guy and I like the set up of his grading and curve. Allows you to drop one exam and has 3 (3 pt) extra credit practice exams. Grades are based on 3 exams (and the extra credit) and you can even drop the final. I sort of wish he assigned more structured homework as I didn't really find the textbook all that helpful. I also didn't really like his exams, there was a lot of multiple choice, fill in the blank, and true or false. If you're good at these kinds of questions, take Davis. I had Koppel for orgo 1 and did so much better on her exams and in her class overall since it was very mechanisms based and gave a lot of partial credit.

This was Dr. Hirschauer’s first semester as Orgo 2 lab coordinator and she exceeded my expectations. She’s hands-down the best lab coordinator I’ve had so far and the first who actually showed that they cared. Also, she responds to emails SUPER quickly and considerately. She came into my lab section a few times early in the semester to troubleshoot the faulty IR machine but was always willing to talk to students while there. The course itself is still a decent amount of work, and I could have certainly put in more effort, but her weekly resources were super helpful for the assignments. I also had a solid, chill TA who made the experience better in general.

I heard bad things about this professor, but it couldn’t have prepared me for this disaster. She goes over things really quickly leaving you to have to review and figure things out on your own. She does have CAN, which i found kind of helpful, so thats a plus. But multiple of her homeworks have numerous errors not only in the questions themselves, but in the grading and answer key, I have seen exam keys and homework keys blatantly wrong answers. Her homework will cover things you don’t learn in class, leaving you to have to either somehow ask her things at her very busy office hours, asking friends, or using AI to make it make sense. To be honest, the GSS is useless because they constantly have misinformation and the same thing with the answer keys to the discussion worksheet. I will be honest, I aced a thermodynamics class before and she made it seem 10x more confusing than it really is. Her exams are easy…when they don’t have errors on them. But they are incredibly long and difficult to finish on time. Overall, the poor quality control of homework and exams, along with the lectures and videos posted being insufficient. I would say I learned most of the topics on my own with google than with the little she gave. She is by far, the worst teacher I have ever had the displeasure of taking. If someone else teaches general chemistry 2, take that. I would rate her negative stars if possible.

She's so chill. The grading is the easiest and most laid back, definitely more than any other chem lab. Yeah, you probably won't learn a ton, and yeah you probably won't go to many of the chem lectures, but just make sure to keep up with the lectures or the exams will get you. You'll learn some good skills from a chem lab and helpful with data analysis, and the labs themselves ain't all that long either.
One of the most understanding, knowledgeable, personable, and funny people I've ever met within the professional sphere of computer science. This dude is great, and buy his game on Steam.

Absolutely terrible, if you want a stress free life, don't take her as your professor. Her lectures don't teach you anything at all; she often skips over thins in class and unexpectedly puts them in exams. She doesn't take her class seriously at all, and instead just giggles around most of the time. You will hear a lot about how she was part of an IT company long back, and very little about the course content at all. If you like self teaching content, then take this class. P.S. You'll find that only 7 people end up attending lecture regularly at the end of the day, because her classes are absolutely useless at the end of the day.

Really well ran course. The projects were pretty instructive, especially the Assembly project. Considering that the tests are borderline open internet, they're surprisingly easy, and if you can do the projects, you can definitely do well on the exams. There's so many places to get bonus points, so even if you lose some points here or there, you can get them back really easily. The lectures can be a bit slow at times, but physical attendance isn't mandatory so if that's an issue you can just watch the lecture videos at your own pace. He loves answering questions, so if you're struggling with a concept, he'll make sure you understand it. Taking 216 with Kauffman really is a no-brainer, just do it.

i literally loved his class, but thats coming from someone who just loves riddles tbh, because i know our final hurt hella people who didnt know what was happening since everything was so vague also he does not curve or drop at ALL so expect your grade to be your grade imma be honest i took a makeup once and our TA didnt even show up til 1.5hours later which was kinda annoying but honestly its very passable

Max has roughly 20 years of experience as a data scientist prior to teaching and everything he does in class (exams, homework) is geared toward preparing someone to work in the industry, which is something I really appreciate. I think the reviewer who said "Overall a great change of pace from the rest of the CS meatgrinder classes and highly recommend" was very accurate. I'd highly recommend taking 320 with Max for this reason. (I can see why something like 250 or 351 might be awkward with him, though, since that's not his passion.) Exams are somewhat difficult but are not a huge portion of your grade individually. Homeworks are designed to mimic real-world data science assignments and are decent resume fodder, and in terms of grading, are easy 100s to boost your grade. Extra credit is also available for homeworks if you put in extra effort. As many other reviewers mention, he is disorganized, but I still found his lectures to be entertaining and educational. I would recommend attending his lectures as he deviates from his slides a lot.

Good professor. Quite literally no difference between him and Cliff. Though, Anwar, being more senior, might be slightly better at teaching. The exams for both professors are more or less the same. In fact, it's pretty evident that Cliff and/or the TAs make the exams given the incorporation of gen z humor. Regardless, the exams are fairly easy, and the only way you fail is if you don't actually do the projects (i.e. don't GPT projects). Both professors' resources are accessible. In fact, most of the resources can be accessed without being enrolled in the class, just search up UMD CMSC 330.

I don't really understand all the hype around Nelson; he comes across as a condescending teacher. For 335, the first midterm felt like a chore, requiring you to memorize a bunch of random information. The only effective way to prepare was by studying previous midterms. For fall 2024, our midterms were nearly identical to those from the previous spring, but they’re always subject to change—spring 2024's midterm, for example, wasn’t like fall 2023's. Our semester got lucky with similar midterms, but overall, you don’t learn much in this class. I was in the 8 AM section, and while I didn’t mind the early timing, Nelson's lectures were quite boring. He often makes jokes and gets off-topic, which isn’t what I want to deal with at 8 AM. It feels like he doesn’t fully understand the material he's teaching. When asked for specifics, he often can’t provide clear answers. If something in his code doesn’t work, he doesn’t seem to know why. I already knew the basics of HTML and CSS but wanted to learn more about JavaScript and MongoDB. Unfortunately, I was disappointed—Nelson simply gave us the code for those topics without explaining how the systems work. The final exam was super easy and almost identical to Project 5. You could literally reword that project and still get full points on the final. The TAs are often PhD or master’s students, and they’re difficult to work with. They don’t provide helpful answers most of the time. This class is definitely worth taking if you’re in it for the grade, but it has its downsides. For example, the midterms aren’t given during class; instead, they’re held at 6:30 PM in a different lecture hall. While I understand Nelson’s intent to prevent one section from sharing answers with another, this setup is inconvenient. I would much prefer taking the midterms during class. Overall, I think 335 needs to be restructured. It feels outdated and poorly designed. We had to learn things from JavaScript ES5, which is deprecated—why bother teaching it? I wish they’d reduce the focus on CSS and introduce more relevant topics, like React, into the projects. A more modern framework would make this course much more worthwhile.

I don't really see the hype. Don't get me wrong, he is good, but so is Fawzi. On pure lecturing, Fawzi is actually better, but overall interaction with students in office hours and stuff like that, I'll give that to Justin. There are a couple of other Lecturers too. The hype for Justin is RIDICULOUS, lol. The class is heavily weighted on Exams. You make a small mistake, you lose a lot of points -> you get a bad grade in the class. That's not Justin's fault, I guess, since the class is a theory course. Justin made A LOT of errors on the midterms. How's that for the GOAT teacher, huh? What a joke. Oh I almost forgot, lectures being 8 AM, I wish he recorded the lectures. Well, bro wakes up at 4 AM everyday so. Just take Ting.

Excellent professor. As others have said, she is extremely responsive to students during class, in office hours, and on Piazza. In fact she was probably the most helpful and responsive professor I had in all four years of my college experience. With that said, her lecturing can be on the weaker side but she makes up for it by again being very helpful, having excellent slides, and an abundance of practice questions. wonderful lecturer and really cool guy! it's a hard class but he's super passionate about the material and it shows in every class, so the course was really enjoyable despite the difficulty and i feel like i learned a lot projects and exams were really challenging and grades take a while to get back, but tas and class materials were pretty helpful with both of them

The lectures were sufficient and you would do great on the exams if you supplemented with the Top-Down Book (NOT the Systems Book; it is really strange that the professor recommends the Systems book instead of the Top-Down Book even though the ROI for reading the former is small compared to the latter). However, the way the projects were designed is comically laughable. Everyone here is complaining for no reason, i'm taking this class right now and the exams and projects are challenging but not to the point that some of these reviews are saying. I'm by no means coasting through this class and I am not a particularly bright student but I enjoyed this class and would take it again despite the 7 exams.

Pratap is pretty good as a professor. He explains concepts in a coherent way, he's pretty understanding, and overall just a solid professor. Any complaints I have are directly against the organization/logistics of the class. Practice exams had some wrong answers which tripped me up, and responses on Piazza vary a LOT. Usually, it's on the much longer end. Class content itself is alright. I did learn a lot, but the content is directly taken from Berkeley's class. It's funny too; I looked up something from the slideshow for more information about that topic and all I found was the same slideshow on 4 different universities' websites. I'd recommend taking Pratap, and probably 421. Class is relatively easy too.

I have never actually had such a bad professor that makes me want to write a review for them here. Her slides are extremely vague and barely help. You are expected to memorize so many things even when she doesn't explicitly state it, and the practice problems are practically useless considering that the exam will be some theoretical concept she mentioned maybe once. It also seems like this class is at the bottom of her priorities and as if she needs half the class to fail in order to enforce high standards. I would advise you save your mental sanity and take this course with someone else as you'll put in hours on end to still end up lost during lectures and exams.

I think a LOT of the reviews below saw his high reviews before last semester (that have gone down since) and thought this would be an easier class to skate through. Prof Abadi is incredibly knowledgeable about databases and it shows. This guy wants his students to learn, and if you want to do well in this class, you will have to. The biggest qualm I have with this class is that the textbook can be confusing/quite boring at times. As an extension of this, the reading quizzes based on them can get a little challenging, especially as you cover DBMS internals towards the 2nd half of the semester (though these are a pretty small part of your end grade). However, from my experience, his lectures/slides covering the info again really ironed out everything for my understanding. You will have to come to class to answer clicker questions, but most are simple and he usually gives credit for most wrong answers. Even if you picked an answer that received no credit, you could defend your thought process and he'd usually be nice enough to mark it correct anyway. Projects 3 and 4 are not trivial by any means, but I didn't find them devastatingly hard. The midterm was a bit challenging, but nothing compared to the final. You will have to study your butt off for the final, but if you can put in the time to really understand everything (mostly B trees and the DBMS algos), it's very doable. And that learning will most likely stick. Overall, I think this class is dragged the most down by the admittedly boring textbook. Maybe changing reading quizzes to be due after you learn the content in the lecture would be beneficial for this, but I'm not really sure. That all being said, if you read textbooks well and strive to truly learn in your classes, I don't think you'll regret taking this. You will have to work hard, but if you are used to doing that to excel in your other classes I wouldn't view this as some insane challenge. It's definitely been the most valuable topic I've learned, maybe just behind OS.

I enjoyed this class a lot. His lectures are super disorganized, yes, and perhaps not at all relevant to projects/the midterm, but he's such an interesting person to listen to. I did learn a lot about computer vision from him (I did end up attending every lecture) and it has definitely pushed me into vision research. His midterm is quite something, though, and there was very little review for this, which can make it challenging to study for. However, the TAs are amazing and are super helpful when it comes to studying for the midterm and working through the projects. He's a cool guy, definitely give him a chance if you see that he's teaching this class, but be prepared to do a lot of studying on your own to catch up for the exam and projects.

Amazing professor and really great class to take. She was teaching for the first time and using David van Horn's curriculum, which is generally quite good. Projects are fair and the head TA, Pierce, is ruthless in a good way. There are secret tests, thankfully, so we actually have to think about our code, proofread, and test. You are writing a compiler to x86-64 assembly, which means you don't really get helpful error messages, especially in the second half of the semester. So you have to walk through everything to make sure it's good which really builds patience and computer science skills. I was screwed over by the second midterm so badly I might not end up with an A despite getting perfect scores on everything up to that point. I trust that they'll refine the assignments so that the difficulty is not so jarring. But by itself the exams are very fair. There are 2, 24-hour (midterm) exams and 3-week final exam. I personally think the first 2 weeks were too easy but this might have been based on David van Horn's curriculum and she still had very effective lectures for people who needed the Assembly review. She goes over Racket (which she shouldn't for a 400-level class, you should just pick up on it from writing code and from the notes) and has an entire project dedicated to writing Racket. Hopefully this is refined but the second half being insanely hard really makes up for the first half being insanely easy and it cancels out.

I took this couse in Fall 2022, and having now graduated, I can now safely say that Li is the worst professor that I have had the displeasure of having, CS or otherwise. Pros: + Sometimes when responding on Piazza, Li gets to fed up, that he will just post answers to graded assignments + Exams are online + Late policy: 20% docked off, but you get an additional four days to complete the project. Since the 20% penalty is flat, regardless if you take 1 or 4 days, it is pretty generous as far as late policies go Cons: - Li is a horrible lecturer. Some reviewers below mention his accent, and while that is an issue, I feel like the bigger issue here is that Li can't properly explain any concept for the life of him. He essentially just reads off the slides without elaborating further on any concept. Whenever he does attempt to try to explain something, it just ends up muddying things up. - Many crucial processes (ex. combining bucchi automata) are not explained - There are too many assignments. The class had as many as four sites active at once, each with different stuff and no reminders about due assignments. It is extremely easy to miss assignments. - He claims you get 2 weeks to do every major programming project, but since multiple programming projects are active at a time, you really only are spending one week on each, since the previous week is spent on the previous project. One week is not sufficient. - Announcements on finals were confusing. Additional clarification was required on exam timings, and he kept saying that there would be zoom proctoring, only for him to randomly not do it at the last second.

I took this class Fall 2023. I'm personally really interested in HCI, so I attended every lecture and participated frequently. Maybe it was because I was so interested in the material, but I genuinely thought Golub was a good lecturer. He did his best to make things interesting and regularly engaged with students. He's a bit old-fashioned and some of his material looks outdated so I'm not sure if I truly learned about HCI as well as I could've, but to me it was an easy A and a chill class. The group project does take some effort depending on the platform you choose and your group members, and there was one part of it that was graded somewhat harshly. But everything else was straightforward and the exams were easy, so if you do well on these you should do grade-wise. Out of all the 400-level CS classes I've taken, this was by far the easiest.

The other reviews for this course pretty much cover what the class is like, but one thing I want to add is that at the beginning of the semester, each student is assigned a TA that grades all the phases of your individual project. Your grade in this class depends on which TA you get. I was lucky enough to have a fairly lenient TA but my friends had TAs that were extremely harsh. Because of how Marsh's grading scheme works, this delayed them from working on later phases, resulting in a huge pile-up of work at the end of the semester. Maybe it's because this is my first Marsh class, but CMSC436 was NOT easy. Even when you don't procrastinate, this class is a huge time commitment outside of lecture (which no one went to). I'd only recommend this class if you have previous experience either with Marsh or Flutter and you're okay with teaching yourself the material.

For clarity, I'll quickly explain the class format. 5 assignments that are worth 40% of your grade with the lowest score being dropped, one midterm (that is awkwardly placed at about a third of the way through the semester) that is worth 20% of your grade, and a final that is "cumulative" and worth another 40%. There is also a hefty curve in the class which can be upwards of 6-7% some years -- typically depends on the difficulty of the exams that year. Regarding the assignments, they are pretty challenging. They often can take between 10-20 hours (especially dynamic programming one) and lots of work since each problem involves understanding all the underlying concepts, inventing/creating an algorithm, proving it works with some reasonable degree of certainty (instructors tend to be lenient about how "good" your proof is if you're right though), and proving it works in the runtime bound. Definitely start early, and definitely make frequent visits to office hours to bother the TA's and ask them to review through your work since ultimately they are the ones grading the assignments. Regarding the midterm, it was weirdly placed. The midterm was placed at the same time classes that typically have 2 midterms have their fist midterm (around end of first week beginning of second week of October). Otherwise, that midterm was relatively straightforward conent-wise -- those who didn't do well either couldn't brainstorm the gimmick to answer the question on the exam, or simply didn't review and study enough. The average on that exam was about a 68%. The final, in my opinion, was slightly harder. It covers a significantly higher breadth of topics than the midterm. In my opinion, the depth that each question goes into in the topic was a bit lower since most of the questions were very similar to questions on previous practices or other CMSC451 finals practices you could find online. The final on its own isn't that challenging, however, with much of the content being straightforward from the textbook. So long as you practice the standard questions, you really should be fine. The best part of Child's class is lectures. His lectures are just amazing. They are well put-together, easy to follow, and also have just enough "question the class to see what the class is thinking" but enough "let's guide through the class so we get some sh*t done". Laxman (the other well renowned and highly rated CMSC451 teacher who also taught Fall 2024) came and gave in a guest lecture, and I was absolutely surprised in the difference in quality between the lectures. Although Laxman's lecture wasn't "bad", it just really pointed out to me how much Child's lectures have an almost 3blue1brown feel because of how nice they flow. Some other misc things: he's pretty active on Piazza so that's really nice. Some of the TA's don't know a lot about these problems (and that follows because a lot of them naturally don't work in this field and might have other preoccupations), so they might also get stuck or not be able to help out on problems so try and exhaust all the TA's office hours and Child's office hours when stuck on homework. Child's expertise is in quantum algorithms so if you need anything with that or are interested, definitely feel free to talk to him about it. He tries to spend a lecture covering basic quantum algorithms at the end of the course but sometimes he doesn't have time to do that (like this semester), but regardless, you should look into it if interested. Overall, I had a lot of fun in this course and it's a definite recommend (even over other CMSC451 sections -- including Laxman's). While you might not necessarily get much practical implementation value out of the course, it's a lot of fun, and definitely molds your brain to become better and more versed in the world of reading and understanding algorithmic problems (which can be infinitely valuable when doing things like Leetcode or software interviews). If you have any math background or are interested in any algorithms stuff, definitely take the course!

Amazing professor. First time in college I got a math course where concepts were explained and intuition was built up rather than just being given definitions and theorems and examples and proofs. He really builds up the concepts and the homeworks are very good at having us prove things that we use later - this meant that there wasn't much to study because It's a rigorous proof-based math class so any low-star reviewers don't realize they need to put in more effort if this is not their strong suit (as it wasn't mine). If you're working really hard and still not getting the grade you want then you have to go to office hours to figure out what YOU'RE doing wrong (in fact Gorjan suggests you email him about this too). I did well because I went to office hours every or multiple times a week to find that I was doing the homework wrong and getting hints and spending time in a homework group with my peers. I eventually got the hang of it. The first homework took me like 12 hours but after that not that long. Most homeworks are <5 questions. I also had a pretty strong background in classical cryptography, which is only the first week of class, but it made things less overwhelming. Would definitely recommend a homework/study group but also spend time by yourself on the homework. Would recommend participating in class. This is a VERY fascinating course and he has very good lectures, very good at making you think for yourself when answering questions, and everything is very fair. Textbook is not required but helpful to review the content a second time and learn about a few other things. I recommend reading the textbook AFTER the lecture on that topic because he explains things much more plainly than the textbook (for me doing it in reverse would mean I just kind of forget the content of the textbook, or I needlessly take notes on everything in the textbook and then the lecture would be kind of useless). He doesn't grant extensions but that's to be fair. No one is entitled to a curve. No one is entitled to an extension. No one is entitled to a homework drop. Great course and great professor!
avoid this teacher. He is bad. I wanna fall asleep every lecture. To his credit, he actually follows his syllabus (nothing gets delayed)

I know nothing about the professor. The class itself is pretty easy. The slideshows can be confusing since some of the slides are the same with a few numbers changed between them and the formatting is messed up, but overall the class was easy.

This course is 1 credit, but she makes you do so much work. The homework has tons of questions, and she goes over Python pretty fast. I didn't learn much from Cruz. The two quizzes, while not worth much of your overall grade, each had an average of about 55%. Everything else I want to say has already been said in other reviews. All in all, don't take this professor!

There’s one required discussion, optional lectures (in my opinion), and a semester-long project. Most of the work is asynchronous, so it’s pretty manageable. I actually liked the assignments, they’re straightforward and teach you exactly what you need to know. You don’t interact with the professors much (there are two), but Professor Duffy stands out as super understanding and clear about expectations. She’s chill, and overall I enjoyed the class.

Dr. Szczekutowicz is a very kind but firm professor. Let me clarify she is not the reason I failed the course, this was solely because I had no algebra/trig basis prior to the class. Dr.S was always reaching out to me to make sure I was on track or doing okay, moreover while her class was very firm on absences during discussion, quizzes and tests she was willing to help me as much as her policy allowed. Overall, I would say that her lectures are fast paced and missing them would set you back, moreover the discussion worksheets and homeworks are really useful so be sure to utilize those. I really have nothing negative to say about Dr. S I just wish she was little more accommodating but with such a large class I understand she'd wanna have a fai environment.

Dr Williams is a good lecture, super intelligent, and is happy to answer any questions that you have in person. However, any other communication is spotty and could easily take multiple weeks to respond to you. During the Fall 2025 semester, he changed his office hours multiple times and only let us know the morning of. His MATH141 class is super demanding and because there are so few homework assignments to help fluff up your grade that every single assignment you have needs to be an A, or else your grade is going to plummet. Multiple people in my class compared his exams with other professor's exams and Williams' were noticeably more difficult. This course marks the worst grade I'll have ever gained during my entire 90 credits of higher education so far. I was literally teaching people within the course and still got a D. I know people that totally no-life'd the Fall 2025 semester as a whole and they have fine grades in the class. Not passing this class set me back an entire year in the degree pathway I was pursuing and I've resulted to completely changing my major. I'm surprised that basically every single professor that is offered during the Spring 2026 semester is rated higher than Williams (who was the highest rated available professor when I registered for the Fall 2025 semester).

Good professor. Lectures can be a bore but if you do the homework the quizzes are straightforward. Midterms are also nothing too difficult just like the sample exams he posts on ELMS. Nice guy who will cut you some slack if you really ask.
Exams are fair and u get a lot of partial credit. She's also nice and her lectures got better throughout the semester.

Taken in Summer '25. Professor S had this designed this course very well to correspond with the textbook. Lectures were daily and she even provided a notes sheet that she would fill in. Examples ranged from easy to difficult. There were two homework and two quizzes each week which were open book. Homeworks were time consuming and had some difficult problems but not bad overall. Final exam was not open book and contained a mix of problems. One thing the professor could have done better is given more practice problems as the questions had some overlap but not a whole ton. Had I done better I would have gotten an A. A great choice for 310 but requires a decent time commitment so if you're looking for an easier class not great but definitely a great choice to prep for 410 as she does some 410 for the last couple weeks.

Horrible professor. His lectures are boring and scrambled.
